- His warning: "we'll wake up one day realizing we've been busy, but not becoming."
- His priority is maintaining intentionality "even in the mess", rather than obsessing over how fast you grow or how visible the progress is.

chunks.heading: The illusion of passive learning
chunks.text:
Cris says most people consume information passively, hoping life will hand them a shortcut if they accumulate enough. He compares it to collecting seeds you never plant.

- "Just because you've consumed the information doesn't mean you've learned the lesson."
- Every book, conversation, or hard experience is raw material. The insights won't chase you down; you have to pull them out, sit with them, make them yours, and let them disrupt your comfort.
- A common failure he sees: people get exposed to powerful information, then file it away like a document they'll "get to later", and later never comes.
- Real learning takes effort and honesty. It means looking at things you'd rather avoid and letting go of stories you've outgrown.
- He points to Alex Hormozi on The Game podcast, who repeatedly says transformation requires active work. Cris's version: if you expect transformation to never challenge your identity, you'll be waiting forever.

chunks.heading: Two questions that separate growers from the stuck
chunks.text:
Cris says two questions, which many people avoid, separate those who grow from those who stay stuck: "What's in it for me?" and "What do I learn from this?"

When something goes wrong (a failed business, or work that feels meaningless), growth-minded people switch into "extraction mode" and get "ruthlessly curious" about their own experience:

- How can I change this?
- What pattern am I missing here?
- How can I do better next time?
- What does this teach me, and how do I need to evolve?

He stresses these are asked from ownership and insight, not blame or self-pity. Most people instead treat setbacks like bad weather, something that happened to them, and move on without mining the lesson buried in the mess.

chunks.heading: Courses and paid learning: you pay for the chance to do the work
chunks.text:
Cris criticizes people who pay for courses and then sit back expecting transformation to happen automatically.

- His framing: "you don't pay for transformation, you pay for the chance to do the work."
- That chance is only valuable if you engage with it fully. Otherwise "you've just paid for the privilege of owning unused potential."
- The same logic applies to any purchase of information, whether a course, book, or program: the value is in how much you apply, not in owning it.

chunks.heading: Habit: regular honest conversations with yourself
chunks.text:
Cris says people who consistently evolve share one habit: they regularly sit down and have honest conversations with themselves about what they've learned and how they're applying it.

- Consuming and moving on only creates "the illusion of progress."
- They ask hard questions about how new information challenges their current way of thinking or operating.
- He says this should be done without "the burden of overthinking or self-criticism". The goal is intentionality, not rumination.

chunks.heading: Treat every experience as raw material for becoming
chunks.text:
Cris's core framework is to treat every experience, good or bad, as input for who you become:

- Every book becomes a mirror.
- Every failure becomes a teacher.
- Every success becomes data for what actually works.

He ends on personal responsibility: information is everywhere and opportunities to learn are endless, so the only question is whether you take responsibility for extracting what you need or keep "expecting change to find you". As he puts it, "the human you become is entirely up to you."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cris Pop writes about visiting Dragoș Pătraru's Biblioteca Nației and why he wanted Pătraru as a voice at The Thunder Way's first event. The essay is mostly values-driven, but it holds a few usable founder lessons: build around ordinary people, recruit trusted voices when launching something that matters, and ask for the seemingly impossible.

chunks.heading: Cris's reason for backing Dragoș Pătraru's Biblioteca Nației
chunks.text:
- Cris spent a Saturday in Ploiești supporting Dragoș Pătraru's new project, Biblioteca Nației. He treats Saturday as the start of the week, reserved for his most meaningful, mission-driven work.
- He had watched Pătraru's TV show with his dad as a child. Sitting at the same table as an adult, he thought: "As a child, I watched him from a distance. Today, I sit beside him, part of the same purpose."
- Pătraru's directness is what Cris admires most. He says things as they are, with no polite silence, and Cris says that takes courage.

chunks.heading: Investing in what's missing instead of debating what's broken
chunks.text:
- Pătraru reinvests his energy, resources and potential into projects that help people. One result is Teatrul Nației.
- Teatrul Nației is a hub with Biblioteca Nației, a restaurant and a coffee shop. All are staffed by people who have faced hardship at home, at work or in life, and Cris says Pătraru gave them second chances rather than just jobs.
- The hub has rooms for rest and healing: a space to sleep, a ping-pong table, areas for therapeutic and recreational activities, and massage. Cris says healing comes from feeling supported in a place that cares, not only from words.
- Cris contrasts this with how most people spend money. He says many invest in "expensive things that we don't actually need, collecting objects while the world collects problems."
- Pătraru instead invests in people: their education, their growth, and a legacy "rooted in community, knowledge, and care" that will outlast us.
- Cris is inspired that Pătraru, his wife and his team "took nothing and built everything that matters," changing thousands of lives through hard, lasting work.

chunks.heading: Integrity means making tough choices daily
chunks.text:
- Cris calls Pătraru "the conscience of Romanian media" at a time when many others have lost theirs. He sees him as more than a journalist or TV host.
- Watching him over the years taught Cris to live with integrity. In Cris's words, that is not just saying the right things but making tough choices every day.
- Integrity means facing the issues most people avoid and choosing what's right even when it's unpopular.
- Through the show Starea Nației, Pătraru gave people a reason to pay attention again. Cris argues that journalism at its best "is not entertainment. It's public service."

chunks.heading: Making people feel responsible rather than passive
chunks.text:
- Cris says Pătraru's power is that he makes you feel responsible. You can't just consume content and complain, and he won't let you settle for "well, that's just how things are."
- Cris's call to action is: "Don't be passive. Don't be indifferent. Be awake. Be loud. Be human."
- His question to the reader: if one man with a mic and a mission can hold power accountable, what could all of us do together if we chose courage over mediocrity?

chunks.heading: The Thunder Way: ordinary people who choose to act
chunks.text:
- Pătraru will speak at The Thunder Way, Thunder's first major event. Cris says he couldn't imagine launching it without him.
- Cris's launch principle: when you build something that matters, you need voices that carry weight, ones people trust, respect and find genuine. He treats landing Pătraru as something that seemed impossible until he found the courage to ask.
- The event's theme is ordinary people. Cris argues that "none of us are born special or destined for greatness" and that what sets some people apart "is not talent or luck, but choice."
- The people the event celebrates saw something wrong and couldn't walk away. They saw injustice and didn't wait for someone else to fix it. They took the leap while everyone else was still thinking.
- The moment he wants to showcase is when ordinary people stop being bystanders and become "the change they want to see."
- He closes with: one honest, unafraid voice can shape the narrative for a whole society, and it can "remind the rest of us that silence is not an option."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cris Pop explains how Thunder Talks events start from an imagined newcomer's feelings rather than logistics or content. He extends the same empathy to feedback and to product or community decisions, asking what the other person actually needs and designing for people instead of personas.

chunks.heading: Designing events by sitting in the empty chair
chunks.text:
Cris starts event design from the attendee's seat, not from logistics or content. For Thunder Talks, the team imagines an empty chair and asks: "I've never been here before. I'm not sure if I belong. How do I want to be welcomed?"

- Attendees arrive from many contexts: introverts, extroverts, tech people, creatives, skeptics, community-seekers. Each carries different hopes, questions and hesitations.
- Planning begins with those people, not with the program.
- He frames it as welcoming "not as guests, but as friends stepping into our home": meet them, try to know them, make them comfortable, create "a human experience."

chunks.heading: Small gifts and personal welcome as part of the event
chunks.text:
At each event, Cris's team prepares small gifts: a book and a message "that might land close to the soul."

- The gift is part of the hospitality, not a sponsor or promo item.
- The goal is that people feel understood before they realize they needed to be.
- Welcoming is treated as a design task with the same weight as content.

chunks.heading: Reverse engineering through empathy: designing for participation
chunks.text:
Cris wants Thunder Talks to be collaborative spaces where people "don't just receive inspiration but create it together through questions, conversations, and genuine engagement."

- Tactic: make space through words and a quiet animation that signals "this is a safe place to ask, to share."
- The design target was the introvert in the back row who carries a question they won't ask out loud. He asks what would nudge them just enough, and what might quiet the noise of self-doubt.
- Principle: "One question can open a door, and your voice might give someone else permission to use theirs."
- He calls the method "reverse engineering through empathy." Instead of asking "Will they like what we've built?", ask what they actually need, then shape the experience from that answer.

chunks.heading: Giving feedback and hard truths so they land
chunks.text:
Cris notes people often act in ways they would not accept from others: abrupt feedback that they would call cold if received, or fast, raw truth that frustrates them when teammates do the same.

- He cites Marshall Rosenberg (Nonviolent Communication): "The greatest gift we can offer is honest expression, delivered with compassion."
- Being right is not enough; you have to be effective. If your truth only hurts without helping, or shuts people down instead of opening them up, "what was the point?"
- He does not advocate diluting the truth. The aim is to give it a place to be received, "Not just heard, but actually felt."
- Before a difficult conversation, picture yourself on the receiving end:
  - How would you want to hear this?
  - What tone would make you feel respected, even if the message is tough?
  - What space would help you stay open rather than defensive?
- Honesty anchored in empathy is where strong communities and relationships start.

chunks.heading: The mirror test: how Cris stays grounded
chunks.text:
Cris calls turning the mirror on yourself "something of a golden rule." He asks three questions from the other side of the table:

- If I were part of this community, what would I care about?
- If I were the customer, what would I expect, and what would make me trust or return?
- If I were attending this event, what would make me feel like I belonged here?

He admits this is not always easy: when you're close to the work or focused on efficiency, pausing to shift perspective feels unnatural. The habit of asking is where clarity begins, even when answers aren't immediate.

chunks.heading: Design for people, not personas
chunks.text:
Starting from your own humanness strips away assumptions. In Cris's words, "You stop designing for personas and start designing for people."

- This reconnects the work to real human experience.
- The value is in the effort to see from the other side, even when the answers aren't obvious.
- The same principle applies across his work: community building, events (Thunder Talks), customer experience and team communication.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cris Pop argues school fills heads with information but doesn't teach you to build or change. He shares the personal framework he built to outgrow mediocrity: an honest inventory, forgiving and accepting your past, a scout mentality, and small intentional daily steps. Mostly mindset, with little on business tactics.

chunks.heading: Starting from an honest inventory
chunks.text:
Cris left school with a lot of information and almost nothing he could use. He says education is "built to fill our heads, not change our lives": it teaches people to store facts, not to become someone who can build, create or solve real problems.

- He was mediocre early in his career despite an IT degree, because he "didn't know much that actually mattered".
- His first framework step is a "brutal inventory of potential": where could he have been versus where he is now.
- He checks four questions to take his pulse:
  - Am I on the right road?
  - Am I actually following my goals or just talking about them?
  - Do I have the activities I crave?
  - Am I spending time with people who elevate me or drain me?
- He admits this can't be measured perfectly, but says you can feel the difference when you ask.

chunks.heading: Building the foundation: forgive, accept, become a scout
chunks.text:
Cris builds a foundation before any plan or productivity system. He says you "can't build greatness on a foundation of self-criticism".

- **Forgive yourself** for past decisions he isn't proud of.
- **Accept your past**: those decisions are exactly why you may not be where you want to be today, "and that's okay". This lets you move forward "with clarity instead of shame".
- He warns that if you're not good with yourself, you'll sabotage every self-help book and every chance at growth "from the inside out".
- **Develop a scout mentality**: question your beliefs "like your life depends on it". When you find that 1, 2 or 5 beliefs are wrong, have the courage to seek new ways of seeing reality.
- He contrasts the soldier, who fights to prove everyone else wrong, with the scout, who is willing to be wrong if it means finding the truth.

chunks.heading: Focus attention with structure and small daily steps
chunks.text:
After the foundation, Cris focuses attention with intention.

- Develop a clear plan.
- Set limits: spend less time on the phone and on time-wasting activities.
- Invest in what he actually wants "with small, intentional steps every single day".
- He closes by saying the gap between who you are and who you could be "will never close on its own". It takes three things:
  - brutal honesty about where you stand
  - the humility to unlearn what doesn't serve you
  - the courage to take small, intentional steps daily

chunks.heading: Personalize your road and own your learning
chunks.text:
Cris says only you know your specific problems, fears, needs, dreams and the destination that will make you feel alive, so the road has to be personal.

- Everything you know can change, including what you think is possible for your life.
- Don't wait for schools, workplaces or the world to hand you the tools you need.
- Learning starts when you take ownership of it, when you stop treating knowledge "like something to collect" and treat it "like something to live".
- He refuses to set a finish line for his potential. He sees it as something that evolves with every challenge and every moment of doubt he pushes through.
- His line on mediocrity: "Mediocrity is crowded, and it's time to stop accepting it."

chunks.heading: How Cris got through his early developer years
chunks.text:
Cris became a developer without a passion for it. He didn't like mathematics, informatics or algorithms.

- **Put passion in on purpose.** He allowed himself to put passion into the work, because "without intention and fire in your work or learning, you'll extract nothing but disappointment".
- **Commit to a trial window.** On his first day coding he wanted to quit because it was too hard and confusing. He promised himself he would give it everything for 1-2 years and then see if he was up for the challenge.
- **Hunt for mentors.** He sought people willing to help, because when you're truly paying attention you can learn from anyone walking a similar path. He extracted every drop of wisdom, applied what felt right for him, and eventually became a mentor himself, "paying it forward".
- **Keep learning outside work.** He spends much of his free time on history, philosophy and physics, learning from people online who teach them in ways that spark curiosity.

chunks.heading: Turning the framework into a habit
chunks.text:
Cris built the framework because what he learned at university and what he needed in the real world were "separated by an ocean of irrelevance".

- Through constant use, it became part of him and shaped how he approaches learning anything new.
- He frames the goal as becoming "the kind of person who can grow endlessly".
- His definition of real education: "not passing exams, but continually passing the test of becoming".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cris Pop argues that success/failure is a false binary and that quitting strategically is a real edge. He offers a red/yellow/green "battle traffic light" and a cost-benefit table to decide which fights deserve time, energy and attention, and which to drop.

chunks.heading: Strategic quitting beats the success-or-failure binary
chunks.text:
- Cris rejects "manifest your dreams" absolutism: "everything I want will happen if I just want it badly enough" does "more damage than good."
- He argues people are taught only two outcomes, success or failure, with no in-between. When you aren't "winning," you assume you're "failing," so you keep fighting battles that no longer matter and force puzzle pieces that don't fit.
- His reframe: "I don't believe in failure. I believe there is only information." Stopping something that isn't working makes space for something more aligned with your needs.

chunks.heading: When to stop: the signals and the capital logic
chunks.text:
- Sometimes what you want doesn't happen. Sometimes it isn't supposed to. If you try different approaches, push harder, and still hit the same wall every time, Cris says there are "no better signals to stop than those."
- He treats time, energy and attention as capital: "why spend capital (time, energy, attention) on assets that don't grow?"
- Pushing calibration:
  - Push too little: nothing moves.
  - Push too much: things break.
  - Push wisely: life opens.

chunks.heading: Strategic quitting as an edge
chunks.text:
- Cris says the real edge is strategic quitting: "deliberately saying no to 99% of opportunities so you can say yes to the 1% that could change everything."
- It requires patience, and progress may look slow. In his words, "what looks slow is often leverage others can't see."
- He frames abandoning a fight as a gift to yourself: "Every fight you abandon is a gift to yourself."

chunks.heading: The battle traffic light: a decision tool for which fights to take
chunks.text:
Cris uses a three-color filter for deciding which challenges are worth pursuing:

- **Red**: not worth it. Drop it.
- **Yellow**: maybe worth it. Weigh cost against benefit.
- **Green**: go for it, because the battle has real impact.

chunks.heading: Cost-benefit table for yellow situations
chunks.text:
For anything yellow, he suggests a simple table with these columns:

| Battle | Potential Benefit | Cost (time, energy, relationships) | Worth It? |

- The cost side counts time, energy and relationships, not just money.
- The rule: if the cost outweighs the benefit, move on.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cris Pop frames his leadership philosophy through an intern story: when Sabina asked to write outside her role, he said yes and the result surfaced a voice that rigid job descriptions would have buried. The essay argues that trust, psychological safety and betting on potential produce stronger people than micromanagement.

chunks.heading: Trust over control: how Cris builds leaders instead of workers
chunks.text:
Cris's core claim is that if the goal is building leaders, the method cannot be control. He frames his role as "not about drawing boxes around people" but "breaking the walls that confine them." He says the aim is recognizing raw potential and nurturing it "even when it takes us places we didn't plan to go."

- "Micromanagement builds workers. Trust builds giants. And the world is starving for giants."
- "People grow in freedom. Trust is the ultimate accelerant."
- "When people feel trusted, they rise. They don't just deliver, they soar."
- He argues that trust produces things "no amount of micromanagement could ever manufacture."
- He says expectations placed on people are "usually too small to begin with."

chunks.heading: Saying yes to out-of-role requests: the Sabina example
chunks.text:
Two interns, Mălina and Sabina, joined Thunder's dev internship program about two months before the essay (September 2025). A few weeks in, Sabina asked to write and lend her voice to Thunder's story, which is outside a dev intern's role.

- Cris says he did not see this as stepping out of role. He saw "a spark beginning to be ignited" and said yes.
- Sabina wrote a personal first-person piece (her doubts, fears and returning hope) that he published in the essay.
- His takeaway: if he had focused on job descriptions and staying in lanes, or "managing instead of listening," her voice "would have stayed buried" and the story would never have been told.
- He asks the leader's question: how many people sit in meetings, follow processes and complete tasks while carrying stories like this inside them?
- The principle: bet on potential instead of policing boundaries, and you get transformation.

chunks.heading: How Thunder hires: warm interviews that look for the person
chunks.text:
Sabina's account shows the interview process Cris and his team run for the internship.

- The technical interview was built to be warm. Two interviewers (one she vaguely knew from a lab, one a stranger) were kind, spoke to her "not as a candidate, but as a person," offered patient smiles when anxiety made her stumble, and did not pounce on weaknesses.
- They asked about her passions and her vision for the future, and listened.
- The final interview was with Cris. She says it "wasn't about my qualifications, it was about my essence." His questions were: what makes you tick, and what lights that fire in your soul?
- Cris entered "not as a titan of industry, but as a person," and smiled.
- Sabina's reaction to being hired was pressure as well as relief ("Now I had to be worth the chance they took"), which shows that the trust placed in someone also creates motivation.
- Thunder also recruits through visible community presence: she found it by slipping into their talks and labs and saw a community before applying.

chunks.heading: Onboarding: give permission to learn at your own pace
chunks.text:
Sabina describes the first week as the thing that changed her relationship with the work.

- The team started interns with familiar faces from the interviews and gave them "permission": to take their time, to learn at their own pace, to ask, to question, to be imperfect.
- They took interns back to the bare bones of web development, stripping away the academic pressure that had smothered her passion.
- Result by her account: she went from dreading the morning alarm to looking forward to the next challenge, and her old love for coding returned.
- Her day-one instinct was to be flawless and give nobody a reason to regret hiring her. Removing that pressure through explicit permission is what let curiosity replace fear.

chunks.heading: Culture: an ecosystem, not a zero-sum corporation
chunks.text:
Cris publishes Sabina's description of Thunder as the culture he has built, and endorses it as "our story."

- Contrast with the zero-sum world she came from, where you don't help the person next to you for fear they'll take your spot.
- Thunder's operating idea is that "we all grow better together." Every person is a pillar, and their wins are each other's wins.
- Knowledge sharing is treated as the only way to build something that lasts, not as a weakness.
- Safety is the precondition: Sabina says she could be honest only once she felt "safe enough," and Cris says that is when people bring their whole selves to the table and create "what they create will be unforgettable."
- The outcome Cris points to: someone who arrived demoralized now wants to "help build more places like it," so the culture reproduces leaders who want to build the same kind of place.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Cris Pop recaps a Thunder Talks session with RebelDot's Tudor Ciulean and adds his own view on company culture. The core idea: transparency builds trust, trust builds ownership, and open, meritocratic teams beat "factory culture" companies.

chunks.heading: Cris's view: work with people, not for them
chunks.text:
- Cris frames collaborative entrepreneurship as the future of building companies, in contrast to "toxic competition" and the "zero-sum game." At Thunder Talks he welcomed people from RebelDot, a company that could be seen as a rival, and traded stories and lessons openly instead.
- He endorses Tudor Ciulean's (RebelDot co-founder) principle "work with, not for": stand shoulder-to-shoulder with people instead of above them.
- When you work with someone, you share the weight of uncertainty, and their wins and struggles become yours.
- Cris endorses the idea that it is not enough to dream together; "we have to be willing to fail together." Shared risk and a shared stake in an uncertain outcome turn colleagues into collaborators.
- Every conversation is a choice that either builds or diminishes trust.

chunks.heading: Honest communication as the foundation of workplace relationships
chunks.text:
- Cris argues most workplaces run on "polite half-truths and carefully curated feedback." He backs the principle of truth even when it is uncomfortable.
- Lasting business relationships are forged in the vulnerable kind of honesty, the kind that risks rejection to invite trust.
- He treats honesty as a practice, "a way of working, leading, and showing up for one another," and says that when you are building something meaningful, "transparency is everything."
- The chain he endorses, quoted from Tudi: "Transparency builds trust. Trust fuels ownership. Ownership generates care and sparks creativity."
- Most companies do the opposite: they hide struggles, micromanage the process, and then wonder why people are disengaged.

chunks.heading: Case study: how RebelDot was built on radical transparency
chunks.text:
Cris holds up RebelDot as proof that this approach works.
- Vision: "A thriving society built on fair relationships." Mission: "We bring value through technology with honest partnerships."
- Origin: as co-founder of a software company, Tudi was asked to fire good people simply because a client hadn't paid its bill. That was the "rational," safe business decision. He refused, walked away, and built a new company with the people he was meant to let go.
- Early days: the company was losing money. Tudi told people the uncomfortable truth and gave them the choice to stay or leave. Some left; others believed in the mission and stayed.
- He made no false promises and kept everyone informed about the reality they faced together. Over time this produced a team that felt genuinely invested in the outcome and understood "not just what they were doing, but why it mattered."
- Result, per Cris: one of the fastest growing tech companies in their area, "not because they had the best rules, but because they focused on people and values," and because everyone understood what they were fighting for, not because of a perfect strategy.
- Lesson: give people not just the how but the why.

chunks.heading: Integral factory culture versus a meritocratic culture
chunks.text:
- Cris describes most companies as having an "integral factory culture": everything systematized, standardized and optimized for efficiency, so people become interchangeable parts. He says this is why innovation dies and talent walks out the door.
- He also stresses the gap between the culture a company actually creates and the culture it thinks it is creating.
- Collaborative entrepreneurship instead rests on a meritocratic foundation: the best ideas win regardless of who suggests them, whether CEO or newest hire.
- Merit-driven decisions cultivate trust, and trust compounds.

chunks.heading: What trust and transparency produce for a business
chunks.text:
Cris lists the compound effects of a merit- and trust-based culture:
- Quality, because people care about the outcome.
- Speed, because there is no bureaucracy slowing things down.
- Flexibility, which leads to real performance and partnerships that last "decades, not quarters."
- Requirement: complete transparency and clarity. "No politics. No 'need to know' basis. Everything in the open."
- His claim: collaborative entrepreneurship "is never the reason we fail, it's what prevents failure."

chunks.heading: Entrepreneurship with human values and civic responsibility
chunks.text:
- Thunder's mission from day one, per Cris, was "entrepreneurship with human values and civic responsibility": work can be meaningful, done alongside people you care about, pursuing goals that matter both personally and collectively.
- He argues consumers and business builders have more power than they realize: every company supported, partnership formed and hire made is a vote for the kind of world we want to work in.
- He says the open question is not whether this approach works (RebelDot proves it does) but whether more people have the courage to choose it.
- He is writing a book called "Leadership before it has a name," on why self-leadership is the most important leadership, to be launched at The Thunder Way.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Romanian Q&A in which Cris Pop explains why he founded Thunder around generosity, self-leadership and civic entrepreneurship. He shows how small, consistent acts and organic community growth (Thunder Talks) beat grand strategies, and why a leader should stay the same person in every role.

chunks.heading: Why Cris defines himself as an "ordinary man" and what drives his leadership
chunks.text:
- Cris founded Thunder, and says its approach rests on human leadership and civic entrepreneurship.
- For him, being an ordinary person means choosing every day to make a small effort for others: help, contribute, "leave something good behind you," even if nothing is spectacular.
- He believes real meaning sits in simple gestures: a word or an act that changes someone's day.
- He learned this from his parents, simple people who were always present for those around them. What mattered was how sincere the gesture was, not how big.
- His lesson: real impact comes from the consistency of choosing to be good every day, not from big things.
- Generosity is the value under everything he does, personally and at Thunder. He defines it as creating contexts where people can grow, collaborate and support each other, not just giving.
- He sees the world's challenges as chances to offer more and build together, not just obstacles.

chunks.heading: Self-leadership: where it came from and what it changes in teams
chunks.text:
- He reached the conviction out of frustration. He worked in environments where people waited to be told what to do, waited for permission to decide, or complained about problems without acting. He realized he did the same in some areas of his own life.
- His core realization: "nobody comes to solve your life for you." No boss, partner or magical opportunity will. The only one who can change something is you.
- What changes when people adopt it:
  - They move from "I can't because..." to "what can I do with what I have?"
  - Motivation comes from inside; they stop waiting for validation or instructions at every step.
  - They take initiative, first small, then bigger.
- In a team, the difference is felt immediately. When people think like leaders and own their work and results, meaning stops being something to search for and is built every day. Work becomes part of their identity, and people become more involved and more grateful.
- He frames self-leadership as "taking your power back."
- He admits it is not easy: it takes courage to take responsibility for everything around you. But once you understand it, you can't go back; the power was always there and you forgot to use it.

chunks.heading: Thunder Talks: how a 4-person meetup grew organically into a movement
chunks.text:
Cris's example of civic entrepreneurship starting small:

- **Start:** 4 people in Thunder's own office ("Thunder home"). No grand strategy; he wanted a space where people could talk openly about things that truly matter.
- **First editions:** about 4 editions, max 15 people, because the space allowed no more. People kept coming, asking questions and bringing friends.
- **Step up:** rented a room at ABC Incubator. 35 people the first time, then 60. Growth was organic, "without forcing anything."
- **Edition 7:** even more interest, with Alexandra Crăciun as speaker. Later speakers included Mădălina Hotca, Tünde Macarie, Cristina Frei and Tudor Ciuleanu.
- **Speaker principle:** always bring people with authentic stories, close to the community, who "live what they speak."
- **Today:** the event runs at Cinema Florin Piersic.
- **Lesson:** "We don't have to know the whole road, we only need the courage to take the first step." What began as a meeting of four became a movement that regularly brings together curious, involved people who want change, learning from each other and forming real connections.

chunks.heading: The problems that motivate him: authoritarian leadership and education
chunks.text:
- The biggest challenge that pushes him to act is authoritarian, rigid leadership that puts control above people and limits their potential.
- His response is to build a different model: human leadership and civic entrepreneurship based on empathy, collaboration and real involvement of people in decisions that affect them.
- He is also concerned that the education system often fails to prepare young people for real life.
- Thunder's answer: events for students to help them build a solid foundation, professionally and personally. The Thunder Way offers 15 scholarships for students who want to grow and contribute actively to the community.
- He treats these challenges as opportunities for transformation, not barriers. The goal is a community of leaders defined by how they do things, not by titles, who put values, empathy and generosity at the center of their decisions.

chunks.heading: Who you are when you're not the leader: no mask, same person
chunks.text:
- His answer: he is the same person regardless of role. His relationships with colleagues, friends and community members rest on respect, empathy and openness.
- He argues a leader should not put on a mask when moving into a leadership position. Too often leadership is understood as authority, when it should be "a space of support, listening and collaboration."
- Leadership doesn't change him; it only gives a bigger platform for what he does anyway every day: listen, encourage and build authentic relationships.
- Regardless of title, he stays a curious, involved person eager to learn.
- Core line: being a leader "does not mean rising above others, but staying close to them and to your values."

chunks.heading: Learning from ordinary people: his mother's village shop
chunks.text:
- He names several ordinary people who inspire through their growth (Dragoș Pătraru, Andra Pintincan, Marius Balo, Alexandra Crăciun), but picks his mother as the single example.
- She runs the shop in the village with a healthy respect for work and responsibility. For her it isn't just a business but a service to the community: many people can't get to town, so she makes sure they find what they need, even if that means extra trips or stocking products that aren't profitable.
- Specific habits:
  - Sets aside bread for someone who comes late from work.
  - Buys certain products for just 2-3 people who need them, because it makes them happy.
  - Is attentive, helpful and always present with each person.
- Result: the shop becomes a meeting and connection place; people come to talk and be listened to, not only to buy.
- His takeaway: real impact doesn't come from big actions but from "small, consistent gestures done with care every day." The differences that truly matter happen daily, "not just once a year."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa argues that teams say they trust the process but treat it like a suspect, confusing control with care. She reframes the problem as self-trust, which she says is built from knowledge, skills and results. She reports Cris Pop sharing a formula at Thunder Talks 10: Confidence = Certainty + Faith.

chunks.heading: Trust the process, or process that trust? Control versus care
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack essay, Andreea Popa writes that teams repeat "trust the process" like a mantra, but treat the process like a suspect: they audit it, timeline it, and call it inefficient or unscalable when it wanders. The essay argues that confusing control with care is the root problem. Care is "patient" and "spacious"; it listens when the process says it needs more time. Control, by contrast, is "the fear of uncertainty and failure," and the more teams rush, question and box in the process, the more they "choke the life out of it." Popa describes real process as "a living, breathing collaboration between trust, time, and the human heart," not a button that produces brilliance. These are the author's own views, not statements attributed to Cris Pop.

chunks.heading: Reframing the question: trust yourself enough to let the work breathe
chunks.text: Thunder's Substack essay by Andreea Popa proposes replacing "do you trust the process?" with "do you trust yourself enough to let the process work without your constant supervision?" She poses a set of tests for leaders and makers: Can you hold the tension of not knowing without rushing to fill it? Can you sit with silence without assuming something has gone wrong? Can you stop refreshing the timeline and start listening to what the work is trying to say? Her conclusion is that "the process doesn't need your trust. You do." The point is that supervision-heavy behavior is a symptom of low self-trust, not a sign of professionalism or maturity.

chunks.heading: Self-trust as something built: Zoltan Veres's three pillars
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack post, Andreea Popa argues that self-trust is not only a feeling but something built "piece by piece, through experience and results." She cites Zoltan Veres, who says self-trust rests on three things: what you know (the information you hold), what you can do (your skills), and what results you have achieved and can achieve again. Her practical advice is to flip the doubt statement "I don't trust myself" into a sharper question: "Trust myself in what, exactly?" This turns vague self-doubt into specific, addressable gaps.

chunks.heading: Cris's formula at Thunder Talks 10: Confidence = Certainty + Faith
chunks.text:
According to Andreea Popa's Thunder Substack essay, at Thunder Talks 10 Cris shared the formula "Confidence = Certainty + Faith." The essay explains it this way (the elaboration is the author's reading, not a direct Cris quote):
- **Certainty** comes from looking back at what you have already accomplished. The question is which wins prove you can trust yourself. No one is expected to believe they can do everything, only what matters most to them. A skills gap is simply the next thing to grow, bit by bit.
- **Faith** comes from looking forward: believing in your potential before there is proof, and trusting that even if the path is unclear you will find your way.

chunks.heading: Fighting negative self-talk with a "BUT"
chunks.text: Thunder's Substack essay by Andreea Popa names negative self-talk, the inner voice that erases your wins, as what kills self-trust. Her counter-practice is to catch the thought and add a "BUT" after it: "I'm not good at this, but I did X before, and I can learn." She pairs this with reminding yourself of consistent achievements, which feeds the "certainty" half of Cris's confidence formula. The essay frames neither the process nor your doubts as the enemy; the power lies in holding steady without seeing what comes next.

chunks.heading: The bird and its wings: faith without a guaranteed path
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes in Thunder's Substack that a bird never senses whether a branch is weak or about to break, yet it trusts its wings regardless. People often say yes to a challenge while quietly bracing for the fall, which is why trust feels distant. The essay's closing message, "Before there's a path, there's a pulse," is to act with faith in your own ability rather than waiting for certainty about the route: "So fly anyway. Wings were made for this moment."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa argues that sounding smart matters less than being felt, and that a voice is a place people enter and either stay in or leave. She cites Cris Pop's rule from his newsletter, "only teach what you've lived", and builds on it with a case for lived truth and for clarity as respect. Her stories about chasing clever words are her own.

chunks.heading: Voice as a place: why sounding smart fails and lived truth lasts
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack post, Andreea Popa writes that she used to think the goal was to sound smart. She believed polished phrasing and vocabulary would make people nod and admire her. She now argues that "if you have to explain the brilliance, maybe it's not," and that words which do not change something (a mind, a belief, a habit, a decision) are doing nothing. Thunder's Substack argues that in a world saturated with information, people rarely remember a single sentence. Being understood, meaning helping someone take away something meaningful, matters more than looking clever. People may admire what they do not understand, but they will not follow it, remember it or change because of it.

chunks.heading: Words that touch versus words that perform
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that she catches herself reaching for clever paraphrasing, and that a "shiny inner voice" tells her to use a new word because it sounds smart. When she returns to the page a day or two later, a humbler inner voice shows her what matters. Thunder's Substack contrasts sounding smart with being felt, calling them "two different universes." It lists what stays with a person:

- A sentence that cuts through the noise and lands like truth.
- Honesty that makes you look away for a second, just to recover.
- Words that "don't perform, but recognize."
- The line they whisper to themselves when the room goes quiet.
- The simple phrase "you're not the only one."
- Something they always knew but needed permission to believe.
- Questions that remind them who they are.

The post's test for anyone writing, speaking or leading is a question: "is this performing, or is this touching something real?" Only the second one stays and makes someone feel a little less alone.

chunks.heading: Cris's rule: only teach what you have lived
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes that Cris shared a rule in his last newsletter that stuck with her: "Only teach what you've lived. Only say it if it changed you first." The post treats this as the base for credible communication and leadership. Andreea adds her own extension, which is not Cris's: "If your words don't scare you just a little, they're probably not the truth yet." She also advises starting a piece with a sentence your past self needed to hear. Her advice is to speak for the version of you that felt small or confused, because "that's where resonance begins."

chunks.heading: Your voice is a place people walk into
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack argues that a voice works like a world, borrowing the world-building idea from fiction. It credits Tolkien with understanding that a world must follow its own internal logic or the magic collapses. The same applies to speaking and writing: if you break your own truth, your message loses its weight. Andreea Popa writes that every time you speak or write you invite someone into a feeling, a memory or a worldview. As with walking into a room, people know within seconds whether to stay. They ask whether it is grounded, true, safe and alive, or designed to impress rather than invite.

If the words offer nothing real to stand on, people leave. The reason is not rudeness or distraction. There are too many rooms to walk into, and too many voices say too much that does not mean enough. The post says the aim is not to decorate ideas but to build a world so honest that people believe it while inside, and where someone pauses and thinks "I need to sit with this."

chunks.heading: Clarity as an act of respect
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that the target is not brilliance, polish or even value, but something "alive. Real. Clear." She urges people to talk as if it matters and to speak as if someone's future hinges on the sentence they are about to say, because sometimes it does. Thunder's Substack argues that words should not be safe, and should be something that wakes people up.

The post also makes a case for knowledge distillation. In its words, "We don't simplify because people can't handle complexity. We simplify because clarity is an act of respect." The reasons it gives are that the world moves fast, attention is thin, and the brain remembers what it feels, not what it decodes. The practice is to take everything you know and have lived and strip it down to the sentence that hits "straight in the chest," a truth someone can carry into a hard day. The post concludes: "Smart words can impress. But simple words, spoken with lived depth, those connect. Those change people." Its closing line is "Say less. Mean more."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes about a line Cris Pop shared with her that changed her mindset: "If your own story doesn't inspire you, it's time to change it." She argues that the narratives we hold about ourselves shape our choices, that one miss shouldn't define us, and she offers reflection questions for rewriting the next chapter.

chunks.heading: Cris's line: "If your own story doesn't inspire you, it's time to change it"
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack post, Andreea Popa writes that Cris Pop shared a sentence that changed her mindset: "If your own story doesn't inspire you, it's time to change it." She says she can't recall exactly when he said it, but she remembers how it landed, "like a moment that shifts your perspective entirely." Before that, she writes, she had never asked herself whether the story she lived inspired her. She was comfortable in her own bubble and accepted that "this was simply how things were." The rest of the post is her own reading of Cris's line, not something the source attributes to him.

chunks.heading: Why the stories we live by shape identity and choices
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack argues, through Andreea Popa, that everyone lives by a story about who they are, where they've been and what they're capable of. That story shapes identity, choices and ultimately life. The problem comes when the story "no longer inspires us," when it feels too small or too limiting. Popa lists the self-limiting lines people repeat without noticing how much they hold them back:

- "I'm just not good at that."
- "I'm not the kind of person who..."
- "This is just who I am."

Her claim is that these outdated narratives work quietly and that most people don't realize they are repeating them.

chunks.heading: Your story is not set in stone: you are not your mistakes
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that a person is not the mistakes they've made, the failures they fear, or "the version of yourself that settled, played small, or got stuck." She illustrates this with her own padel experience (her anecdote, not Cris's). She obsesses over missed shots, and the good shots and won points fade into the background. She saw her playing partner do the same: after one missed shot the partner fell into frustration and forgot how well she had played until then. Popa reminded her not to let one shot define her game.

Her lesson is that we replay the misses and downplay the wins. We carry one moment "as if it defines the whole match," but it doesn't and shouldn't. Stories can evolve, and if the current chapter feels uninspiring, "you have the power and the responsibility to rewrite the next one."

chunks.heading: Five reflection questions for rewriting your story
chunks.text:
Under the heading "Turn the page," Popa offers questions to ask honestly in order to begin changing your story:

- Do my words about myself make me feel stronger or weaker?
- What parts of my story do I keep repeating that no longer serve me?
- Am I following my own path or what others expect?
- What would my story sound like if I believed in myself more?
- What beliefs about myself do I need to challenge or let go of?

She advises letting the story "sing with possibility, rooted in your values and expanding toward the future you envision."

chunks.heading: An uninspiring chapter means readiness for growth, not failure
chunks.text:
The post argues that an uninspiring story does not mean someone has failed: "It means you're ready for growth." Popa frames the choice as staying stuck in a story that drains you or rising into one that empowers you. She closes with two forward-looking questions:

- What story do you want to tell a year from now?
- What needs to change today for that to happen?

The post treats self-reflection and personal narrative as a leadership starting point. It places the responsibility for rewriting the story on the individual, rooted in their own values rather than other people's expectations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa's year-end reflection argues that 2025 was the year Thunder stopped waiting to feel ready and simply began: launching The Thunder Way event, writing the leadership book, and choosing collaboration over competition. It reports Cris Pop speaking at the New York and Cluj events and guiding Thunder Talks conversations, and describes the Thunderometer, a shared values check-in.

chunks.heading: The Thunderometer: a shared compass of principles for when things feel unclear or rushed
chunks.text:
In a Thunder Substack post reviewing 2025, Andreea Popa describes the Thunderometer. Thunder created it because "some things can't be measured in numbers, but they still need attention." The team wanted a shared way to check in with themselves, with each other and with the work.

She describes it as a set of principles the team returns to when things feel "unclear, heavy, or rushed." Thunder uses it to:
- stay honest with itself
- notice when it is drifting from its values
- catch moments when "the pace gets louder than the purpose"
- catch moments when "good enough starts replacing care"

The post says it works on three levels:
- **Relationships:** lead with trust, listen with intention, uplift one another.
- **Work:** craft with meaning, decisions made consciously, responsibility for what you leave behind.
- **Personal:** self-leadership through owning your choices, your energy and your standards.

Popa calls it "a compass." It doesn't tell people what to do. It helps them sense whether they are moving in the right direction: toward work they're proud of, relationships that feel real, and a way of being that stays true "no matter how fast we grow."

chunks.heading: Lessons from the 2025 work: self-leadership in development, presence in marketing
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes in Thunder's Substack that every piece of Thunder's 2025 work "carried the trust we placed in each other and the daily decision to show up fully, to care about both the work and the people we share it with." She draws one lesson from each side of the company.

**Development.** Colleagues took on complex systems, unfamiliar technologies and higher expectations with "a strong sense of self-leadership." They understood that "quality is something you take responsibility for." Time spent thinking before building paid off, and many of the best solutions came from asking the right questions. Her takeaway: "Lead yourself through the work. Take ownership beyond your tasks, hold your standards high, and build with intention. Create work that carries value beyond yourself."

**Marketing.** The focus moved closer to people. Popa writes that digital presence has its place, but "real connection still happens soul to soul." Being part of the community meant being present, listening and organizing events where ideas grew stronger by being shared. Her takeaway: "Show up where people are. Pull chairs to the same table, invest in gathering together, and build community the timeless way."

chunks.heading: Collaboration over competition: RebelDot, BitStone, Linnify and the student tickets
chunks.text:
The post says Thunder has "never bought into the idea of competition." In 2025 it connected with Cluj companies that share its vision: RebelDot, BitStone and Linnify. The stated aim is "coming together and contributing to a community worth being part of, side by side."

Popa singles out that these companies invested in students by buying tickets to The Thunder Way. She says this kind of faith in the next generation gives students "trust, wings, and the courage to chart their own path."

The collaboration with Linnify led to two events in New York:
- **AI beyond the BUZZ**, with speakers from Endava, Siena AI and TypingDNA.
- **A panel of Romanian tech leaders and business owners.** Cris Pop took part as founder and leader of Thunder, alongside Simona Vasile (BDO), Andrei Papancea (NLX) and Gabriel Păunescu (Naologic).

Popa says the events sharpened the need to stay connected to tech communities: "Technology doesn't evolve in isolation, and neither should the people building it." Thunder wants to share what it learns and stay close to ecosystem conversations.

Thunder also spent the year building a platform to broadcast events at Teatrul Nației, the cultural hub founded by Dragoș Pătraru. Popa says it reminds the team that "the work we do is only as meaningful as the people it serves."

chunks.heading: The Thunder Way event: beginning before certainty
chunks.text:
Popa writes that the Thunder Way idea lived quietly inside the team for more than a year, "paired with doubt, questions, and the feeling that it might be too big." In 2025, "instead of waiting for certainty, we chose to begin." The event took place at Cinema Florin Piersic.

She says it was born from a line the team keeps following: "before a path exists, there is always a pulse. You just have to listen to it, and step in fully, body and soul."

The post frames the year as a lesson in momentum: it "comes not from having everything figured out, but from showing up fully, believing in what you're creating, and trusting that the people around you will meet you there."

Speakers included Dragoș Pătraru (simplicity and responsibility toward each other), Andra Pintican (work doesn't have to hurt to have meaning), Marius Balo (resilience and inner freedom) and Alexandra Crăciun (curiosity and authenticity). Popa says Cris Pop's talk reminded the audience that "when you lead with belief in others and a commitment to service, you lift a vision that carries the weight of many hearts and minds."

chunks.heading: Thunder Talks, Bookclubs and student events: community built around people
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack describes how Thunder ran events "for people, by people" in 2025. Thunder Talks included voices from outside the team:
- Tudor Ciuleanu on collaborative entrepreneurship and honest communication at work.
- Cristina Frei on drawing your own path.
- Tünde Macarie on saying less but meaning more.
- Mădălina Hotca on trusting yourself and fighting for your vision when no one else does.

According to Popa, Cris "contributed to each conversation with his own stories and struggles, always seeking the next layer of truth and searching for the questions that would take us all deeper."

Cris also guided the final event of the year, with Cluj Startups at the opening of Founders Hive. The question was "what does leadership look like before it has a name?" He drew from the book and from years of learning "what leadership looks like when it's stripped of the polish."

Bookclubs continued as a space where people "came thirsty for meaning and left feeling less alone." Marius Balo joined to share his book "Păturica roz."

On students, Popa argues that the education system often leaves young people "at the edge of the real world, unprepared." She says "preparing them for careers just feels hollow" next to helping them understand who they are and who they can become, and know they have a community behind them.

chunks.heading: "Leadership Before It Has a Name": the book as a call back to being
chunks.text:
Popa writes that the book began as a simple guide to capture Thunder's philosophy and what leadership looks like "when you strip away all the polished theories." As they wrote, it grew into a book, one the team "never planned to write."

She says the book is proof of "how essential humanity is in everything we do." It is a reminder of how easy it is to get caught up in "the doing, the building, the achieving, and lose sight of the being," and it calls the team back to "who we are beneath all the roles we play and the masks we sometimes wear."

Its core claim, in her words: "leadership is not about titles, nor about authority. It will always come back to showing up, fully human, fully present, and leading from that place of authenticity." She calls it a promise that the team will never drift too far from who they are and are becoming, however far they go.

chunks.heading: Welcoming interns and gathering as a team
chunks.text:
Popa writes that two interns from the AI web internship, Mălina and Sabina, joined Thunder in 2025.
- Mălina is described as dedicated and dependable, with a warm, positive presence.
- Sabina arrived with "a fire for tech and a hunger to learn." She wrote candidly about her journey before and during the internship, and the team found her words "profound, honest, and moving."

Popa says they "arrived as two, but worked as one," leaning on and challenging each other in a way that "raised the bar for everyone around them."

The team also travels together. In 2025 that meant a winter trip to the mountains with skiing and snowboarding, Amsterdam, New York, and a closing gathering in a cabin near Cluj-Napoca to reflect on the year.

For 2026, the post names events in Berlin, The Thunder Way in Bucharest (June) and Cluj-Napoca (November), one stop in Zurich and plans to return to the United States. Thunder Talks will likely drop to two or three "with the same depth and intention." Thunder will keep running student events and Bookclubs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa recaps Thunder's February: coaching, culture outings, a hackathon, and the book launch. She reports Cris's coaching question (rules or guidelines?) and that Cris handed interviewing, once mostly his, to Florina, Iuli and Cosmin. She argues growth comes from trust, ownership and consistency.

chunks.heading: Group coaching and the rules-versus-guidelines question
chunks.text:
In a Thunder Substack post ("10 stories from February"), Andreea Popa describes Thunder's first group coaching session with Tünde, focused on deepening relationships, being more connected and intentional with one another. In the coming months the team planned to split into two groups to share perspectives on communication, friendship at work, and how stronger relationships shape both work and life.

Cris also began 1:1 coaching with Tünde to find areas where he can grow as a leader. In one session she asked him: "Would you rather set rules or offer guidelines?" Andreea Popa writes that this question "opened something up." Her reading: rules make people stop feeling they own what they do, so work becomes compliance, "ticking boxes and staying out of trouble," with no heart in it. Guidelines trust people to find the path; the framework is given and they fill in the details, which creates ownership. People then choose how to show up, and the focus shifts from getting the job done to "who they're becoming in the process." Her takeaway: "When you give people guidelines instead of rules, they take ownership, and in doing so, they work on their own becoming."

chunks.heading: Transferring recruitment interviews to the team
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack describes February as the month recruitment ownership was "fully transferred." Interviews, which had mostly been Cris's territory, were run by Florina, Iuli, and Cosmin, who decided who belongs on the team. Andreea Popa notes the role reversal: not long before, they had been the candidates. Cris trusted them to do it well.

Cosmin said the experience strengthened his own understanding of key concepts, since explaining ideas to candidates forced him to structure his thinking and revisit fundamentals ("Teaching, in a way, becomes learning"). The post traces Florina's path at Thunder: intern, contributor, developer, initiative owner, interviewer, and mentor to colleagues such as Mălina. The author's view: growth like this is "built through trust, ownership, and consistency. You can't manufacture it. You can only create the conditions for it, and then get out of the way."

chunks.heading: The hackathon as a hiring process
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack describes a recruitment hackathon held February 20-21. Out of nearly 200 applications, nine participants were selected to spend a weekend building a mission-driven software product. They split into three teams, and most projects centered on skills and meaningful exchanges between people.

Cris opened the day by sharing Thunder's culture, values, and the thinking behind how the company works. Florina guided the technical side so each team had clarity and support. The tone mixed deep focus with lightness: pizza, laughter, conversation about hobbies between coding sessions. Some participants stayed until 4 AM, and Sergiu worked continuously until 10:30 PM the next day without sleeping. On day two, after breakfast and lunch together, each team presented.

Andreea Popa writes that what stood out was the thoughtfulness of the ideas, how the teams worked together, and "care in what they built." Denis and Andrei joined Thunder part-time, a decision based on long-term fit, team dynamics, and shared values. For others, the door stays open, with Thunder aiming to support all participants through future initiatives, tools, and mentorship.

chunks.heading: Culture as stepping into a colleague's world
chunks.text:
In a Thunder Substack post, Andreea Popa describes a team outing to BT Arena on February 11 to watch U-BT play basketball. It mattered because Anda, a huge basketball fan and former player, was there, and seeing the game through her eyes made it feel more alive. The author writes that there is "something powerful about stepping into someone else's world for an evening."

The stated culture goal: someone's passion doesn't stay theirs alone but becomes something everyone experiences together. "We weren't just there for the game. We were there because it matters to her, and that's reason enough." The post's closing invitation extends this: think of a colleague or friend, identify what lights them up (a sport, hobby, or passion they rarely get to share), and show up for it.

chunks.heading: Bookclub, podcast, and ceasing to wait for the right moment
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack reports that bookclubs returned on February 12, with four people presenting four books from four different worlds; some of the group continued to a screening of Hamnet, Gabi's pick. Andreea Popa shared her own journey, from authoritarian systems to growing inside a workplace that puts people first, and the shift from seeing leadership as a title to understanding it as "a lifelong process of becoming," which she says sits at the heart of Thunder's book.

On February 13 the team set up its podcast room and recorded its first episode, with Iulia as guest. Deni handled the technical setup and Anda helped make it happen. The post notes the equipment had been owned for a long time; "What we were missing was the courage to stop waiting for the right moment." The team was still deciding whether to publish or re-record. The author's lesson: "The barrier was never out there. It was always just us."

chunks.heading: Cris visiting student builders at UTCN
chunks.text: On February 13, per Thunder's Substack, Cris visited students at the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca (UTCN) building a solar-powered car aimed at a race in Australia. The students had earlier visited Thunder's office to share their goal. In their workspace, surrounded by tools, wires, and "controlled chaos," Andreea Popa observed that everyone had a role and moved with clarity and purpose, "like a system that only works because each individual takes responsibility." The post calls being around young people who care that much "both humbling and energizing."

chunks.heading: Leadership in Tech event, book launch, and Project H.U.M.A.N.
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack announces an event on Leadership in Tech in Austin, Texas on March 3, where Cris would moderate and Mir Hwang would share his story. Mir, a touring session drummer, hit inefficiencies in booking live entertainment and built the solution himself. The post frames this as the leadership Thunder believes in: "Seeing what needs fixing, taking ownership, and creating meaningful solutions for the community."

On February 26 Thunder held the official launch of its book, "Leadership before it has a name," with Iulia, Gabi, Ioana, and Marius (author of "Păturica roz") reflecting on human-centered leadership, followed by a Q&A with Cris and Andreea Popa. Andreea writes about her first time speaking to a large audience: trembling voice, then relaxing once she stopped fighting the emotion. Her reflection: "The very things we fear are often the ones that free us once we face them," and joy and fear in the same breath "is what leadership is truly about."

On February 27 Cris joined the Project H.U.M.A.N. podcast, aimed at young professionals. He spoke about his professional path, lessons from wins and struggles, and the intention behind the book: resources for young professionals trying to understand what leadership, growth, and healthy work environments mean, encouraging them to seek and build healthy, mission-driven workplaces.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa recounts a March in which Thunder's SXSW event in Austin drew 7 of 70 sign-ups, then Berlin and a home Thunder Talks on self-doubt. She reports Cris opened that talk framing self-doubt as caring and preparing, not something to fight. The post argues for staying in the process, learning rooms by being in them, and treating culture as behaviour.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on organizing events abroad: the Austin SXSW empty room
chunks.text:
In a Thunder Substack post titled "March: Self-doubt pulled up a chair," Andreea Popa writes about Thunder taking its community-building work to the United States, which she calls unusual for a small company from Cluj. The stated belief is that exposing the team to different cultures and ways of thinking is how Thunder breaks "the ceiling of what we think is possible." The first two New York events went well, so the team felt confident going into Austin during SXSW.

At Austin, 70 people signed up, many on the same day, yet only seven walked in. Cris, Deni and Gabi stood in a room that was supposed to be full. The post says none of them knew what to say, because none had been there before. The lesson the team drew: during SXSW people sign up for dozens of events and attend only a few. This was "a cultural nuance, and a local rule nobody told us," learned only by being in enough rooms. The post's takeaway is "You learn the room by being in it."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on how Thunder reads the Austin setback
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that the empty chairs "don't tell the whole story." Thunder organized the Austin event with Linnify. Cătălin and his team helped find the venue and connect with people, and then took the Thunder team to live concerts and around the city, creating space for informal conversations that, the post says, are "the foundation of any good long-term relationship." Through Cătălin the team met Mir, a founder running a business that makes millions, described as humble and as someone who leads by investing in people first. The post says meeting him in the middle of what felt like failure showed that a company can grow and still stay grounded in what matters.

The post also credits Cris, Deni and Gabi for staying late, joining meetings and working on projects alongside the event, noting that being in the States "comes with a lot of hard work behind the scenes."

The wider point: growth is not a straight line. "Sometimes you win first. Sometimes you lose twice. The order doesn't define the outcome." Thunder's stance: "We'll keep trying. We'll keep failing. We'll keep doing it."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on the Berlin event and "culture is behaviour"
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack describes a Berlin event on the theme "Culture under pressure," run with Irina, founder of Brightroom. Thunder brought its book, as it does wherever it goes. Unlike Austin, people signed up and most showed up. The post notes a ticket price, which it says created a different kind of commitment. Engagement ran deeper in the panel, the conversations after and the smaller groups, and discussions moved into real workplace situations, challenges and unfinished decisions.

The idea that resonated most with the team: you can't separate culture from behaviour. "Culture is behaviour. How you show up, how you speak, how you treat the person next to you, that's the culture." The post's closing reflection repeats it: "If you want to understand the culture of a team, just look at how people actually behave." Thunder says it is still learning how to build community across cultures but is more convinced it is worth figuring out.

chunks.heading: Cris's reframing of self-doubt at Thunder Talks (15th edition)
chunks.text:
At the 15th Thunder Talks, with guest Iulia, a long-time member of the Thunder community, the post says Cris opened the conversation with a perspective on self-doubt. It is an emotion you don't need to fight but can learn to understand differently. People usually treat it as a problem that blocks or pulls them back. Seen from another angle, the post says Cris suggested, self-doubt can mean you care, are paying attention, are willing to prepare better and go deeper, and are ready to take responsibility for what you are about to do.

Andreea Popa adds that self-doubt "doesn't disappear, and maybe it's not even supposed to." What changes is the meaning, depending on how you relate to it. If you stay involved in your own process, it becomes part of how you grow.

chunks.heading: Iulia's reframes of self-doubt, shared at Thunder Talks
chunks.text:
The post summarizes Iulia's talk. She recalled first feeling self-doubt as a child, and how it kept returning in different forms through her life. The post lists unspoken ideas many people grow up with: if you're scared, maybe it's not for you; you're either good at something or not; life happens to you; if you're not sure it will turn out well, don't try. Iulia didn't deny them but looked at them differently, with these reframes:

- "I want to do this and I'm scared."
- "(Almost) everything is a competence I can build."
- "Life is happening and I'm creating it."
- "If I can't guarantee the result, I will guarantee my involvement and my character."

The post connects this to Thunder's long-held intention for Thunder Talks: a space where people grow and invest in who they are becoming.

chunks.heading: The month's theme and practice: let go of the outcome, hold on to the work
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa frames March as being about continuing: staying in the process when things don't look as expected, and being willing to understand, adapt and learn from different contexts. She notes the team seemed to live the self-doubt lesson before putting it into words. A near-empty room in Austin could have been read as a sign to step back, but the team went on to Berlin and then home. "At times, you don't first understand and then go through the experience. You might go through it first, and only after... you start to see what it was actually teaching you."

The post offers a small practice: when doubt shows up, ask whether it is fear telling you to stop or a request to prepare. Then change the sentence from "I want this but I'm scared" to "I want this and I'm scared," and see what changes. Another reflection carried forward: "Technology comes from humans. Don't forget to invest there first."

chunks.heading: Cris's talks beyond the team in March, per Thunder's Substack
chunks.text:
The post lists Cris's external speaking that month:

- A Q&A with students, which made the team want to do this more often to stay closer to what students are going through.
- A TEDx Avram Iancu talk on not choosing to change the world but choosing to become, and how things that seem impossible at first are not really impossible, sharing defining moments from his journey.
- A talk at Liceul Elf, as part of a school project, on how he built a business with meaning and how students can start doing the same in their own way.

Other Thunder activity noted in the post: continued discussions with Tünde on building close, healthy relationships honestly and naturally; Vlad and Horațiu taking part in interview simulations with students at UTCN; and padel and a stand-up show as informal team bonding.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa recounts Cris Pop and Anda's three-week US trip (San Francisco, Las Vegas, New York) and argues that surrounding yourself with driven, trusting people lowers your own threshold for action. She reports Cris attended the New Narratives retreat, joined padel games with strangers who became contacts, and that the team met young Cluj founders.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on why US trips raise ambition: absorbing a culture where failure is expected
chunks.text: In an April post on Thunder's Substack, Andreea Popa describes Cris Pop and Anda spending three weeks in the US (San Francisco, Las Vegas, New York) making connections and chasing opportunities. The post argues that "exposing yourself to other people and places opens new ways of thinking." Its core claim: "If you're open to being inspired by others, you can lower your own threshold for taking action." The author contrasts San Francisco, where failure "has crossed the threshold of just being accepted. It's expected" ("Fall down, get up"), with Eastern Europe, where founders start businesses already asking "If this doesn't work out, what's my backup?" Thunder's Substack summarizes the contrast as "Falling upwards, that's the whole philosophy" versus a mind that "goes downward before it ever looks up."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on the New Narratives retreat: trust and co-creation feed audacity
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that Cris began his trip at the New Narratives retreat in California, organized by Renee Lynn Frojo for entrepreneurs building intentional, human-centered businesses. It was small by design, with conversations of real depth on marketing, business strategy, team dynamics, productivity and solopreneurship, all told through lived moments rather than abstractions. The post argues that stories stick because seeing a principle applied by a real person with real stakes gives it "texture. Nuance. Color."

The author says the retreat's openness came from people who wanted each other to succeed. Questions like "Have you ever considered doing it that way?" or "Are we missing something here?" carried no criticism, though in Eastern European culture they can easily land as such. The post concludes that "that culture of trust and co-creation is what feeds the audacity," and quotes Renee's newsletter: "If we want to create the change we want to see in the world, we have to stop thinking we can do it alone." Cris also noticed a pattern: most attendees had left corporate life, tired of hierarchies and processes that slowed everything down, to build one-person businesses on their own dream.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on Las Vegas and padel: a city built from desert by commitment
chunks.text:
The post describes Las Vegas, setting aside the casinos, as a city that "rose from nothing," built by people with "a vision, a strategy, and the nerve to follow it all the way." Andreea Popa writes that whether or not you like it on a moral level, it is hard not to be humbled by what committed people can build.

The same energy followed Cris onto the padel court. He plays regularly back home, and in the US he joined games with strangers and connected with them instantly. Through those matches he met people who believe ideas only matter if executed boldly, including founders of a New York-based startup using AI-powered cameras to record padel matches, analyze performance and improve the player experience. They were in Vegas setting up for the biggest padel tournament in the USA.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on New York: reconnecting and strangers offering support
chunks.text:
According to Thunder's Substack, back in New York two weeks later, Cris and Anda reconnected with people they first met in November, people who "share our story and our book" and believe in Thunder with the conviction they bring to their own dreams. Cris also met people with no reason to care about what Thunder is building who nonetheless "pulled their chairs closer and offered to support our vision."

The author reads this as people who had decided "scarcity was a lie, and that helping someone else go further costs you nothing and might just change everything." She says the journey felt "less like pushing against the world and more like moving through it, with the right people appearing at the right time."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on young Cluj founders: ambition close to home
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that audacity also exists a few streets from Thunder, in Cluj. She describes Vic, 19, who built two startups and sold one.
