He started at 13 following a love for computers, and at 16 opened his own company under his father's name and built his first product with friends; that is the one he sold. He then created Listener, a startup helping podcasters track their efforts, now based in San Francisco, where he is head of engineering.

Vic is also part of Cluj House, a co-living and co-working space that began when Bantu proposed hanging out with friends while each worked on their own projects; about 12 young people now live there. The Thunder team visited them and discovered another product they build, Anara, an AI workspace for scientists, students and research teams. The following month, the Thunder team hosted them at the author's home. The post says the more such people they find, "the more we believe that a different culture is being built. By all of us together."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack takeaways and monthly commitment: pick an environment that expands your sense of possible
chunks.text:
The post closes with four takeaways:

- "We're so busy avoiding the fall that we forget to look at how far we could go."
- "The culture you're in shapes the ceiling you believe exists."
- "When people move in the same direction and commit to the path, even empty ground can become a city."
- "Every connection you make is a door that hasn't revealed itself yet. Go further and meet more people."

The monthly commitment draws on a thought from Anda: traveling to places that feel more evolved, among driven people, changes you, and you return "more awake and ambitious." Thunder's Substack asks readers to seek out at least one place, community or environment that makes them feel that way, let themselves be inspired by others, take action, and then ask others to join in.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa's August newsletter recaps Thunder's trips to Tallinn and Helsinki. She reports that Cris and colleagues went to observe how others build, and Cris concluded Thunder isn't missing much, only consistency and bravery in sharing its work. It also covers Cris's long-term dream of Thunder as a place where people start projects and get mentorship, plus Gabi's reflections on confidence and inner authority.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on travelling to Tallinn and Helsinki to learn from other startup scenes
chunks.text: In an August recap on Thunder's Substack, Andreea Popa writes that Thunder people have been showing up in different corners of Europe and America. The stated reasons are curiosity and "that familiar Romanian feeling of, 'if they can do it, why can't we?'" The post says some cities are ahead of the curve and have livelier ideas, so Thunder goes to see them in person. Cris and other colleagues go to observe how people build, what they talk about, and what they do differently, then bring ideas back to try in Cluj. The post frames this as checking your "North Star": you may not be lost, but watching how others work can teach you about your own path.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on what Cris took from Tallinn and Helsinki: being consistent and braver about exposure
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that in Tallinn and Helsinki, Cris left with the sense that Thunder is "not really missing much." The post lists what Thunder already has: the right people, lots of experience, good work happening every day, and hard-earned lessons. What it needs, per Cris's takeaway as the post reports it, is to be more consistent and a bit braver about getting outside its usual places, to find out how far it can go and to get more exposure for its work.

Thunder's Substack describes a shift already under way. For a long time, in the community space, Thunder focused on its own culture and did not share its work, the product-building knowledge it gained, how it navigates change, or the opinions it formed. Now some people give talks, moderate discussions and meet new people, becoming more visible voices for Thunder. Andreea Popa argues this is also practice in talking about what you know, being seen, and saying yes when you don't feel completely ready. She adds that when things go well, networking and sharing feel non-urgent, but tough times are a reminder not to take good ones for granted.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on Cris's long-term dream of Thunder as a place to start projects
chunks.text: Thunder's Substack reports that while looking at the startup scenes in Tallinn and Helsinki, Cris considered a long-term dream: that one day Thunder might become a place where people not only come to work but also come to start new projects, meet other people, get mentorship, and find support while their ideas are still taking shape. The post says this dream is still far off but that Thunder is working towards it. For now, the near-term step it names is to use what Thunder has more consistently and share it with the world.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on Estonia and how success becomes permission for the next success
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that Gabi, a Thunder colleague on the trip, tends to study an ecosystem or country and "come back talking about us as people", returning "with a principle for the inside." His reflections on Estonia, as quoted in the post:

- Estonia has around 1.3 million people yet produced an extraordinary number of startups and unicorns for its size. Infrastructure, regulation and capital matter, but the story starts earlier.
- After regaining independence in 1991 it had to reinvent itself almost from scratch, and a young generation of reformers built new institutions.
- Skype became proof that something built in a tiny country could matter globally. Its first employee, Taavet Hinrikus, co-founded TransferWise (now Wise). Alumni of Skype, and later Bolt and Pipedrive, became founders, mentors and investors.
- Success creates capital and knowledge, but also confidence. "One success becomes permission for another. And over time, confidence becomes cultural."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on inner authority and difficult conversations on the trip
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes that travelling together gave the Thunder team uninterrupted time with one another, which led to some profound and at times very difficult conversations that "brought us closer" rather than creating distance. She connects them to Richard Rohr's idea of inner authority from *From Wild Man to Wise Man*.

Her reading of it: inner authority is the capacity to trust your own perception and experience without constantly needing outside validation. Without it, people look for heroes and authorities, and when those fail the projection, admiration turns quickly into judgment and resentment. Developing it does not mean being certain you are right; it means being secure enough that another person's perspective no longer threatens yours. "I can tell you honestly how I see something without requiring you to agree with me. You can challenge me without becoming my enemy."

The post says the team said hard things, heard hard things and stayed in the conversation, and that relationships deepen by discovering "that the relationship can survive truth." It contrasts two kinds of confidence: an ecosystem's cultural confidence built from successive wins, and the quieter personal confidence of no longer needing every difficult conversation to end with a winner and a loser.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on team members representing Thunder at the Festival of Thinking
chunks.text:
According to the post, a friend met in New York invited Thunder to the Festival of Thinking in Bucharest, a festival for young creative entrepreneurs with sessions, events and labs where people who have been there before can poke holes in ideas and help them grow. Cosmin joined as a mentor and gave a masterclass. Andreea Popa describes him as someone who gets involved beyond the work: speaking at events, contributing to things around Thunder, and caring about the spaces the company is part of. Cosmin said he valued meeting inspiring people and the chance to share his thoughts, noting that "having the feeling that you might have given somebody a boost of confidence is even better."

Bianca went along to capture the festival, her first time covering an event like this solo with no one to guide her. She said she gave a lot of herself while a voice asked whether it was enough, and that she is trying to do her best "while still being gentle with myself." She returned wanting to go deeper into video and writing. Deni, separately, made her first vlog-style video of the Tallinn and Helsinki trip, and Thunder's Instagram is where she shares what she sees.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on care at Thunder Home and the "time travel" closing idea
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa credits Alexandra, who joined Thunder's office, with taking care of the team: trying new recipes, cooking nutritious food, asking what people like, and putting "a little bit of herself" into what she makes. The post says the team has been "doing a little better" since she arrived.

The essay closes on its title idea. Andreea Popa argues we already time-travel through memory, revisiting and reinterpreting moments, wishing we had acted differently. We cannot change the beginning, but "we can start where we are and change the ending." Changing the course of things often needs only a decision in the present, and then fighting for it and giving it everything so it becomes the best decision we could have made. She also notes that the book on Thunder's philosophy, which began as a document about her own distance travelled, is soon to have an audio version.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa's July recap argues that Thunder is built around togetherness: bringing promising people close when paths cross, pairing newcomers so the unknown feels smaller, and caring about people beyond their role. It reports Cris's recurring reminder that "we don't have to fight our battles alone" and that he reminds her what she can do when she forgets.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on why growth starts with the people beside you
chunks.text: In a July 2026 post on The Thunder Way, Thunder's Substack, Andreea Popa argues that "we're not made to do life alone." The post says Thunder was built around that idea from the start: "building relationships that go beyond the work itself" and finding communities around the world to contribute to or join. It says the people around us make good moments better, hard ones easier to carry, and keep pushing us to grow, often without either side noticing. The post is framed as small July proofs of that idea.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on bringing in people who fit the culture, without a job posting
chunks.text: Andreea Popa describes two people who joined Thunder in July to learn, practice and "figure things out together." The post says Thunder never announced an opportunity: "We just crossed paths." Its stated approach is that when Thunder meets people who feel right for the culture it is trying to build, it doesn't like "letting the moment pass," and instead brings them closer to see what becomes possible. One was David, Iuli's brother, a student at the Technical University who came to start building his way into engineering. The other was Bianca, who studied photo and video in Timișoara, lived in Germany, and came back home looking for a place to put more of herself into the work she loves. Andreea writes that Thunder is always looking for people with "hunger, discipline, and willingness to work for the life they want."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on raising the bar for the people around you
chunks.text: Andreea Popa uses David and his sister Iuli to make a point about example-setting. David spends his days at Thunder full-time learning to become a better engineer, and also delivers food for Wolt by bike to earn extra money. The post says he already understands that the life you want later is built through the choices you make now. It credits Iuli with setting that example "probably long before either of them realized how much it mattered." She is described as ambitious, as having carried high-stakes projects, and as having repeatedly shown what it looks like to take responsibility and deliver outstanding work. Andreea writes that one of the most powerful things we can do for each other is "to live in a way that raises the bar for the people around us."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on doing new things scared, but not alone
chunks.text: The post tells how Bianca and Deni went to Linnify for a photo shoot with its team. It was new for both of them, which meant nerves, and Thunder had just brought Bianca in to help tell more of the stories happening around Thunder through visual storytelling. Deni wrote that she couldn't have done it without Bianca, who showed her things about lighting. Bianca wrote that she was convinced they would figure it out together, helped by talking beforehand about their approach, and praised Deni's ease with people, which created a relaxed atmosphere. Andreea's reading: Bianca knew her way around light and Deni around people, and "the unknown got a little smaller because neither of them had to step into it alone." She notes the messages said "Look what we did together," not "Look what I did."

chunks.heading: Bianca on her first three weeks as an intern at Thunder
chunks.text: In a section written by Bianca herself, she describes her first three weeks as a mix of peace, surprise, gratitude and some frustration. She says colleagues took the time to explain how things work, with special thanks to Deni, who she works with most closely and who answers all her questions. She reports that coming to the office gave her energy on days she wasn't feeling right, and that she can take breaks in the downstairs living room with people who "feel like a breath of fresh air" and already feel like "more than colleagues." She also names a tension: she values autonomy and independence, so balancing openness to others' opinions with feeling that her creative view counts can be hard, and adjusting to others' work pace as an intern is another hit to that. She says she is glad there is "always space to talk about these things."

chunks.heading: Andreea Popa on three years at Thunder and Cris's reminder that no one fights alone
chunks.text: Andreea marks three years at Thunder, the longest she has stayed at any company. She writes that Adi told her, three months in, that she acted like she'd been there forever, and that Thunder made belonging feel easy by welcoming "all the parts of me." She describes the 23 July all-hands in the lounge: she arrived tired after a full week, including work on the website rebrand, and people shared ordinary stories that left a mark on them. By the middle of it she wasn't tired anymore, which she says shows people can refill you just by being there, sharing and making you laugh. She is candid that the three years haven't been all easy; she overthinks and pressures herself. She writes that "as Cris always points out, we don't have to fight our battles alone," and that reaching three years made her hear that differently. She names Cris as the person "who reminds me what I'm capable of when I forget," alongside colleagues who give her energy when hers is gone. Her conclusion: "It really does take a team to build one person's dream," and the task is to notice who has carried pieces of the journey with you and let them matter.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on caring about people beyond the role that brought them in
chunks.text: Thunder hired a cook, Alexandra, a friend of Deni's who is also a singer and songwriter and wants to become a musician. Andreea writes that Thunder hopes to help her get closer to that dream while she's there, possibly through opportunities along the way or by having her perform at a future event, or something not yet thought of. She states the principle: "We want to care about the people we bring close beyond the role that brought them through the door. To know what they dream about, what they hope to build for themselves, and, whenever we can, make a little more room for those dreams to grow."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea writes that values are proven only when they are inconvenient; otherwise they are just preferences. She extends this to forgiving others who are still growing, and to choosing what you pay attention to, using David Foster Wallace's "This Is Water". It is her reflection; she only references Cris's earlier newsletter on seeing the invisible.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on values that cost something
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack essay, "We carry values, but do we let them carry weight?" (2025-06-27), Andreea Popa argues that people claim values such as honesty, empathy, loyalty and presence because they feel right, without always paying for them. She says that "real values show up when picking them feels like choosing against your ego." The essay is her own reflection, not Cris Pop's words.

chunks.heading: When a value becomes inconvenient, according to Andreea Popa
chunks.text:
Thunder's Substack argues that values only mean something once they are tested. Andreea writes that honesty is easy until it means saying something someone doesn't want to hear, kindness is easy until we're angry, and loyalty is easy until it's no longer convenient. Her test is: "If it's always easy, always convenient, maybe it's not really a value yet. Maybe it's just a preference."

She lists what living a value often looks like: taking the longer route, keeping your mouth shut when you want to win the argument, showing up for someone when you're tired, not choosing revenge when the chance is there, and making the harder choice even if it hurts a little. She adds that the choices that matter most often happen in complete solitude. She admits, in her own voice, that she caught herself being kind only when it felt easy and patient only when she wasn't in a rush, and realized she was "chasing the feeling of being good, not the weight of actually living it."

chunks.heading: Expecting more from others than we give, in Thunder's Substack
chunks.text:
In the essay, Andreea Popa points to how naturally we expect the best from people: friends who understand our silences, colleagues who read between the lines, family who know how to love us without being told. When they fall short we say "They should've known" or "If they really cared, they would have...". She asks readers to turn the question around: have I ever misunderstood or hurt someone without meaning to? She writes that most people are "doing the best we can with the emotional maps we've been handed," and those maps can be incomplete.

Her proposed shift is from "why did they fail to show up the way I needed?" to grounding questions: can I hold space for someone who is still growing, and can I accept the version of them that exists today rather than the one I wish they already were?

chunks.heading: Forgiveness as a lived value, per Andreea Popa
chunks.text: Thunder's Substack defines forgiveness not as pretending the hurt didn't happen, but as "choosing not to reduce someone to their worst moment." Andreea frames it as remembering that others, like us, are works in progress. She calls that "soft remembering" on some days "the most honest value we can live," placing forgiveness among the values that cost something.

chunks.heading: "This is water": noticing what is invisible
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa retells the parable from David Foster Wallace's commencement speech *This Is Water*: two young fish meet an older fish who asks "Morning, boys. How's the water?" and one later asks the other, "What the hell is water?" Her reading is that the most obvious, important realities are the hardest to see and talk about.

She says real awareness is about learning how to think "in the deeply human sense": choosing what to pay attention to and building meaning from your own experience. She links this to Cris, noting that Cris explored "seeing what's invisible" in the previous Thunder newsletter. This is the only place the essay references Cris. Her warning: "if you don't choose your attention, the world will choose for you," and you drift through life as if the water is something happening to you rather than something you swim through.

chunks.heading: Where values actually live, according to Thunder's Substack
chunks.text:
The essay closes by arguing that most days we forget: the traffic jam is not about us, the slow person at the pharmacy may carry a burden we'll never know, and the world is not a movie with us as the main character. Andreea writes that real life, "the true work of being human," is not achievements or goals ticked off, but "what we notice, what we choose to care about, over and over and over again."

Her conclusion is that values live "in the moments when being good costs us something and we choose it anyway." Surfacing, she says, means "not into a different life, but into a different way of living."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes a personal essay about spending three years in work that didn't fit, mistaking inaction for patience and complaint for progress. She argues people hold the pen on their own careers and should invest in skills, network, narrative and standards. Cris Pop is not mentioned; the views and anecdotes are the author's.

chunks.heading: Andreea Popa on the cost of waiting and why you should lead yourself first
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack post, Andreea Popa (writing for the Thunder team, not Cris Pop) argues that most people's careers stall because they stop acting, not because they lack options. She frames it as forgetting "we're the ones holding the pen": we can rewrite the rules and build a new world. The post is a personal essay about leadership of the self, published on The Thunder Way in July 2025, and its views are the author's, not Cris's.

chunks.heading: Popa's own story: three years of staying put
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes that she started her career in environments that valued quick results over thoughtful process, where "leadership often meant control, not care." Those places taught her to doubt her gut and silence her voice. She spent years asking whether she fit and never acted, because the discomfort was familiar and felt safe. She says that waiting cost her three years doing work that didn't mean much to her, years she could have spent growing among people who "saw more in me than what I could deliver on a deadline." Her line: "Sometimes we don't see the price of waiting until it's already been paid." She says she now writes from the career she once thought she couldn't build. This is her anecdote, not Cris's.

chunks.heading: When patience becomes inaction
chunks.text: Thunder's Substack, through Popa, argues that patience is only a virtue sometimes. Holding out for a role that fits who you are can be a form of self-respect, especially if the alternative is another draining environment. But patience can become "the story we tell ourselves to justify staying still": waiting for the right moment while avoiding the truth that you aren't moving. Popa admits she told herself she'd start searching but wasn't doing the work, just hoping the right thing would find her. Her warning is that "eventually, waiting becomes a wall."

chunks.heading: Complaining is not the same as changing
chunks.text: Popa writes that complaining without action is "another form of procrastination." Venting about jobs, managers, missing mentorship and lack of support can feel productive, but it avoids the fact that change requires risk. She describes raising feedback with her manager and getting defensiveness or personal criticism instead of effort to fix the system, then staying because known frustration felt safer than the unknown. Her diagnosis: people build lives around pain they can predict and call it patience or realism, when "really, it's fear."

chunks.heading: Lead yourself before anyone else does
chunks.text:
The post's core mindset shift, according to Popa, is moving from "Why is this happening to me?" to "What can I do about this?", focusing on what you control. She lists four areas to invest in:

- **Skills:** learn a tool, take a course, build something out of curiosity; "you don't need permission to grow."
- **Network:** connect with people in roles that interest you, ask questions, join a community, attend events.
- **Narrative:** reframe your experience around what you gained (resilience, clarity, direction) rather than what you endured.
- **Standards:** don't adjust yourself to fit every opportunity; look for the ones that fit you.

Her advice is to start with what you can carry today and let the first step be the proof you're ready.

chunks.heading: Your world is waiting: act on small steps
chunks.text: Popa closes by arguing the career you want won't arrive through perfect timing or wishing. It "will exist because you chose to create it." She says somewhere there is a team that needs what you bring, a project that could move faster with your perspective, and a problem only your mix of experience can solve, but they can't find you while you hide in a job that doesn't fit. The bridge is "built from small, consistent actions taken by someone who decided they deserved better." Her final framing is that the question is not whether you're ready but "whether you're willing."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa interviews Cosmin, a Thunder team member, about music and utopia, and draws a leadership lesson from it. She argues leadership is a balance of courage and vulnerability, not a set of techniques. It does not report anything Cris Pop said or did.

chunks.heading: Utopia as balance: Thunder's Substack on leadership as the harmony between light and darkness
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack post, Andreea Popa writes that leadership, like utopia, is "not perfect, not free of struggle, but a balance between courage and vulnerability, vision and reality, ambition and care." The post frames utopia as the balance of joy and sorrow, the ordinary and the extraordinary, rather than a distant ideal. Thunder's Substack argues leadership invites deeper questions: what it means to live authentically, how to grow into who we are meant to become, and how to find possibility in everyday moments. This is the author's reflection and an interview with her colleague Cosmin, not words from Cris Pop.

chunks.heading: Leadership as becoming "the kind of human others want to be around"
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa writes in Thunder's Substack that through emotions and the music we listen to, "we begin to see leadership differently. Not as a set of techniques to master, but as the art of becoming the kind of human others want to be around." She describes three traits of such a person:
- Someone who gives emotions permission to be real.
- Someone who finds balance between light and darkness.
- Someone who uses their passions to grow into who they're meant to become.

The post presents this as a counter to technique-driven views of leadership: the emphasis is on character and authenticity rather than methods.

chunks.heading: The leaders who stay with us are "brave enough to be human"
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes that the leaders who have truly stayed with her were the ones brave enough to be human. They helped her see possibilities she couldn't see before and made her feel she had permission to be herself. She names her colleague Cosmin as an example of this kind of leader. The Substack post positions permission to be yourself, and the ability to open up new possibilities for others, as the lasting marks of leadership, more than results or authority.

chunks.heading: "Harmony we create together": people over task
chunks.text: According to Andreea Popa, Cosmin often says he would rather do work he doesn't love with people he cares about than the other way around. She reads this as a reminder that "leadership is less about the task itself and more about the harmony we create together." Thunder's Substack uses this to argue that the quality of relationships on a team matters more than how enjoyable the work itself is.

chunks.heading: Cosmin's interview: music as emotional permission and authenticity
chunks.text: In the interview, Cosmin says music "takes your emotions and gives them permission to come into reality." He says the version of himself that listens to music the loudest is the truest, allowing him to be brave and loving, and to shed tears, which he rarely does. He adds that without music he would likely lack his confidence and his personal style, and might never have formed the purpose of "bringing light into people's lives." Thunder's Substack uses this as the basis for the first of its leadership lessons, the courage to feel authentically.

chunks.heading: Cosmin on utopia: balance, ordinary moments, and growth
chunks.text: Cosmin explains that his idea of utopia comes from Travis Scott's album *Utopia*, which treats light and darkness, happiness and suffering, as combined. He argues that laughing until you cry would be impossible "if life was only funny," and that "utopia is a balance of all things, take some steps back, you might be living it some days," such as a cozy night at home with a partner or friends. He also says music pushes him to grow: he travelled to several countries to see favorite artists live, which "forced me to be the type of person that can afford that," and he wants to become "the type of human those people would like to meet." It brings him close to believing "that anything in this life is possible."

chunks.heading: The symphony of leadership: five lessons from Cosmin's lens
chunks.text:
The Substack post summarizes Cosmin's reflections as five leadership themes, each tied to a quote:
- **The courage to feel authentically:** music gives emotions permission to become real.
- **Shaped by growth:** being pushed to become the kind of person your idols would want to meet.
- **The freedom to imagine and create:** "Music is anything you want it to be and can be used as a tool to achieve whatever you'd like."
- **Utopia in the ordinary moments:** balance of all things, possibly already lived.
- **The boundless self:** the belief that anything in this life is possible.

The post closes by asking readers whether they are listening to what this teaches about "who we could become."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Andreea Popa profiles Manu, a Thunder team member who runs marathons and Spartan races, and argues that leadership grows from practicing self-leadership, not from holding a title. She draws lessons from Manu's answers: keep a plan, push a little further, lift others, believe in yourself, and treat every finish line as a start. The post does not report anything Cris said or did.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack: leadership starts with leading yourself
chunks.text: In a Thunder Substack post on The Thunder Way (published 2025-09-05), Andreea Popa argues that "we develop leadership not by holding a title, but by practicing the activities that teach us to lead ourselves." The post is written by Andreea Popa of the Thunder team, not by Cris Pop. It profiles Manu, a Thunder team member who is also a runner and Spartan race competitor, as an example of "quiet leadership that inspires growth." Her approach to code, collaboration and races is presented as one way of moving through challenges: excellence as a habit, not a single act.

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on discipline: have a plan and stick to it
chunks.text: Thunder's Substack post "We develop leadership by learning to lead ourselves" shares Manu's discipline practice, in her words. Her "secret is having a plan": when she sets a goal, she creates a plan and sticks to it. "Rain, snow, or scorching heat doesn't matter, if I've scheduled four runs in a week, I complete them." She adds a personal rule: never skip more than two consecutive days. In her words, "the voice saying 'not today' disappears because there are no excuses." Andreea Popa frames this as showing up regardless of conditions, mood or excuses, and as the way discipline becomes freedom: "progress is built step by step."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on pushing past perceived limits
chunks.text: The post's Q&A with Manu covers the biggest mental barrier she has faced. She describes moments in training and races when she felt she could not go any further. Her lesson: "when you feel like you can't, you actually can go a little more. Our bodies are stronger than we think, and our minds just need a small push to keep moving." Andreea Popa lists this as the first of six elements of leadership in the post: "the courage to take one more step." Her message to her younger self is "Believe in yourself, you're capable of more than you imagine," which the post calls "the belief that shapes all other beliefs."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on community over competition
chunks.text: Manu describes her first Spartan race as full of emotion and uncertainty. She had trail-running experience, but Spartan races differ because "it's not just about you; it's about community." After racing in her own country and abroad, she now sees them as a team experience, where people offer encouragement or "a hand over a difficult wall." Her words: "Nobody competes against each other; we all share the same goal: to finish the race together." Andreea Popa treats this as the post's version of true strength, which "lives in lifting others up." The post concludes that leaders practice "lifting others as we climb."

chunks.heading: Thunder's Substack on endings as beginnings (the infinite mindset)
chunks.text: Asked how she avoids feeling low after a big goal such as a marathon, Manu explains that she has never felt discouraged after reaching one, because there is always something to improve: a longer distance or a faster time. Last year she ran her first half marathon, and then decided to aim for a full marathon. "Every achievement opens the door to a new challenge." Her closing advice: "There's no finish line for ambition. Every goal you reach is just the beginning of the next challenge. Enjoy the journey, the progress, and the person you're becoming with every step you take." Andreea Popa calls this "the infinite mindset where endings become beginnings" and "the continuous act of becoming." The post's subtitle is "Every finish line is simply the start of a new journey."

chunks.heading: The six-part summary of leadership in the post
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa distills Manu's story into six elements of "leadership distilled to its essence":
- The courage to take one more step.
- The commitment to show up regardless of conditions, mood or excuses.
- True strength that lives in lifting others up.
- The belief that shapes all other beliefs: believing in yourself.
- The infinite mindset, where endings become beginnings.
- The continuous act of becoming.

Her conclusion is that these practices, "showing up when it's hard, pushing a little further than we think we can, lifting others as we climb, and seeing every ending as the start of something new", are the steps that "turn discipline into freedom and action into quiet, lasting leadership."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The opening chapter argues that leadership is not a title or authority but ownership: taking responsibility for who you are and where you are going. Andreea Popa recounts that Cris handed her Jocko Willink's Leadership Strategies and Tactics, which reframed leadership for her. She then argues leaders act where they are, grounded in humility, courage and honesty.

chunks.heading: Leadership as ownership: the chapter's core definition
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, "Leadership Before It Has a Name" (written by Andreea Popa, coordinated by Cris Pop), opens by arguing that "leadership is not a title, nor is it about authority. Leadership is about ownership." The chapter defines it as taking responsibility for who you are and where you are going. Its image is a ship. Leadership means leading your ship, and ownership means owning it. "Not everyone will sail with you. Some will come aboard. Some won't. But the journey? That's yours to command."

The book builds Thunder's philosophy on this base. Leadership is not a position that someone grants, and it does not depend on having a role.

chunks.heading: Lead yourself first: how Andreea Popa came to this view
chunks.text:
Andreea Popa, the book's author, tells how she reached this idea. This is her own story, not Cris's.

- She began as a creative writer and ended up in leadership roles in tech, where she never felt at home.
- She had never seen leadership that inspired her to follow. Her attempts to bring "humanity, empathy, and understanding" were mistaken for weakness.
- She left, and at a later job she found leaders who cared. But "big bosses" who insisted on controlling everything meant she would "never be fully understood."
- About three months into her time at Thunder, "leadership found me." She watched people who "cared," "served," "thought bigger" and "moved with purpose." She saw that the software work was only part of the story.

Cris is the only action the chapter credits to him. He gave her *Leadership Strategies and Tactics* by Jocko Willink, which she says "rewired" her. From it she took what she calls the secret of leadership: "lead yourself first. Then, and only then, can you lead others." She notes that people are taught to perform before they are taught to be, and to lead others before they have met themselves. She started with self-reflection, and she found that this gave her better ways to lead others.

chunks.heading: A self-check: what do you feel when you think of yourself as a leader?
chunks.text:
The book asks the reader to close their eyes and think of themselves as a leader. It lists four feelings:

- Courage, "the kind that makes your heart race because you know you're about to do something that matters."
- Joy, the lightness of knowing you might help someone or change something.
- Fear, the honest kind: that you're not ready, that you'll mess up, that people are counting on you.
- Craziness, the recognition that you will take responsibility for things, people and outcomes you can't control.

The chapter argues that feeling all of these together means you are ready. Leadership "isn't clean or comfortable. It's not a steady state. It's a constant dance with uncertainty," and courage comes "not from having answers but from staying in the dance anyway."

It also says who the book is not for. If you see leadership as holding a role, making the calls and getting "more money, more status, more control," then "this conversation isn't for you," unless you let it change your perspective entirely. Leadership is "the human you become when you realize that someone needs to care this much."

chunks.heading: Why you: care as the reason to lead
chunks.text:
The book argues that people lead because they care, and that this care has a price: "Time. Energy. Comfort. Certainty." What it gives back is "Connection. Meaning. A glimpse of what's possible when people choose courage over convenience."

The chapter lists why someone chooses to lead:

- Something in them refuses to wait.
- Pretending not to care would feel like betrayal.
- They felt the weight of injustice and couldn't look away.
- Someone once believed in them, and now they carry that forward.

Leaders are described as "flawed, unsure, and still showing up." Leadership is "yours to do. Even if that doesn't come with a title or a role." The chapter says that when systems are stuck you move anyway, when the room goes quiet you show the way, and when doubt sets in you return to your why. Its line: "real leadership doesn't begin when you're ready. It begins when you're needed."

chunks.heading: Where and when: start now, start where you are
chunks.text:
The book argues that leadership starts here and now, not "someday, not somewhere else." It asks: "If not here, where? If not you, who? If not now, when?"

Its points on permission and readiness:

- Permission is something you give yourself "when you decide to try, to fail, to grow anyway."
- "Polish comes later, and honestly, it matters less than presence."
- Waiting makes the leap feel further away.
- You can trust that your essence is already enough, that your clarity is already disruptive and that shaky courage is still courage.

The chapter adds that you "don't have to save everything. But you do have to start something." Its picture of a leader is not someone born extraordinary but someone who thinks, "If something must change, let it begin with me."

chunks.heading: How: humility, courage and honesty
chunks.text:
The book answers "how" with three qualities, "humility," "courage" and "deep, uncomfortable honesty." It sets them against the usual image of the leader as a charismatic, certain, controlling visionary who never doubts. It calls that image "incomplete. Sometimes, dangerously so."

- **Humility** is "the kind of quiet strength that listens, that seeks to understand, that carries others on the shoulders to the top, and that leads with a grateful heart." The chapter says this is what gives leadership its moral weight.
- **Courage** means keeping your heart open when cynicism would be safer, telling the truth even if it disturbs something, and choosing "the long road over the quick win."
- **Honesty** means risking being misunderstood to stay true to your values. It opens the door for others to be real too. The chapter's reason: "without honesty, trust cannot live."

None of this happens in one defining act. It happens "in a thousand small choices. One moment at a time." Leaders do not pretend to be invulnerable. They reveal their humanity and make it safe for others to reveal theirs, and they keep showing up "even when it's thankless... Especially then."

The chapter closes with its thesis: "leadership is not a role. It's how you approach life. And who you become is ultimately how you lead."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues leadership is built through self-reflection, purpose, daily action and small acts of care, not inherited or mystical. It reports Cris's formula Confidence = Certainty + Faith, his habit of living one idea deeply, and Thunder's commitment to build, fail, learn and rebuild without waiting for permission.

chunks.heading: Leadership is built, not born: the premise of Thunder's leadership book
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, "Leadership Before It Has a Name" (2025), opens its chapter "The Foundation" by telling readers to discard clichés about being born a leader, management-book bullet points, and the idea of a mystical leadership factor. The chapter argues that leadership is something you build. It is "shaped in your collaboration, sharpened in your humility, and strengthened in your quiet work of showing up again and again." It is born "in the small spaces where you decide to care enough to act."

The evidence it offers is ordinary: someone with no title and no "leadership gene" steps up when no one else will. The chapter concludes that leadership is available to anyone willing to do the work. It closes the same way, with a "Keep digging" image. Leadership accumulates "like dust, decision by decision." There is no exact day you become a leader. You dig each time you choose the harder conversation, admit you don't know but commit to finding out, or stay when others leave. What you uncover is not hidden talent but "your capacity to care about something bigger than yourself." Leadership is "something you do, again and again, until doing it becomes who you are."

chunks.heading: Self-leadership and purpose before frameworks, per Thunder's leadership book
chunks.text:
The book argues that leadership starts with the question "Who's leading your life?" If you don't decide who you want to be, your past, your habits, fear or ego will decide for you. The chapter asks readers to reflect on:
- who they are at their core
- what shaped them
- what matters to them
- what they avoid
- what they stand for when the world isn't looking
- how they will pay it forward

It calls purpose the step people keep skipping, "overused... but strangely, still... underlived." The chapter says to ask why you are leading, beyond the company mission or team goal. It also asks what leadership gives shape to inside you, what you are trying to prove, protect or heal, and who you hope to become. People who chase execution before intention end up in roles that empty them. In the chapter's words, "Leadership without purpose is not quite leadership. It's more like performance," and performance burns you out before it fulfills you.

chunks.heading: Cris's formula for self-trust: Confidence = Certainty + Faith
chunks.text:
The chapter argues against hovering over a process. Monitoring every step is not care, and the more you control a process, the more you lose what makes it powerful. It reframes "Do you trust the process?" as "Do you trust yourself enough to let the process work without your constant supervision?" The author, Andreea Popa, writes that self-trust rests on three things: what you know, what you can do, and what results you have achieved and can achieve again.

At one talk, Cris shared the formula "Confidence = Certainty + Faith."
- Certainty comes from looking back at accomplishments, the wins that prove you can trust yourself.
- Faith comes from looking forward, believing in your potential before there is proof.

The book names negative self-talk as what kills self-trust, because it erases your wins. Its fix is to catch the thought and add "BUT": "I'm not good at this, but I did X before, and I can learn." The word is the bridge "from doubt to possibility."

chunks.heading: Extracting growth from setbacks and living one idea deeply
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book says people who eventually lead differ from those who stay stuck by asking two questions: "What's in it for me?" and "What can I learn from this?" After a failed project or meaningless work, future leaders "flip into extraction mode." They ask what pattern they are missing, how to do better next time, and what the experience is teaching them. Most people treat setbacks as bad weather. In the chapter's framing, every book becomes a mirror, every failure a teacher, and every success data on what works.

The chapter says Cris has a habit of sitting with an idea until it transforms him. He reads one book ten times and replays the same podcast episode again and again, instead of chasing the next big thing. The book turns this into a four-step practice:
1. Choose one powerful idea that fits your current leadership challenge.
2. Ask how it applies now, where you are resisting it, what would change if you acted on it today, and who you would become if you embodied it.
3. Take one small action daily based on it.
4. Teach it to someone else.

The chapter's line is: "Most people are drowning in insights but starving for integration."

chunks.heading: Break the old playbook and write your own rules
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that the old management playbook has expired. It cites managers running meetings "like it's 2010," executives who think digital transformation means buying software, and leaders who measure hours instead of impact. It names remote work, AI and Gen Z's different expectations as changes already here. The authors recount Thunder's commitment when it launched its first tool: "We're going to build, fail, learn, and rebuild until we create something that changes lives. We won't wait for permission, perfect conditions, or complete information." Readers are asked which assumptions, methods and comfort zones no longer serve them.

The book also sorts the rules governing your life into three types:
- **Moral rules (what you must keep):** the ones that shape integrity and how you treat others.
- **Intentional rules (what you choose to keep):** the ones you create to move toward your vision.
- **Limiting rules (what you need to break):** unspoken expectations such as "Don't ask for more than you deserve," "Don't challenge people above you," "Don't start before you're ready," and "Don't show your flaws."

Limiting rules show up as hesitation: not speaking in meetings, not applying, not starting. The test is to ask "Which rule am I following right now?"

chunks.heading: Kindness without reason, and excellence beyond the minimum
chunks.text:
The book argues for being good to people "for no reason at all." It says that if kindness is treated as currency or reciprocity, it is not leadership. It asks leaders to give kindness "like air," like a lighthouse that shines without asking who deserves it. In the chapter's words, "if your leadership requires a reason to be kind, it isn't leadership but rather performance."

In "The minimum is crowded," the chapter argues that in every project you choose between what is expected and what is right. Leaders care about the work because they care about the impact and the people behind the tasks. Half-hearted effort creates half-hearted results and then half-hearted teams. Mediocrity spreads, but so does excellence. Before submitting work, the chapter suggests asking: "What am I capable of that I'm not giving? What would make this matter more?"

chunks.heading: Noticing, and culture built by example at Thunder
chunks.text:
The book says culture does not come from rules or posters but from people who lead by example. A leader's job is "not to have all the answers" but to hold the vision, protect the values and model what matters most. It gives Thunder examples of unassigned leadership:
- Anda noticed the Instagram links page needed clarity. She reorganized it into thoughtful categories without being asked.
- Deni started cooking lunches to bring people together, which grew into a quiet tradition.
- Colleagues give up their birthday gifts to support a cause.

The chapter says this happens constantly at Thunder: someone spots a problem early, improves a process unprompted or offers help before it is requested. "No one assigned them these roles... The rest of us followed."

It asks leaders to become "a detective of the human experience." That means noticing small changes, such as a quiet teammate who now offers three insights per meeting instead of one, or a collaborator whose replies slowed from hours to two days. It also suggests asking:
- what invisible behaviors shape culture more than words do
- who is quietly leading without a title and how to amplify them
- what moment of kindness or courage to acknowledge before the day ends

chunks.heading: Why Thunder was built, and the invisible backpack
chunks.text:
The chapter says Thunder was built because its founders heard a call that "the game itself is broken." It names hierarchies that crush creativity, metrics that measure motion instead of meaning, and cultures that reward conformity over courage. Its stance is "We're not here to climb someone else's ladder. We're here to build bridges to places that don't exist yet." It gathers people who stop asking permission and start taking responsibility, and who understand that "true power comes from empowering others."

A section on gratitude argues that leaders get to prove "high performance and deep care multiply each other" and that command-and-control leadership is crumbling. Grateful leaders see broken systems as opportunities and frustrated colleagues as people "waiting to be unleashed."

The chapter ends with a story of a teacher and an "invisible backpack" of beliefs. A student asks whether things can be taken out, and the teacher answers, "Yes, but you have to notice what's inside first." The book's lesson is to take inventory, own your shadows and choose your burdens with intention. It says the leaders we need "are not perfect," but are brave enough to unpack, face themselves and keep walking.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that true inner fire is the quiet flame of responsibility, not magnetic passion: a decision to own outcomes regardless of motivation. Andreea Popa describes going first, quiet care, claiming what is "mine to take care of", trusting people, and owning your shadows. It reports that Cris told the team in a growth meeting they were "waiting to be told what to do", sparking a shift to ownership, illustrated by Cosmin's story.

chunks.heading: Inner fire as the quiet flame of responsibility, not passion
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, in its chapter "The Inner Fire", argues that inner fire is usually mistaken for passion, "that magnetic spark that draws followers". The chapter says that kind of fire "burns hot, and it burns out fast." It defines true inner fire as "the quiet flame of responsibility": showing up consistently when you least want to, owning outcomes, and carrying weight others won't bear.

The chapter argues this fire comes from a decision to take ownership. Ownership "doesn't wait for motivation" and "carries the mission even when you barely believe in it." Once a leader has done the inner work of building a foundation, ownership shows in how they move, how they respond under pressure, and in people trusting them "with things that actually matter."

chunks.heading: "I'll go first": leadership as vulnerability before certainty
chunks.text:
The book argues that leadership happens when everyone waits for someone else to speak up, try something, or admit they don't have it figured out. "I'll go first" is described as small to say but heavy to do. It means being vulnerable before others are brave enough, saying "I was wrong" so others know it's safe to be wrong, and trying something new so people know experimenting is allowed.

The chapter's points on readiness and courage:
- Readiness is "a myth we made up to avoid jumping in."
- Nobody knows enough, and "we figure it out as we go."
- Courage is "fear with its walking shoes on."
- Going first is not about certainty but "lighting the path so others feel brave enough to follow."

The practical move is to say "Here's my thought . . . but I'd love to hear yours." The book says this gives people "permission to be human": safe to try, to stumble and to figure it out together.

chunks.heading: Quiet leadership: care, presence and taking the blame
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book argues that leadership used to mean being the loudest voice in the room and now feels "quieter, softer." It is less about proving you're in charge and more about making sure people feel cared for. The chapter gives concrete examples:
- Saying "I could have been clearer about that" instead of "You should have understood."
- Spending extra time fixing something nobody will notice so someone else doesn't stumble over it tomorrow.
- Asking "What part of this is mine to carry?" without waiting to be handed responsibility.
- Giving space to a strong person having a hard day, without making a scene.
- Saying "I've got bandwidth for that" when someone is drowning.
- Saying "That's my mistake," even when it's not technically yours, because "taking responsibility moves things forward, and pointing fingers just keeps us stuck."

The chapter describes this as leadership that "sits beside you". The question it offers is "What would make this easier for you?" in place of "Why isn't this done yet?"

chunks.heading: "This is mine to take care of": claiming what nobody owns
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that "when everything belongs to nobody, nothing gets cared for." It says people have been trained to say "Not my problem" and have forgotten the "revolutionary act" of saying "This is my responsibility." It treats the inner voice that says "Somebody should do something about this" as a sign that the somebody is you.

The book calls this "the underground work of leadership": people claiming responsibility for things nobody else wants, and saying "mine" to what has been abandoned. It argues that the deepest ownership comes "not from having but from being claimed by something worth saving." It ends with the question "What's yours to take care of?"

chunks.heading: "I trust you": how ownership starts
chunks.text:
The book argues that ownership is not really a skill to be coached and measured. It says ownership happens when someone stops micromanaging your potential and says "I trust you". The person then realizes "I'm not working for them, I'm building with them."

The chapter calls this trust abnormal and unsafe in most workplaces. It says trust given before results is what makes people "stop executing and start owning," because they feel seen. It closes the section with the practice of saying "We trust you" to someone who doesn't expect it, and meaning it.

chunks.heading: Owning your shadows: "the part of me I'm still working on"
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book argues that ownership also applies to oneself. It calls this "shadow work" rather than a leadership course, and says "what you don't own will eventually own you." Its examples:
- The fear you won't name makes your decisions for you.
- The discomfort you avoid shapes the culture.
- The struggle you never made peace with "is still running the show."

The chapter argues that saying "this is the part of me I'm still working on" can feel like weakness. It says this is the only way to lead without "contaminating everything you touch with unresolved baggage" and the only way to build something that "won't rot from the inside out." It also says the admission doesn't disqualify a leader: "It's the reason I can." Owning your own shadows makes space for others to own theirs. The chapter links this to the next chapter's theme of dropping polish worn "like armor."

chunks.heading: Story: the growth meeting where Thunder chose ownership, and Cosmin's interview
chunks.text:
In the chapter's closing story, the author (Andreea Popa) recalls a growth meeting about "who we were becoming." Cris told the team: "We're not owning our work. We're just waiting to be told what to do." The team had been defaulting to Cris or Adi for decisions they should have made themselves. They had the skills but were waiting for permission. The author calls it their "Matrix moment" (red pill or blue pill) and says the team chose the red pill. It was messy at first and people still slipped into old habits. One person showing up differently inspired another, and the ownership mindset grew bit by bit.

The chapter then describes a test during a hard stretch of winning projects, when some projects were ending, others were just starting, and the dev team was putting in extra hours preparing for interviews and technical challenges. Cosmin told the author he was ready and would "rock the interview", but he didn't get the project. He didn't defend himself or blame the process. He kept working on what had held him back. Months later he was chosen for another opportunity, even though the other candidate had more technical expertise.

The feedback he received said the other candidate was "the most qualified on resume" but the person choosing would go with Cosmin: "His message is what I look for in a team. Someone who cares and has the willingness to learn with me as a partner." The chapter's lesson is that ownership "might not guarantee you win today, but it shapes the person who will win tomorrow." It adds that what people bring as humans can matter even more than what they bring as experts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that the leader's wall of hidden feelings is defensive armor that makes leaders unreachable, while real mental toughness protects values and stays open to connection. It offers practices for the inner voice, flexibility, fear and recovery, and tells Thunder's story of hitting 2 RON in the account, where it reports Cris carried four projects alone while Adi knocked on every door.

chunks.heading: Thunder's leadership book on why defensive armor fails and protective armor works
chunks.text:
In "The Armor," Thunder's leadership book (written by Andreea Popa, coordinated by Cris Pop) argues that leaders are expected to wear armor that hides feelings, masks doubt and never lets them fail visibly. The chapter calls this a defensive armor "designed to protect your image." Its logic is that "if nothing gets in, nothing real gets out either," so the leader becomes unreachable, and "unreachable leaders don't inspire."

The book proposes a different armor, one that safeguards your values while keeping you open to connection. It defines mental toughness as "your ability to stay grounded when life gets chaotic." Toughness doesn't remove challenges. It gives you the strength to move through them "without losing who you are." The chapter closes with a toolkit for building this resilience.

chunks.heading: The book on rewriting your self-story and training your inner voice
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that the story you tell yourself about who you are shapes everything. People often tell themselves they are weak, unlucky or undeserving, and the mind then collects evidence for that story. The book's answer is to rewrite it by collecting counter-evidence: search for the moments you truly succeeded, the small wins and the times you refused to quit. It treats every challenge as a test and every setback as "a vote for resilience." If you forget your strength, it says to look to the people who have seen you at your worst and still believe in your best.

It also argues that the toughest battles are fought in your head, and that most people never train their inner voice. They let it replay failure on a loop and mistake it for truth. The book says to build a voice that can hold pressure:
- "Yes, this is hard, but you've done hard things before."
- "This is not the end; it's feedback."
- "You've got more in the tank; now prove it."

The goal is a voice that is "honest, but never cruel" and that is on your side.

chunks.heading: The book's quiet strength: the tree, the water and the ice
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that strength is not only fighting back harder. It uses the image of a tree in a storm: the tree that survives bends with the wind but keeps its roots deep. The book lists what this strength looks like:
- Staying calm when everyone else panics.
- Being kind to people who aren't kind to you.
- Not needing to win every argument.
- Taking care of yourself quietly.
- Listening more than you speak.
- Being there for people who can't pay you back.

It argues that our culture celebrates "never give up, fight harder" and so overlooks people with an internal shelter no one can see.

On the mind, the chapter contrasts an attached mind, "like ice," frozen in one shape, with a free mind, "like water," which adapts and flows around problems. Gripping plans and beliefs, replaying old conversations or worrying about outcomes you can't control keeps you in "a mental time machine." The book says a mind that is "nowhere" can still plan and want things without being a prisoner to them, and is ready for the present.

chunks.heading: The book on fear, recovery and choosing hard things
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book argues that fear is not a signal to stop. It shows up "at the edges of growth," before the hard conversation, the job change or the launch. The chapter says fear means "you're standing exactly where your life is ready to change." Its advice is to get curious about what the fear is telling you and which old pattern it asks you to release, then notice it, feel it and move forward anyway.

On setbacks, it rejects the idea of "bouncing back." Recovery is "not a rewind button. It's a rebuild." After a hard fall you become a different person, with a new normal that includes resting more, saying no more and letting go of old chases. The chapter's line is: "You're not returning. You're becoming."

It then argues for choosing discomfort on purpose. Comfort "kills your drive," and confidence and strength must be earned by doing hard things. Its conclusion is that self-mastery, mental toughness, ownership and purpose are how discipline is built and how leaders are made.

chunks.heading: Thunder's near-collapse: the "2 RON" story in the book
chunks.text:
The chapter tells a story from Thunder's own history. After a peak, when business was thriving and projects were rolling in, the book says everything began to unravel over eight months:
- Thunder lost partnerships it believed in most, ones that had stood for years.
- Its decision to give back more to the community split the room. Some potential collaborators welcomed the civic work and others did not, and "many still aren't" on board. The book says this was because Thunder "dared to break the mold."
- Projects ended abruptly, new ones were nearly impossible to find, and salaries kept going out while income stopped.

The breaking point was "2 RON left in the account." The book says that for most, this would be the time to quit or "even fire a few people (because that's the trend these days)." Instead, "for Cris and Adi, and for all of us," it was the start of something. The team had tried to prepare, having talked openly that the mission could backfire, but the book says preparation only goes so far.

chunks.heading: How Cris, Adi and the team responded, according to the book
chunks.text:
The book says two things were clear even at the lowest point. Looking back, the team was grateful for every struggle, failure, win and person who stood by them, and the journey was "about memories and moments" rather than business. Looking forward, "we still had one another," so they could start again even from nothing.

The chapter describes what each person did:
- Cris went out and created opportunities. He carried four projects on his shoulders alone, pushing forward "when every instinct screamed to give up."
- Adi knocked on every door and reached out to every contact until doors opened, while working on the projects he had taken on.
- Every other team member doubled down on their own growth, "investing more in ourselves than ever before."

The chapter presents this as what leadership looks like in the hardest moments: "When everything inside you wants to say stop, true leaders find a way to say go." It adds that the aim was to pull themselves out so they would never be caught in that place again.

chunks.heading: The book's three options at a wall, and its tools for mental toughness
chunks.text:
The chapter says that when you hit a wall you have three options: back down, break down or break through. It argues the truth is more complex than "always break through." Sometimes backing down is right, from a wrong path or something chased for the wrong reasons, and that "is growth." Sometimes breaking down is needed, to understand what you're made of. The book says "the danger is in staying there," and that what matters is what comes after. To build something meaningful you will eventually need to break through, and to get back up for the people who believe in you and for the mission.

The chapter ends with five tools:
- **Pre-decided practice:** choose in advance how you will respond to a kind of adversity. For example, when overwhelmed, take three deep breaths and respond with clarity. If you are rejected or lose a project, let it hurt, then reengage within twenty-four hours.
- **Reverse visualization:** imagine loss or collapse to strip away illusion, asking each morning or evening, "What if I lost everything I take for granted today?"
- **One move past breakdown:** at your edge, do one more thing, such as one rep, one sentence, one breath or one step.
- **Neutral observation:** witness thoughts and emotions without calling them good or bad, for example by saying "This is frustration. This is heat in the chest."
- **Shadow contact:** once a week, confront on purpose something that triggers fear, shame or insecurity. It can be emotional, physical or social.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that motivation is a feeling that vanishes when life gets heavy, and that leaders are built on discipline, which shows up regardless. Andreea Popa writes that discipline needs a settled nervous system, fewer commitments, goals that are truly your own, and pre-made decisions. It closes with Manu's running story. The chapter does not attribute specific statements or actions to Cris.

chunks.heading: Discipline as a system, not a feeling
chunks.text: "Leadership Before It Has a Name," Thunder's leadership book (written by Andreea Popa, coordinated by Cris Pop), argues in its chapter "The Weapon" that motivation is the wrong foundation for leadership. Motivation is a feeling, and feelings "vanish the moment life gets heavy." The chapter says most people lose here because they are "addicted to feeling ready," not because they lack capability. Leaders, it argues, are built on discipline: doing what needs to be done whether they feel like it or not. The chapter's advice is to stop waiting for inspiration, build systems that work regardless of mood, and follow them "whether you want to or not."

chunks.heading: Safety before discipline: you can't build on shaking ground
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that people have discipline backwards. They treat it as force: push harder, fight resistance. But the body "responds to safety," not force. Under stress or anxiety, the nervous system goes into survival mode, and a system in survival mode cannot build habits. It can only protect itself. Layering discipline on top of chaos leads to starting strong and then burning out. The book's point is that this isn't a personal flaw. The person needs "less chaos," not more discipline.

Its suggested checks are three deep breaths, a walk, permission to rest without guilt, or acknowledging that you are safe in this moment. Once the system settles, discipline becomes "a conversation you have with yourself" and stops being a fight.

**Practice from the book:** when you miss the mark, pause and ask what support your body needs. Meet that need first, then try again from a stronger foundation.

chunks.heading: Discipline as subtraction: less becomes light
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book argues that discipline is not about adding more habits, goals and systems, such as the 5:00 a.m. routine of meditating, working out, journaling, reading and networking. It compares this to curating "the perfect Instagram feed of productivity," and to scrolling a feed where everything competes for attention at once and leaves you overstimulated and still empty. The chapter says that "every yes you give is a piece of your energy you're lending out." Lend out too many pieces to things that don't matter, and nothing is left for the things that make you feel alive.

**Practice from the book:**
- Once a month, list everything you give your time, energy and attention to.
- Circle what truly nourishes you and cross out the rest.
- Let go of at least one item that month and reinvest the freed time in what matters.

chunks.heading: Don't borrow someone else's goals
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that much of what people chase is borrowed: a morning routine from a podcast, productivity hacks from a followed entrepreneur, even the career path, lifestyle and definition of success. The author suspects that at least half of most people's current goals are not really theirs. The chapter claims the nervous system senses the gap between performing and being, and eventually stops cooperating. It calls this the "internal weapon," a deepest sense of truth that protects you from a life that doesn't belong to you.

**Practice from the book:** audit your goals, drop the expectations you inherited but never agreed to, and listen for what is actually yours, "even if it's less impressive on paper."

chunks.heading: Make it matter at the level of identity
chunks.text:
The book argues that when something matters at the level of identity, it stops feeling like a chore. Its test question is: "Why does this matter to me more than comfort? More than distraction? More than staying the same?" If you can't answer, the chapter says not to force action but to dig until you find a reason that anchors you for a lifetime, not just for a day. Once the reason is found, the ritual is easy: the same time, the same place, the same small ceremony to begin. Discipline then becomes something you honor instead of something you endure.

The author gives a personal example: leadership may become less about having a role and more about starting the day with something that belongs only to you. She also admits that the writing-as-conversation-with-yourself reminder is one she still needs.

**Practice from the book:** before starting, ask "How do I make this meaningful enough that I want to do it?"

chunks.heading: Protecting mental energy: time-boxing and pre-decided reactions
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that discipline feels impossible because the brain has spent its energy on small, unnoticed decisions (what to wear, what to eat, whether to work out now or later, whether to check a message). All of these draw on "the same mental energy account," so by the time the hard, meaningful work arrives, you are "mentally bankrupt."

The book's two practices:
- **Time-box the non-negotiables.** Decide once when the work happens and repeat it daily, instead of asking each day. The author's own schedule: creative work from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. every weekday, with a 10-minute break after each hour and no exceptions, then smaller tasks afterward.
- **Pre-decide reactions ("If X happens, I do Y").** Examples: if the phone rings during deep work, check it during the ten-minute break. If you don't feel like working out, do five minutes first before deciding.

chunks.heading: Story: Manu and running toward who you're meant to become
chunks.text:
The chapter closes with a story about Manu, who is drawn to running competitions and Spartan-style obstacle races. It began in college as a way to relieve stress and became a ritual of reconnecting with her body. The author asked her what keeps her moving, and Manu gave two pieces of wisdom:

- **"Never skip more than two consecutive days."** The chapter reads it this way: one missed day means the body needed rest, two means life happened, and three is "where dreams go to die."
- **"When you feel like you can't, you actually can go a little more."** The chapter reads the urge to quit as the mind's "first negotiation," while the body still has fuel and capacity.

The book draws the lesson that discipline is "loving yourself enough to show up, even when you don't want to," making space for humanity while refusing to let comfort become a prison. It says discipline is built in "the stumbles and the comebacks," not in perfection from day one, and that every time you push past the voice saying "enough," "you're not just training your body, you're training your life."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that vision is relational, not a blueprint: a leader carries it rather than owns it, leaves it open for others to shape, and proves it through daily action until it lives on without them. Andreea Popa reports that Cris hires for resonance with what Thunder is building, asking about who someone is more than what they can do technically, and says the vision belongs to everyone.

chunks.heading: Vision as something lived, not announced
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book (chapter "The Vision") argues that most leaders try to speak their vision before they have lived it, treating it as a blueprint or a clean statement. People do not follow words or a nicely designed plan; they stay because of resonance, and "resonance can't be faked." The chapter frames vision as relational: you do not hold it over others, you invite them in. If it truly lives, it will outgrow the leader, so the job becomes holding it lightly and walking it humbly rather than controlling it. Vision, the book says, "has always been a frequency you learn to live at until others can hear it, too."

chunks.heading: The leader as messenger, not owner
chunks.text: The chapter argues that the visions that matter belong to no one. A leader is "a messenger," carrying something that was already trying to happen. Great movements may start with one person but only become real when others help shape them. This changes how a leader leads: you are not convincing people to follow your plan, you are inviting them to witness how moved you are by what you carry, and letting them contribute. The book asks leaders to hold the vision with integrity, make space for other voices, and walk it daily in their choices and priorities. The more a leader serves the vision rather than using it to serve themselves, the more faithfully it moves through them to others.

chunks.heading: Vision should show people their place in the story
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book argues that vision is not just a picture of a destination to pump people up. Visions that work help people see themselves inside it, answering the quiet question "Do I matter here?" The chapter contrasts "We want to grow our business" with "You are the reason we're able to grow": one is a statement, the other tells people why they matter to the story. People want to be part of something bigger, but also to know their specific chapter is essential and that the story wouldn't work without what they uniquely bring. When they feel that, they stop working for something and start building it with you.

chunks.heading: Keep the vision an open canvas
chunks.text: The book argues that a vision should never be finished or polished. A vision that is too complete is hard to breathe in: it may be clear and impressive, but it leaves no room for new voices or for real life to unfold. A better vision is an open canvas, a beginning waiting for other hands. Its essence is not how much it defines but how much it can hold, above all people, with their change, creativity and courage to show up differently. The chapter's practical advice: "leave space. Write in pencil. Create margins where others can dream."

chunks.heading: The test of a vision: it keeps moving when the leader is absent
chunks.text: The chapter argues that a vision is working when it keeps moving even when the person who started it isn't in the room. That requires trust, clarity and shared ownership from the beginning. The leader doesn't need to obsess over details; they need people to understand what matters most, so they know how to move and feel confident doing so in real decisions. This takes presence: listening, sitting with people when they're stuck, asking meaningful questions, and letting them run with parts of the mission and feel the weight of it. If people aren't stepping up, the book says, that is not about them; it signals the vision isn't clear enough or hasn't reached their hands. A leader still steers the ship, but if only one person touches the wheel, no one else learns to navigate. If the vision lives on in others, "you led in a way that mattered."

chunks.heading: Make the vision touch the ground every day
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book argues that "a vision dies in the clouds if it never touches the ground." Its prescription is to pick one daily act that embodies the vision so clearly it can't be ignored, and keep doing it until people know you mean it. Examples given: if the vision is connection, look someone in the eye every day and make them feel they belong; if it is transformation, take one daily step that terrifies the old you; if it is service, leave one person better each day. A vision you don't walk daily is "just a story you tell," and a leader who doesn't work for their vision won't make others believe in it.
