chunks.heading: How Cris carries the vision at Thunder: hiring for resonance
chunks.text: In the chapter's closing story, Andreea Popa writes about watching how Cris Pop handles vision. Most leaders announce it once and hope it is remembered; she says Cris treats it as something living that needs to be nurtured and protected. Her example is hiring. She describes hearing that Cris spends far more time in hiring conversations asking who someone is as a human being than what they can do technically: what drives them, what they believe in, where they see themselves growing. Andreea says she first wondered whether the focus should be on whether a candidate can do the job, then realized Cris is looking for people who already resonate with what Thunder is building. Systems, tools and methods can be taught, she writes, but you cannot teach someone to care about building genuine community or to be excited about showing up to events and connecting with people.

chunks.heading: Protecting the vision means people who make it more itself
chunks.text: Andreea Popa writes that people who truly get what Thunder is about become "guardians of the vision" too: they suggest ideas that strengthen it, call out what doesn't fit, and bring energy to conversations. In her telling, Cris is not just hiring employees but finding people who were already looking for this story, even if they didn't know it. She concludes that protecting the vision is not keeping it safe from change but making sure every person who touches it makes it "more itself, not less." Cris carries the vision, sometimes through people and sometimes through conversations, and "always points out that this vision belongs to us, and we belong to this vision."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that a leader's voice is not a tool of persuasion or performance but a presence that comes from inner work, honesty and responsibility. It says the strongest voice belongs to the listener, and that leaders should make space for others' ideas rather than be the source of all wisdom. Andreea Popa closes with her own story of seeing, at Thunder, leadership reframed as service rather than dominance.

chunks.heading: Voice starts in fear, not delivery
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, in its chapter "The Voice," argues that leaders mistake voice for "a weapon of persuasion," where everything must be right, clear and compelling enough to drive action. It calls that "old theater" that no longer moves anyone. The chapter says real voice comes from responsibility and authentic alignment, built through inner work on "your fears, your purpose, the places where you've been broken and rebuilt." The goal is not to learn to command a room. It is to become someone others trust with "their half-formed dreams. Their wild ambitions. Their secret fears about whether they're enough."

The book says voice "shelters where your fear lives." When words match a person's life, people lean in and trust it. Powerful voices "don't always sound polished; sometimes they tremble," and a shaking voice is a sign to go deeper, not to pull back. Voice also works as a mirror that shows where you still hold fear. The chapter's line is that you don't just transmit a message, you "become the message."

chunks.heading: A voice is a place people decide whether to stay in
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that every time you speak or write you create a space, and people sense it as quickly as they do when walking into a room. They can tell whether it feels "grounded and real, or like someone's trying to impress you." If it is the latter, they check out, "not rudely, but the space just doesn't hold you."

Thunder's leadership book says people are "starving for something honest, something they can stand on," and that there are countless voices saying nice things that mean nothing. Its advice is not to dress ideas up. Build something honest enough that someone stops scrolling and thinks "Wait . . . I needed that." A space not rooted in truth loses people "no matter how well-crafted the language sounds."

chunks.heading: The strongest voice in the room belongs to the listener
chunks.text:
The book argues that the person who isn't mentally rehearsing their next point becomes "the center of gravity," because being seen, heard and witnessed without judgment is what people are hungry for. Its instruction is "Don't interrupt, invite. Don't compete for space, create it." Listening means offering attention and letting someone else's truth matter more than your own need to be heard.

The chapter says people remember how you made them feel in the silence more than any words you could have said: held, given room to think, and able to discover what they needed to say. It concludes that the voice that changes everything "is not the one that fills the silence. It's the one that makes space for it." It also asks leaders to practice active, intentional listening rather than waiting for a turn to speak.

chunks.heading: The pause between words builds trust
chunks.text:
The chapter focuses on the moment after someone finishes speaking and before you respond. In that pause, the book says, you choose between interrupting to make your point and building on theirs, and between getting defensive and getting curious when someone disagrees. People are always judging whether your voice "adds value to their world or just adds noise."

Thunder's leadership book gives concrete practices for leaders:
- Ask questions that help others think out loud.
- Give quieter voices room to rise.
- Resist jumping in with your own experience right away.
- Remember that sometimes the most profound thing you can offer is silence.

Its logic is that a voice is only as powerful as the trust behind it, and trust grows in the spaces between words. The line is "Earn attention by giving it first."

chunks.heading: Your voice becomes a voice in someone else's head
chunks.text:
The book argues that everyone carries voices from people who spoke into their lives, some lifting them up and some making them doubt themselves. Every time a leader speaks, they plant seeds in another person's internal dialogue that help them grow or make them shrink.

The chapter contrasts people who "speak care into existence" with those who leave you smaller. The first kind give feedback that challenges, ask hard questions that spark curiosity, and disagree in a way that leaves you thinking more clearly. The second point out problems without hope, ask questions that feel like attacks, and make you second-guess good decisions. The difference, it says, is not the words but the intention behind them, and people feel it instantly. The most powerful use of voice is to make people feel more capable: help them trust their judgment, show possibilities and not only missed problems. Say "You're stronger than you think," not "You're not ready for this."

chunks.heading: Be the soil, not the flower
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book argues that leaders don't need to have great ideas if they can hear them. People living closest to problems carry solutions the leader will never think of, and often don't know how good their ideas are until someone listens. The chapter's image is "we change lives when we become the soil, not the flower."

The leader's role, it says, is not to fill every room with wisdom but to hear answers already floating around and connect them: to "spot the connection between what one person said and what another is struggling with." It compares the leader to someone who helps scattered puzzle pieces find each other, since people bring fragments, half-thoughts and frustrations that are "solutions in disguise." The chapter's advice is to stop being the source of all wisdom and become the person who recognizes it and encourages others to spread it.

chunks.heading: Leadership was never meant to be loud
chunks.text:
In the closing story, author Andreea Popa writes about people who grew up as the quiet ones, the observers and question-askers, who assumed leadership was for "the loud ones" who own a room. They believed silence disqualified them and that listening made them invisible.

She writes that at Thunder she "watched leadership being rewritten": less about taking charge, more about taking responsibility, and about service "to people, to values, to meaningful work." She describes seeing leaders at Thunder who were not interested in owning the room but in "building the room so others could thrive in it." The chapter ends by saying the Thunder voice may not echo in every room, but it will reach those who need it, and that the quiet ones may have been meant to "build a new" mold.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues the shield a leader needs is humility, which guards against ego rather than hiding humanity. It says to be useful rather than look important, be easy to work with, stay open to being changed, and lift others as you climb. It reports Adi describing Thunder as a village where no one claims the storm as their own.

chunks.heading: The shield: humility as protection from ego, not from vulnerability
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book (chapter "The shield," from "Leadership Before It Has a Name," written by Andreea Popa and coordinated by Cris Pop) opens by rejecting the advice "Protect yourself. Shield yourself. You're a leader now; you cannot show weakness." The chapter argues the shield a leader actually needs "doesn't protect you from showing your humanity; it protects you from your ego." When status gets loud, humility keeps a leader grounded in service; when ambition turns rigid, it keeps them flexible. The book calls humility "the quiet infrastructure underneath every leader we actually trust": it lets you grow without clinging to old titles, build things that don't center on you, and serve in ways that don't need to be seen. It describes this as "strength that doesn't need to prove itself."

chunks.heading: The empty cup: pride versus possibility
chunks.text: The chapter argues that many people carry "a cup that's completely full": full of pride, of needing to look the right way, of protecting their image. A full cup lets nothing new in. Such a person walks into rooms ready to defend what they know instead of learning what they don't, spends energy maintaining reputation instead of building something real, and misses the bold idea because they are busy proving they're smart. The book's alternative is to fill the cup with humility, which makes space "to listen, space to discover that you don't actually need to have it all figured out." Its line: "Your cup is either full of pride or full of possibility. It can't be both." The payoff is that you "quit trying to look like a leader and just become one," letting work speak instead of ego.

chunks.heading: Followership: leaders begin the story, followers write the path
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book argues that if we honored following half as much as leading, more things would last. Leaders point the way, but followers "make things real": they build the culture and carry the mission through daily behavior. To follow is to take ownership, to put ego aside, trust someone else and believe in the mission "even when no one is there to witness." The chapter also claims following can be a powerful form of leading: moving with the group while carrying a different vision inside, listening, learning, then acting with real impact when the moment comes. Its summary: followers "are not just part of the journey, they are the journey."

chunks.heading: Being easy to work with: the bridge metaphor
chunks.text: The chapter argues that being easy to work with "means getting over yourself." It likens professional energy to a bridge: either one that connects people and smooths everyone's journey, or an unpredictable one that makes people think twice before crossing. Someone acting as if their presence is a favor is "an obstacle with an ego." A working bridge steps in quietly when someone struggles, adjusts pace so no one is left behind, and gives without expecting return. For leaders, the book says you are the main bridge everyone depends on, so you strengthen yourself to hold the weight, and when you can't help you are honest about limits: "I'm at capacity today, but I'll be stronger tomorrow." Its line: "Your talent might get you in the room, but your attitude decides if you get invited back."

chunks.heading: Ego flexibility and usefulness over importance
chunks.text:
The book argues that the rare skill is letting yourself be changed, "ego flexibility: the ability to let go of being right long enough to become wiser." Real growth, it says, usually "shows up wearing someone else's voice." Leaders who stay open and still evolving earn trust because people follow "the way you move, not just where you're going." The chapter urges leaders to let truth "ruin your opinion if it needs to" and to thank the person who showed them what they missed.

It pairs this with a distinction between looking important and being useful. Importance (big words, a busy calendar, ready opinions) is loud and often hollow. Usefulness is staying late to fix what no one saw break, noticing who is struggling and stepping in, setting up chairs, answering the unglamorous questions that move things forward. "Importance is what you claim. Usefulness is what others feel."

chunks.heading: Paying it forward and leaving no one behind
chunks.text:
The chapter argues success is never a solo act: someone opened a door or believed in you, and that is your guide for treating the person coming up behind you. Paying it forward multiplies, since the person you mentor mentors someone else, starting "a chain reaction that outlasts you."

On inclusion, the book states that "We, the Thunders, believe no one should be fighting for a seat at the table. Everyone deserves one by default," and should feel safe bringing their whole self. Diverse backgrounds and personalities are "not a challenge to manage. It's our edge." It lists concrete practices:
- **Mentor when you can:** don't look away from someone stuck or doubting themselves; share what you've learned and walk with them.
- **Connect people:** make the intro, open a door, even without the answer.
- **Be present:** a quick "Hey, you good?" may matter more than expected.
- **Make room:** especially for quiet people still finding their pace; help them speak and stay.
- **Lift as you climb:** celebrate their wins like your own.

chunks.heading: Thunder as a village: Adi's story
chunks.text:
The chapter closes with a story shared by Adi, a Thunder team member: "Thunder is like a village." In a village no one stands alone; the baker bakes, the blacksmith forges, the farmer tends crops, and it works because each is invested in the others' well-being. The book applies this to Thunder: the team is building, creating and dreaming together, and none of it works if anyone believes they can do it all alone. Some lead projects, some solve problems quietly in the background, some bring new ideas to life, and each role is essential.

The book argues humility means knowing "your strength is multiplied through others": listening when you think you know the answer, and asking for help "not as a weakness, but as an invitation for others to shine." In this village "no one claims the storm as their own"; Thunder doesn't chase leadership "for the sake of standing above others" but leads by serving and showing up. When the storm comes, the chapter concludes, "we don't face it to prove our strength. We face it together, because that's what a village does."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that when plans stop holding, a leader's real compass is their own capacity to grow, notice, shift and unlearn, not the strategy document. It urges turning discomfort into a growth signal, acting on lessons rather than collecting them, and choosing the people around you deliberately. It closes with a Thunder story: Thunder Talks, Bookclub and Thunder Lab are meant to build a circle of service, not an audience.

chunks.heading: The Compass: leadership as personal growth rather than strategy
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, in its chapter "The Compass," argues that the usual advice to pick a direction, map the moves and stick to the plan runs into a basic problem: "plans don't last. Because the map keeps changing." The chapter says traditional thinking treats leadership as control, clarity and direction. It argues that real leadership is "becoming the kind of person worth following, even when the path disappears."

The chapter argues that "the real compass is not the strategy document. It's you." That means a leader's capacity to grow, notice, shift and "unlearn what used to work." Strategy matters, but it isn't enough. What moves people is "how alive you are in the face of uncertainty," not how precise the plan is. The book says nobody wants a leader "stuck defending yesterday's map." People want one who is willing to grow so the whole team can.

chunks.heading: Welcoming discomfort as a sign of growth
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, in "The Compass," argues that the discomfort of being at the edge of what you know is a signal of growth, not of failure or danger. It describes this as "the tension of almost, not-yet, still-learning," and compares it to stepping onto a stage before you've memorized your lines.

The chapter says the work is to "press into the discomfort," to "outgrow what once protected you" and to let awkwardness be "a teacher, not a threat." When discomfort arrives, the book's advice is: don't run, don't armor up, don't distract yourself. Breathe, soften, and say with a half-smile: "What a pleasure to feel this discomfort. I must be growing."

chunks.heading: Knowledge without application is the illusion of growth
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that leadership development is full of content (books, courses, keynotes, talks) designed to help people "know more." People can memorize frameworks on motivation, conflict resolution, discipline and strategic thinking. If that knowledge doesn't change how they show up when it matters, the book calls it "unfulfilling busywork."

The book's line is "You don't pay for leadership; you pay for the chance to do the work." That chance only has value if you engage with it. Otherwise you've paid "for the privilege of owning unused potential."

Its practice is to sit down regularly for honest conversations with yourself about what you're learning and how you're applying it. The book warns that consuming leadership content and moving on only creates the illusion of growth. The question to ask is not "What should I know?" but "Who am I becoming?"

chunks.heading: Unlearning: questioning inherited beliefs and outdated internal maps
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book, in "The Compass," argues that people collect beliefs "like souvenirs" and build "museums of certainty." When evidence doesn't fit, the natural response is to reject it, because beliefs have become identity. The chapter points out that most deep convictions were inherited from family, education and culture, adopted "before we had tools to evaluate them."

It describes unlearning as becoming "an archaeologist of your own mind": digging up old truths and asking whether they still serve. The book says "the moments when we feel most certain are precisely when we should be most suspicious," and that growth "lives in the willingness to question your own compass."

The chapter also argues that old internal maps can leave you lost on a familiar road. The ambition that earned a first promotion may now cause burnout. The need to prove yourself may block the work that matters. The hustle that built a career may be destroying peace. Because those drives once worked, questioning them can feel ungrateful. The book reads exhaustion and hollow success as the inner compass saying it's time to recalibrate, not as failure.

chunks.heading: Learning from the people around you and choosing your circle
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that wisdom is not only in books, courses and podcasts, but in everyday people. Its examples are a colleague who stays calm in chaos ("a masterclass in leadership you didn't pay for"), a barista who remembers your order, a child who gets back on the bike, and the person at lunch who handled a hard conversation with more grace than most executives. "The world is your classroom. The people around you are your teachers."

The book also argues that growth is never solitary. People absorb the ambitions, standards and limits of those around them, and it invokes the idea that you become "the average of the five people you spend the most time with." Its advice is to "choose your circle with intention": find people who make you uncomfortable in the right ways, who see your excuses and won't let you hide behind them, and whose drive wakes something in you.

chunks.heading: Becoming never ends
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book argues that becoming is not a destination or "a door you walk through once." It is "a dance you commit to. Again, and again, and again." A title or a job is "not permission to stop" but "an invitation to go deeper," with more curiosity and courage. The chapter adds that if you don't get picked, you "dance anyway."

It calls the belief that once you arrive you get to rest a "dangerous myth." The people who keep growing and contributing "never graduate from becoming."

chunks.heading: Service as a path to growth: Thunder Talks, Bookclub and Thunder Lab
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that everything worth doing starts with wanting to serve the people around you, not in a grand way but "in the small, daily way of showing up for each other." The book says this is why Thunder created Thunder Talks, Bookclub and Thunder Lab. The stated aim is "not trying to build an audience" but "trying to build a circle," where the right people find each other, grow together and work out how to serve.

At one Thunder talk, the room was asked three questions:
- How much of what you do actually serves others?
- How often do you go out of your way to help?
- What if every small act of service was secretly the key to your own growth?

The book then tells the story of two attendees. Andrei, a university professor, was building an internship program for students who needed technology mentors but lacked the tech experience himself, so he asked for help. Mircea, a software developer, said yes without hesitating. Over that summer they built software for an archaeological boat. The chapter says the code was only part of it: they also built trust, created space for questions, and made room for people to become more than they thought they could be. The result was "a circle of care," where "helping others meant growing yourself."

The chapter's conclusion is that change "is what happens when you say yes" and choose "service over comfort, again and again."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that leaders watch the wrong storm: the one that matters is internal, and courage is the daily choice to move first, admit first and ask first. It closes with the story of how Thunder was born from two bold moves by Cris: asking Adi to mentor him for free, then asking Adi to build a company together. The book says Cris understood you don't wait to be chosen, you make it impossible not to choose you.

chunks.heading: Courage as the "actual storm" in Thunder's leadership book
chunks.text: "The Storm" chapter of Thunder's leadership book, "Leadership Before It Has a Name" (2025), written by Andreea Popa and coordinated by Cris Pop, argues that leaders watch the wrong storm. They track market crashes, rising competitors and product failures, and build bunkers for economic hurricanes. The chapter argues the storm that matters is internal, and that it is courage. It describes this as a daily, relentless choice, not a one-time lightning strike: speaking the truth when your voice shakes, making the unpopular call because it's right, holding steady when the people you lead doubt you, and looking fear (of failing, of being misunderstood, of not being enough) in the eye and moving toward it. The chapter says to be "the one who moves first, admits first, asks first," and that "real leadership lives" in facing the storm inside. Markets recover and competitors fade, but courage "keeps you standing no matter what changes."

chunks.heading: Courage is remembered, not built: "You weren't born ready. You were born willing."
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book argues, in its chapter "The Storm," that courage is something people lose rather than find. It says we were born courageous (learning to walk by falling a thousand times) and later learned to hide, to wait and to perfect before presenting, collecting reasons why "not yet" feels safer than "right now." The chapter argues that people who challenge the world did not find more courage than anyone else; they remembered they never lost it and stopped believing they needed permission to be themselves. Stepping into a room where you don't belong yet, or speaking up when your voice shakes, is framed as returning to who you were before you learned to be afraid. The line the chapter lands on: "You weren't born ready. You were born willing."

chunks.heading: Keeping your heart open as an act of leadership courage
chunks.text: The book chapter "The Storm" argues that after early disappointments a small voice says "next time, don't let them get so close," and most people feed it, trading wonder for wariness and hope for realism. It describes the people who refuse: those who still get excited about small things, still believe in people despite the evidence, and choose curiosity over judgment. The chapter says the world calls them naive, but they have felt rejection and disappointment and refused to let that pain become their teacher. Staying soft "doesn't mean avoiding hurt. It means absorbing it without becoming it." The chapter's conclusion: "Your kindness is your rebellion. Keep your heart open anyway."

chunks.heading: Integrity over approval: standing alone when your values aren't popular
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book argues, in "The Storm," that people are "addicted to approval": saying yes when they mean no, apologizing for boundaries they should be proud of, and twisting themselves to fit other people's comfort zones. The chapter argues the hard part is not learning to stand up for what you believe but learning to stand alone when it isn't popular, and to say no to the easy path so you can say yes to the right one. It urges readers to stop trying to be everyone's favorite person and to be "someone you can live with," someone who "knows the difference between being kind and being convenient." It adds that the people who matter will respect this, and the ones who don't may never have been on your side.

chunks.heading: Accountability in the dark: fingerprints on the fix
chunks.text: The chapter "The Storm" in Thunder's leadership book describes the "loneliest kind of courage": picking up the pieces when something breaks and everyone suddenly becomes busy. When responsibility sits "in the middle of the room like an unwanted guest," most people have perfected the vanishing act. The chapter argues the person who steps in is not doing it to be a hero or get a pat on the back, but because someone has to. It says this courage happens where no one will ever know, with only your own reflection as witness. Its line on credit: "We live in a world full of people who want their name on the success story. But the world runs on people who are willing to have their fingerprints on the fix."

chunks.heading: Being willing to be terrible long enough to be great
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book argues, in the chapter "The Storm," that feeling like the most unqualified person in the room is "the doorway to everything you want." It challenges the conditioning that if something is hard you're doing it wrong, or that struggling is a signal to pivot rather than persist. The chapter argues the skill that will define you will humble you before it honors you, and the work that becomes your signature will feel like a foreign language at first. "Everyone wants to be good at something. Few people want to be bad at something long enough to become good at it." In its framing, courage is "not in the trying but in the staying": showing up tomorrow after a day that felt like failure, enduring the embarrassment of being a beginner when you're used to being competent, and trusting that discomfort is temporary while quitting is permanent.

chunks.heading: The two bold moves that built Thunder: "You don't wait to be chosen"
chunks.text:
In the story that closes "The Storm," Thunder's leadership book tells how Thunder was born from "two men who refused to wait for permission." The chapter says Cris, fresh out of college and "completely clueless about programming," walked into a company where Adi was working. The system had given him theories and grades but left him unprepared for the real world. Instead of applying for entry-level jobs, Cris went straight to Adi and said: "Teach me. Mentor me. I'll work for free. I don't want money. I want to learn." Adi saw commitment and drive, said yes, and mentored and pushed him until Cris went from knowing nothing to being great.

The second bold move, per the book: Cris asked Adi to build a company together, with no roadmap or guarantees, only a vision and the belief that business can be different, a company meant to "disturb the status quo." That, the chapter says, is how Thunder began, with one bold move growing into a dream shared by thirteen people.

chunks.heading: The lesson the book draws from Thunder's origin: make yourself impossible not to choose
chunks.text: The book argues that what Cris understood was: "You don't wait to be chosen. You make it impossible not to choose you." According to the chapter, he created value from the day he walked in, showed up every day, put in the work, learned, improved and lifted others up, and when it was time to build something bigger "he didn't ask if he was ready. He simply stepped up." The chapter generalizes this into its view of leadership: it "is not about titles or permission," but about making yourself so valuable, reliable and committed to the mission that people naturally want to follow you. It also frames Thunder's founding as two complementary acts of courage: one person had the courage to ask for help, the other had the wisdom to give it. Its closing call: don't wait for permission, take the responsibility, own the challenge, and "the world is waiting for people bold enough to step up before they're ready."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The chapter argues that a leader's legacy is the human ripple they leave, not titles or systems. It reports that Cris built Thunder on generosity learned from his family and a "we, not me" belief, rejecting the "be loud, put yourself first" playbook. It then profiles team members who lead through service, sharing knowledge, honesty, grit and ownership.

chunks.heading: Thunder's leadership book on legacy as the ripple people carry
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book ("Leadership Before It Has a Name", 2025, written by Andreea Popa and coordinated by Cris Pop) closes with a chapter on legacy. It argues that people think they'll be remembered for "the systems we built, the frameworks we created, the decisions we made," but "roles fade. Titles get reassigned. Even the best systems get rewritten." What stays is human: "the silent stories people carry about you." The chapter asks what shows up when your name comes up: unity when things got hard, kindness at the cost of speed, listening and noticing, or drive and discipline. All matter, but the question is which one "created a chain reaction." Its claim is that "leadership leaks through your humanity" and that what a leader leaves behind is "the ripple," the way they changed how people think about what's possible.

chunks.heading: The book on Cris Pop: building Thunder from "we" instead of "me"
chunks.text: The chapter says Cris grew up watching his family give without expecting anything back; they "never counted the cost," and that generosity became his blueprint. When he built Thunder he started from the same place, believing success was "never a solo act" and that real leadership means lifting others up rather than stepping on them. The book says that when he stepped into leadership the world offered a different playbook, "Be loud. Put yourself first or get left behind," which "sounded like ambition" but "felt like betrayal." It argues that game is a trap: leaders who bet on themselves alone "build monuments to their own isolation." The book says Cris never bought it; he knew "the real game wasn't 'me', it was 'we,'" and that leadership is about the people you empower, the trust you build and the impact you leave. The chapter frames Thunder as built by inviting others in: "a team, a community, and anyone ready to believe in a better way to work together." Not everyone will join, and the book says that's fine, since this is "for the believers."

chunks.heading: Leadership as service without a title: Anda, Gabi and "leadership before it has a name"
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book shows leadership appearing before any role exists. Of Gabi, it says he joined and "simply stepped in and did the work that others didn't have time for." Before he signed a contract or had an official role, "he had already become part of the team." The shelves got built and the desks got organized, and "no one invited him to lead. He simply started leading." The book defines this as leadership "before it has a name": owning what no one asked you to own, cleaning the workspace without being told, researching tools that make colleagues' work easier, showing up consistently. Its advice is to begin small: onboard the new person patiently, organize shared tools, share a resource, "notice what's missing, then fill it, quietly and repeatedly." Of Anda, who works across marketing, event strategy, legal documents and team experiences, it says she is "defined by her presence" and calls modern leadership "being human enough to lean in wherever you're needed," which in its purest form is "service without ego." Its summary line: leadership is "not waiting for permission to care about the work and the people around you."

chunks.heading: Sharing mastery and honest challenge: Adi and Horațiu
chunks.text: The book's portrait of Adi says that when Cris asked him to mentor, he said yes "without hesitation." Adi is described as demanding at first, with tough standards and tougher questions, but someone who "lives for the craft" and codes for the joy of it. He shifts roles as coach, challenger and mentor, and knows "when to push and when to support, when to teach and when to let you figure it out yourself." The principle drawn: "Your knowledge is a gift. Share it. Give it away." His goal is not to be the smartest in the room but to make sure no one is left behind. The book also profiles Horațiu, who questions rules "every time." It argues that raw, unfiltered honesty is "a service" to the team, the ideas and the work, because it sharpens ideas and makes space for better thinking, and that he doesn't pretend to agree to keep the peace. It adds that he delivers it with humor so the goal is "not conflict but progress," and says every team needs someone "brave enough to question the system yet grounded enough to be the glue." A disruptor "who doesn't divide but connects."

chunks.heading: Ownership to the last mile and hard work as commitment: Iuli, Florina and Manu
chunks.text: In the book's account of Iuli, a project near its end was not going to ship on time because of misjudged time estimates and unforeseen challenges. With her contract ending, she could have handed it off. Instead she worked late evenings, documented every blocker and edge case, insisted on a final sync with the tech lead, refined her deliverables and left detailed notes and clear next steps. The feature wasn't complete when she left, but the book says her leadership "wasn't measured by the number of tasks she ticked off, but by the level of care and responsibility she carried until the very last minute." Of Florina, it says hard work is not hours or burnout but "showing up fully, relentlessly, with a commitment to growth." That can mean fourteen-hour sprints or stepping back to recharge, and it comes down to ownership of wasted moments, of the gap between where she is and where she wants to be, and of the process. The book's line: "You don't learn to work smart until you've worked hard, really hard, for a long, long time." Of Manu, it describes quiet excellence: autonomy as her default, punctuality that respects everyone's time, preparedness, attention to detail, and no ego as a follower or leader.

chunks.heading: People first, and leading yourself: Cosmin, Vlad, Anda and Deni
chunks.text: The book says Cosmin's recurring message is "It's all about people," not from a self-development book but because that's how he believes the world should work. It says he would rather do work he doesn't love with people he cares about than the reverse, and it concludes that "the work will never be as important as the lives we touch while doing it," asking readers to show up as humans first and measure success by "the quality of care we bring to the people around us." The book also covers leading yourself. Vlad was "quietly stuck" and found discipline not in a breakthrough but in the people around him: "Their pace becomes your pace. Their standards raise your own." Anda, after leaving a safe accounting path and teaching herself UI/UX before joining Thunder, shows that "you don't need a title to lead." Deni left law school for a creative writing and photography internship with no portfolio, and the book says she succeeded because she "backed it up with grit," built her own proof, and was coachable, curious and committed. Its advice: "Start where you are. The path clears as you walk it."

chunks.heading: "Fight for it": the book's closing call against waiting for permission
chunks.text: The chapter ends with a personal story from author Andreea Popa, not Cris. She recounts playing football as a child in worn-out sneakers, then sandals her mother bought to stop the costs, and finally barefoot, because she was willing to invest in her passion whatever the discomfort. From this she argues adults have traded curiosity for comfort and boldness for safety, and she quotes the excuses that kill leadership before it starts: "If I don't get a raise, I won't lead." "If I don't have the right resources, I won't start." The book's conclusion is that it's time to take ownership, stop letting the world define what's possible, and fight for what you want, "because if we're not willing to fight for it, we'll never have it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: The closing chapter argues that every person carries a spark of leadership, and that the job is to find it, feed it and act on it now rather than keep thinking about it. It describes leadership as built through setbacks, hard conversations and course corrections, and ends with Thunder's promise to stay in readers' corner through mentorship, a newsletter and open contact.

chunks.heading: Leadership as a capacity in every person: the "Lead With Humanity" chapter
chunks.text: Thunder's leadership book, "Leadership Before It Has a Name" (2025, written by Andreea Popa and coordinated by Cris Pop), opens its "Lead With Humanity" chapter with the claim that "every human being carries something inside that makes them capable of leading." The chapter calls this "a spark," "a conviction," and "a quiet instinct to lift, build, and protect." It says the job of leadership is to find that spark, feed it, and fire it, "hour by hour. Day by day. Human by human." The chapter treats leadership as something already present in people, not a title or a position. It adds that every story that broke the ordinary "started with humans". These were people who "chose to be real in a world that rewards pretending" and who "stood up before they felt ready."

chunks.heading: Start now: leadership is something you do, not something you wait for
chunks.text:
The chapter argues that leadership "won't come by itself. You have to do it. Now." It tells readers to stop thinking and dreaming about leadership and to start doing it ("Get after it."). It asks them to commit to the process "not because it's glamorous, but because it's yours." In this view leadership is built through repeated practice:

- Every setback sharpens you.
- Every small win adds weight to your steps.
- Every hard conversation and every course correction is "leadership being built."

The book frames growth as cumulative and ordinary. It does not rely on a single defining moment.

chunks.heading: The leadership behaviors the chapter lists
chunks.text:
The chapter says to lead "with intention. With presence. With a willingness to get it wrong and grow anyway." It lists concrete behaviors:

- Show up before you feel ready.
- Make decisions with care.
- Share what you're learning.
- Ask questions.
- Offer your hand.
- When the moment asks for it, step forward.

The book argues that readiness is not a precondition for leading, and that being willing to be wrong is part of the work. It also stresses sharing and helping others as part of leading, alongside stepping forward. It ends this passage by saying legacy begins "inside ordinary days, shaped by extraordinary integrity."

chunks.heading: "We're rooting for you": Thunder's stance toward people trying to keep their humanity
chunks.text:
Thunder's leadership book closes the chapter with a direct address to readers. It says that "for everything you do to keep your humanity intact, we're rooting for you." The authors note that people often need someone in their corner to offer a vote of confidence, but "it rarely comes." The chapter sets out to be that moment: "you'll always have us."

The book is open about the limits of this support. It says "We may not be able to support you in the ways you need most, like offering a job or a leadership role," but promises to be there as a friend. It tells readers to reach out through social media, email, or the team's personal accounts, and says "we're listening."

chunks.heading: Mentorship, the newsletter, and paying it forward
chunks.text:
The chapter points readers to two Thunder resources for continuing the journey:

- **A mentorship program**, which the book says is "designed to help you grow as a leader by focusing on your foundation first."
- **A newsletter**, which will keep sharing insights on the leadership path.

The chapter's line "Don't fight alone" frames leadership development as something done with others. It then asks readers to pay it forward: "Someone near you is waiting to be invited into their own courage. Quiet revolutions start this way." The book presents leadership as something passed from person to person through invitation and encouragement. It closes with: "Keep going. We see you. We're with you. And we're always rooting for you."

Nothing fuels our growth more than having the humility to accept that others are ahead, simply better at certain things.

There is so much power and peace in being able to honestly feel behind, yet fully content with your own journey.

Having people ahead of us is a privilege, but only once you decide the competition is against yourself. That moment, those people become inspiration and proof.

That’s exactly why we landed in Tallinn: knowing they are ahead, but grateful for the opportunity to become more of who we can be.

We're creating these videos to give young people (mostly 🇷🇴 language - for now) a chance to see what a human-centric culture looks like.

To everyone who has endured leaders who close doors instead of opening possibilities, who impose rules without offering reasons, and who take more than they give, work doesn’t have to feel that way.

There is a light at the end of the tunnel. You can find it within, maybe buried, maybe scared, but still pulsing.

You can earn a human-centric work culture (either joining one or building one) by becoming the kind of person who deserves it.

5 years ago, I bet my so-called “safe” engineering career on this belief by founding Thunder, and I’ll die on this hill.

We’ve been through sh*t, hardship, and tons of boring work.
We suffered, we felt lost, and we got betrayed.
And I’m sure the future holds many more lessons and struggles.

We also shipped many cool projects, grew the business, mentored 900+ youngsters, built tens of community events, gifted more than 10.000 books, wrote a freaking book ourselves, traveled to tens of countries, and collected thousands of memories - all while serving one another’s growth - brick by brick, one day at a time.

Meaningful work is not always sexy, but that’s not the point.
But rather... what does work make of you?

You can grow through failures as much as you can regress through wins.

Whatever happens, good or bad, make sure you keep becoming.

[Translated from Romanian] A while ago, I was talking with Florina about how our growth requires extremely consistent work, but, ironically, the results usually come in waves and with a delay.

Florina, an ordinary person, is an example and an inspiration of perseverance for me. I love people who keep daring even when results are late.

Over the years, I've found myself "moved" by Florina's actions.

Often our impact comes from things that seem small but make a significant difference.

Last year, we went through a complicated period for the team, both financially and emotionally.

There were many weekends when I chose to work, trying to find solutions, even when nothing was visible on the horizon.

On many of those days, Florina chose to be by my side, even though quite often what I was doing fell outside her area of expertise.

It's always a good moment to show the people around you that you care.
Her simple presence showed me a care that deeply inspired me.

For me, that's what leadership means. And not some grand title given to a boss who gives orders from a pedestal.

Everything I wrote about Florina matters, because it reflects character traits and leadership principles. If you choose to make them your own and practice them every day, they can bring evolution and growth.

At The Thunder Way, you'll meet people like Florina, ordinary people who inspire through who they are. People you learn from, but also grow with, sharing the same values.

If you feel you want more from your story, we're waiting for you with us.

I woke up excited about the work ahead, but carrying a strange guilt because, according to the status quo, I’m supposed to hate my work.

Most people I met who dislike their work usually hate the culture, which is simply a proxy term that actually refers to (some) people, because we are the culture. We, the people, are the culture.

I feel them. I’ve been there. It’s hard to give a sh*t about your work as long as you find yourself in the cold water pushing a boat up the river instead of being in the boat and rowing.

You feel unseen, unappreciated, almost invisible. Missing the type of things money can’t buy, while hoping career success will somehow miraculously fill these gaps within one day.

Who you are becoming through your work matters most.

That means emotional awareness, self-reflection, resilience, active listening, leadership, or traits like humility, empathy, and curiosity… not just coding, paid ads, or Jira tickets.

Monday seems like a surprisingly good day to wonder, what if?

What if work were meaningful?

[Translated from Romanian] We all want to feel that we have a purpose, it's part of human nature.

But very few people choose the paths that truly build this sense of meaning in our work and our lives.
Anda, an ordinary person, is among the very few. She gives color, emotion and meaning to the Thunder team and community.

I admire with all my heart the depth with which Anda treats her own work. I wouldn't call what she does professionalism, but art.

Professionalism takes you to a very good transactional level, but if you want to create work that moves people, much more is needed. You need to put your soul into every small step and be guided by an uncommon generosity.

Generosity is the foundation of meaningful work.

Over the years, Anda's work has never stopped amazing me. I'll illustrate with a seemingly mundane but remarkable example.

The other day she made a design for a post with the Foreword of our book: Leadership before it has a name.

Looking at the design, I realized the piece of visual representing a book page has the effect of writing showing through from the back, mirrored... exactly how it would look in a photo of a real book page.

My mind stopped instantly. I simply love people like her.

No job description will produce such a result. That effect is about who you are as a person and how much you respect your work and your life.

I feel privileged to work with Anda. It's clear to me that very few people choose to walk such a path of their own becoming.

Anda, I carry a strong gratitude because you believed in our vision, since back when there was almost nothing, and because you choose to be with us.

Of one thing I'm sure: it's infinitely easier to walk such a path with a community by your side, and not alone.

Together we are all better off. And these very few can become more, growing together.

The Thunder Way will be about such stories. About such values and principles that have a far more significant impact on our lives than any "shortcuts" or "hacks" that promise quick results.

True evolution doesn't come from tricks, but from how you choose to live and work every day. If you feel your story can become more, come join us.

Next week, we’re buckling up for our flight to Austin, Texas. 🦅 

We’ll be taking part in tech events at @SXSW, and we’re also hosting our own event. I love seeing how we’ve grown from small gatherings, major local events, and now to organizing events in the States. We’re grateful that this journey began with the support of Linnify.

This time, when they suggested inviting Mir Hwang as a speaker, we felt a strong sense of resonance. His story aligns so naturally with what we stand for.

As a touring session drummer, Mir experienced firsthand the friction and inefficiencies of booking live entertainment. He noticed the gaps. He felt the frustration. And instead of waiting for someone else to step in, he decided to build the solution himself, especially after realizing he wasn’t alone in facing those challenges.

That’s the kind of leadership we believe in, that’s rooted in ownership. In service. Seeing what’s broken, choosing not to look away, and doing the work to create something better for the community.

I can’t wait to dive into this conversation and explore together what leadership in tech can, and should, truly look like.

Last year, my colleague Manuela inspired me to run my first semi-marathon. I’ve always admired the discipline she brings to making running a habit and the way she shows up for Spartan races with such commitment. 

To me, that kind of discipline is a rare and powerful trait in a leader, and I’m deeply grateful to have been moved by her example.

Of course, I couldn’t keep up with her. She has years of training, countless miles behind her, and the kind of grit that pushes her further every time. But as I was running, I began to feel a glimpse of the weight, the endurance, the quiet fight it takes to keep going. 

A marathon is never easy. For some, years of practice may make it look effortless, but it’s never just about the run itself. It’s about becoming the human you’re meant to be: disciplined, resilient, someone who leads by first learning to lead themselves.

All of these qualities shine through Manu’s work, too. And I couldn’t be more grateful to be inspired by such a human being.

You can read more about how she maintains this discipline in this week newsletter, link in the comments.

My colleague, Anda, wrote a piece on our culture page that captures an essential truth:

"We always said that we all, as humanity, are standing on the shoulders of giants. All those who have worked hard, suffered, or even died for a better future. For something they’ve believed in. They lived in a time of sorrow, so that we may live today in a time of peace. And we, in return, have the duty to pass it on. To give what we already have. Sometimes what we have on the outside, but more often, what we have on the inside."

This is why I strive for building leaders. Building giants. And building giants means giving people ownership, letting them follow the fire wherever it leads. That’s how they grow. That’s how we grow.

Time and again, I’m reminded that when people are trusted to follow their own path, they go beyond, creating work that’s simply excellent.

In today’s newsletter, I shared the story of Sabina, who joined us through the dev internship program. Her journey from college to our team is a bold act of courage, growth, and discovery. 

You can read it through the link in the comments.

I’m obsessed with gifting books.
To this day, I’ve probably gifted over 5.000 books to thousands of people.

I carry this urge because, 7 years ago, a book disrupted the course of my life.
It’s a sense of responsibility.. to give back what was once given to me.

Thinking back to who I was then, I didn’t ask for it, didn’t expect it, and probably didn’t even deserve it. Yet someone believed in who I could become.

And that’s why, deep down, every book I gift is an act of trust.

[Translated from Romanian] I believe in civic entrepreneurship. Entrepreneurship with and for people, guided by meaningful personal and collective goals.

And it's precisely from this belief that I've been walking this path for many years now. From belief in people, especially ordinary people, like me and like you.

One thing is very clear to me... together we are all better off. Together we can do big things. Much bigger than each of us can do individually.

Only that this togetherness needs what we increasingly call the 3rd space. A place of ideas, of dialogue, a place where we incubate the future.

Just last week I was talking with Flavia about this 3rd place. About how much it matters to have more and more such spaces, built with purpose and human values.

For a few years now, together with my colleagues at Thunder, we've been working to build such contexts. Places where we get to know each other, share our stories, our strengths, but also our obstacles. Places that truly put people first.

Soon, we meet (again) in such a space, at The Thunder Way, to explore together why and how we can do extraordinary things, even as just ordinary people.

You can find the story of the event on the website, I'll leave a link in the comments.

I’ve been thinking about this for years, how often we make decisions without really stepping into someone else’s shoes.

Whether it’s a customer, a participant, or just another human on the other side, we miss a chance to see what they see, feel what they feel. And that shapes everything, from how we lead, how we communicate, to how we create experiences that actually feel human.

I wrote a few thoughts on this in today's newsletter, small things that might matter more than they seem. Link in the comments.

Like most of us, I used to think life was binary. You either win or you lose, succeed or fail. But over time, I’ve realized there’s a huge gray space in between, full of moments that don’t feel like clear victories or defeats. That space is where most of our growth truly unfolds.

In this week’s newsletter (link in the comments), I’ve shared a way to navigate that gray area in order to figure out which challenges are worth your energy. 

Learning to sit in that space without rushing to label everything as "success" or "failure" has been game-changing.

I built my own framework(s) because I felt unprepared for real life after school.

I had the degree, the grades, the notes, everything that proved I could memorize. But when it came to solving and creating? I was lost. 

That’s when I stopped chasing more information and started chasing transformation. The result was a system that helped me outgrow myself, again and again.

If you’ve ever felt like you’ve been learning for...ever but not actually moving forward, you might find this week's newsletter helpful.

Link in the comments.

If you’ve got 'the things' in life but still feel unfulfilled, try giving back.

To this day, nothing beats the feeling of giving back. Nothing.

Nothing humbles me more than witnessing people turn the invisible into something seen and understood, without being asked to.

It reminds me, again and again, of how powerful it is to trust. To give people space to notice what others don’t. To let them take the lead, act without being asked, and care deeply about the work.

I’m grateful for the culture we’ve been shaping together at Thunder over the past five years. Most of what’s visible now was once invisible, built slowly, on a foundation of trust.

This week newsletter touches on the power of the small details that often go unnoticed. You can find it in the comments.

Whenever I get the chance to meet someone like Mo, I question my life.

And that’s because I get flashbacks of my early beginnings.. back in the village, when today’s reality was nothing more than a distant dream, yet I never stopped believing. And I kept working for it.

Now, whenever I find myself around such experienced and wise individuals, I feel a deep sense of gratitude and responsibility.

One thing I admire in any human being is the ability to stay humble. Or, as he likes to say, to remain grounded, living by principles like:

"I know nothing. I’m nobody."

Mo, thanks for being such an inspiration.

Here's my single biggest indicator that I only talk the walk, no matter where I'm invited to speak.

At one of the previous events, in the first row, there were Cosmin and Anda, two of my colleagues at Thunder.

The fact that my voice never falters when I look them straight in the eye shows me I’m true to myself and to our mission.

That's it. No fancy systems. Just pure honesty and heart.

One year ago, when Denisa joined us at Thunder as part of an internship, I gave her the best advice I could think of..

Make it impossible for us to let you go.

Since then, I’ve shared this philosophy with many students at different events and mentorship sessions, and I still stand by embracing such a mindset.

Next week, we’re kicking off a fresh internship at Thunder, so I thought it's a great opportunity to remind ourselves that it’s our responsibility not to let opportunities slip.

Take ownership of your journey.
Make every day count.

Today's newsletter is an invitation to rethink the way we create, and who we’re really creating for.

We talk about slowing down, yet keep creating content that screams louder.
We want connection, but build for clicks.
We’re chasing reach, and losing meaning along the way.

What if we stopped performing for the algorithm, and started writing for people again?

I wrote about that tension in this newsletter. Not to go viral, just to go deeper.

Left the link in the comments, quietly waiting.

Yesterday I spent my entire evening talking tech and life with students.
It's hard to find anything more fulfilling and important to be done.

The educational system is doomed, and while there is a lot of talking about improvements that might come, there are generations of young and beautiful humans that won't catch that wave.

If you..
..had a hard time starting your career
..felt lonely and discouraged along the way
..were scared you weren’t good enough
..felt invisible in the room
..craved guidance that never came

And you made it through, then you have an opportunity to give back.

We can be there for them, especially if nobody was there for us.

It's not an obligation, it’s a chance. 
A chance to leave this world better than we found it.

We had Thunder Talks this week, another event that reminded me why I love what we’re building at Thunder. 🙌 

Beautiful human beings, honest questions, perspectives that challenge the norm. And, as always, lessons.

One lesson stuck with me in particular, something I did wrong.

I forgot to introduce Tünde. We were switching mics, things were moving fast, and in that moment… I skipped it. I didn’t pause to give her the space she deserved.

Maybe no one noticed, but I did. And that matters to me because I want to be someone who sees the details. Who shows up with intention. Who gives credit when it truly matters.

No blame, just a quiet promise to do better and to keep myself accountable. Observing failure, and how it often looks like something small, but feels big when your values are on the line.

I’ve been thinking about what I should have said.
So I’ll say it now, because it’s never too late to properly honor someone.

Here’s what I want you to know about Tünde:

- She leads in a way that’s quiet but strong.
- She speaks with purpose, like every word is carrying someone gently forward.
- Her presence is more than a gift.
- She helps people grow into themselves, into real leaders by helping them remember who they already are.
- She equips leaders with emotional intelligence, self-awareness, and the courage to evolve.
- To her, great leadership starts with clear words, thoughtful action, and a deeply human heart.
- She believes that true success is about purpose.
- She brings out the best in others by building trust.
- She offers transformation for those willing to do the work.
- She sees people deeply, and that’s rare.
- She’s kind, compassionate, humble, the kind of human the world needs more of.

I wish I had said that then. So I’m saying it now, because acknowledgement never expires. I’ll take this moment to say thank you for being a light in our community, for inspiring us not just with your words, but with how you live them every day.

And maybe that’s another lesson: that it’s never too late to make something right. That we can be transparent, even when it feels uncomfortable. That we can take ownership, not to blame ourselves, but to grow more intentionally.

Growth doesn’t come from getting it right every time. It comes from noticing when you didn’t, and then doing something about it.

So here’s to the missteps that teach us, to the people like Tünde who lead by example, and to making sure that next time, we don’t forget what matters.

It’s odd how much favoritism still exists. 

We’ve got AI writing poems, rockets landing themselves, and teams working across time zones. But somehow, we’re still promoting people based on who gets lunch with the boss?

Wild. Climbing the ladder, one lunch at a time.

When promotions are based on proximity instead of performance, it sends a message no amount of motivational posters can undo: “It’s not about how well you work. It’s about who’s watching.”

And people catch on fast.

The ones who used to go the extra mile? They stop at the bare minimum. The quiet high-performers? They either become quietly bitter or quietly gone.

And maybe the worst part? The people who are favored rarely feel safe in their roles either. Because when you’ve been handed something you didn’t earn, you live with the fear it could be taken just as easily.

Real leadership isn’t about loyalty points. It’s about clarity. Standards. Giving people a reason to believe their effort actually matters.

Favoritism is lazy leadership.
Merit takes more work but it builds teams that work better.

When mistakes happen, and they always will, what happens next defines a team.

Blame is the easiest reaction. It’s quick, it’s loud, and it makes someone feel momentarily in control. But it doesn’t fix the problem. It just teaches people to play it safe and to avoid risks that could lead to something great.

Fear kills innovation faster than failure ever could. When mistakes are punished instead of studied, progress grinds to a halt. No one experiments. No one speaks up. And slowly, without anyone noticing, the team stops growing.

The best teams don’t avoid mistakes, but they use them. They dissect what went wrong, adjust, and get better. Not because they’re reckless, but because they know the only true failure is refusing to learn.

As a leader, I can demand perfection, or I can build a culture where people are safe enough to chase it. But I can’t do both.

Because in a culture of blame, people play defense.
And in a culture of trust, people build the future.

"Keep on climbing, but don’t forget to pause and appreciate life along the way."

Every time I get replies like this, I just don’t get it.

I’m like… what do you mean by appreciating life?
Or better yet, what do you mean by not appreciating life?

Way too many people hate their work, which leads them to believe that life can rarely be appreciated, and that saddens me.

If you need a pause from the activity you’re investing most of your time in just so you can "appreciate life", then you probably need an exit plan.

I don’t climb to arrive somewhere.
I climb to climb.
Climbing is the meaning.

Money matters. Promotions are wonderful. Metrics and KPIs help us track progress. Growth attracts investment. There are countless amazing destinations in our careers and lives.

But none of these should ever come at the expense of doing work that you truly care about. Work that you find meaningful. Work that nurtures your appreciation for life.

Life comes with suffering, regrets, failures, and all kinds of setbacks.
Yet we should still appreciate every experience, because each one contributes to our becoming.

If you can’t appreciate the climb, you’re probably on the wrong mountain.

Conversations today often feel cold, distant, stripped of real emotion. Somewhere along the way, we’ve embraced, perhaps unknowingly, a culture of detachment.

We’re quick to complain when we’re wronged. Loud in our frustrations. But when there’s something kind to say, something uplifting, we stay silent.

"They’ll just know," we assume.

But they don’t. And even if they do, hearing it matters.

I believe meaningful relationships are built on honest, human, authentic communication. That’s why I choose to be intentional about the way I engage with others. If I want deeper, richer conversations, I have to bring that energy into the spaces I occupy.

So, if no one has told you lately, you’re seen. You’re valued. You make a difference.

Keep going and don’t let your voice fade away.

Code can’t speak for you. You have to.

You can have a genius-level IQ. You can speak Python better than English. But if you can’t tell your story, if you can’t communicate your value, then you’re invisible.

Emotional intelligence beats raw brainpower. Every. Single. Time.

I see too many developers building walls instead of bridges. They hide behind screens, convinced they were born to code and not to connect. No events. No conversations. No community. Just commits and features.

But that’s not mastery. That’s mediocrity.

You don’t grow by perfecting syntax. You grow by showing up. By contributing. By collaborating. You grow by being human, not just someone who ships features.

The moment you stop communicating is the moment you start falling behind.

Want to level up? Start by getting uncomfortable.
Speak. Share. Show up.
Because no amount of tech expertise can replace the power of being understood.

Code might build the product. But people build the future.

You stay late. Answer emails at dinner. Skip vacations. Not because you have to, but because it’s expected.

Unspoken, but obvious.

It’s called commitment. But is it?

If loyalty means working yourself to exhaustion…
If dedication is measured in sacrificed weekends…
If success demands burnout…

Then maybe it’s not commitment. Maybe it’s conditioning.

A culture that normalizes burnout doesn’t create high performers. It creates short careers.

People don’t leave because they can’t handle the workload. They leave because they’re tired of pretending it’s normal.

If success demands exhaustion, maybe it’s time to redefine success.

I believe in people. And that’s a choice I make every single day.

I choose to believe that people want to matter. That they want to do meaningful work, to create something they’re proud of. That when they’re trusted, they rise. And when they’re given a real chance, they leap.

But we learned to expect the worst. We started assuming laziness, not potential. Compliance, not creativity. We built systems for control, not for contribution.

We stopped believing. And that’s when things broke. Not because people changed. But because we did.

Belief isn’t naive. It’s the spark behind leadership, culture, innovation and everything that matters.

The best work isn’t done by cynics. It’s done by those brave enough to bet on people.

So yeah, I believe in people. Their grit. Their genius. Their goodness.

Do you?

Success is not the destination. It’s the way you choose to walk the path.

Every morning, when you open your eyes, the clock resets. It doesn’t matter how much money you made yesterday or how impressive your LinkedIn title sounds. The only thing that truly matters is who you choose to be today.

The world tells you that success is about results. A number in your bank account. A position. A car so expensive you’re afraid to park it anywhere. But if that’s all you’re chasing, you risk losing what’s essential. Because real success doesn’t come with a throne of superiority, but with a collective responsibility.

If success has made you forget respect, integrity, or honesty, then you haven’t won. You’ve lost everything. True achievement is merely about how high you’ve climbed. It’s more about how much you’ve grown as a person.

Every day, you have a choice. Will you chase status like a cat chasing a laser pointer, or will you use your success to actually do something meaningful?

Don’t let success be the beginning of your downfall. Use it as an opportunity to create value, to lift those around you, to make a difference.

Because at the end of it all, nobody remembers your job title. But they’ll definitely remember if you were the person who always took the last slice of pizza.

Before picking up your next book, ask yourself, "Did I really act on the last one?".

It’s a question I keep close. We even printed it on one of our Thunder bookmarks. Not just because it sounds good. But because it’s a reminder we all need, right when we’re tempted to move on too quickly.

I know the feeling. You’re trying to keep up. Another book, another podcast. You’re following the volume and you hope something will stick. But just as notes pile up on your desk, ideas pile up in your mind… unprocessed, unorganized. 

I’ve lived that loop. I still fall into it sometimes. But there’s another way. One that’s slower, quieter, but more profound.

Pick a book, a podcast, an idea and stay with it, long enough to shape you. Come back to it. Reread the same page. Revisit the same question. Not to remember more, but to understand more deeply.

This is how meaning is created. Not by collecting ideas, but by integrating them into your life. Not by reading more information, but by allowing what you read to reach further into you.

This is what I will be talking about tomorrow at Offbeat Sparks Cluj 2025. About how it feels when you start to live that knowledge. When learning becomes less about content and more about clarity.

For Cristian, Sabina and everyone building this event, for the other speakers, and for the ones who will fill up the room with meaning.. I carry a strong sense of gratitude for sharing such an experience with you. 🎉

As a leader, nothing makes me prouder than seeing more people in the tech community offering free mentorship beyond their business roles. It’s inspiring to witness this generosity, and I want to share the resources that make it possible.

Platforms like ADPlist, ProgrammingBuddies, and many others are connecting experienced developers with those just starting out or looking to level up. They create opportunities to make a real impact, to pay forward the knowledge we’ve gained, and to help others overcome challenges we’ve faced.

There is a real need for mentorship in our industry. People want to connect with others who understand their struggles and guide them.

Too often, developers are working in isolation, relying on forums or anonymous advice to get by. But what they truly need is direct, human connection. They need to talk to other developers, ask questions, and get feedback in real-time from someone who’s been there before.

This is exactly why mentorship matters. It gives people a chance to grow and gain the insight that only experience can offer.

If you want to discuss tech or exchange any thoughts on some given topics, you can always book a free mentorship session with me, Iuliana Pap, Andreea Popa, Gabriel Cioflica, or Cosmin Artene. The link is in the comments.

It’s not the market. It’s not the competition. It’s not even the economy.

The real danger to your team? Silence.

When people don’t feel safe, they don’t speak. When they don’t speak, they don’t share the bad news until it’s too late. The problems go underground. Innovation slows, engagement drops, and the best ideas, the ones that could have changed everything, never see the light of day.

And the worst part? It’s invisible. Leaders don’t notice the missing voices. Teams assume that quiet means agreement. And slowly mediocrity sets in.

Psychological safety is about making it possible to take risks, to disagree, and to share bad news early so we can fix it together. 

I’m always ensuring my team knows that speaking up will always be welcomed, because silence might cost us everything. Because if I want a team that’s bold enough to innovate, I need to be humble enough to listen.

So I ask myself often: have I made it safe enough for my team to tell me the truth?

There’s a kind of pressure out there. To consume more, to move faster, to always be onto the next thing. 

Ten books a month. Five podcasts a week. Always scrolling, always queuing up the next recommendation.

But somewhere along the way, I realized I wasn’t really absorbing any of it. I was collecting, not connecting. So I slowed down.

Now, instead of chasing volume, I return to depth. I’d rather read one extraordinary book ten times than race through ten that barely land. I’d rather replay a podcast that shifted something in me than jump to another just because it’s new.

Every time I revisit something meaningful, I catch what I missed the first time. And the second. And the fifth. Ideas sink deeper. Words shape thoughts, not just memory. The message turns into something lived.

Repetition is how things take root.

I’m not here to keep up. I’m here to grow. And for me, growth comes more from depth than from speed.

Perks don’t make up for the essence of a meaningful team culture.

Trust, ownership, care, and respect can’t be replaced by pizzas.

Who shows up for the leader?

We spend so much time talking about how leaders should behave. Visionary. Decisive. Empathetic. Clear.

But rarely do we talk about the other side: how we show up for them.

Sometimes, the most generous thing you can do for a leader is to lead with them.

I’m constantly inspired by how each “thunder” steps in, offering not just support but their own leadership, making even the hardest moments feel like opportunities.

Because the person with the title is just another human, standing in front of a problem, hoping they’re making the right call. And maybe sometimes, they’re carrying so much weight that they don’t have the time to think through the solution or see it clearly.

And that’s when I see my colleagues step in. Not out of obligation. Not because they want to prove anything, but because they truly care. They care about the work. About people.

Care is the difference between waiting and leading. And leadership isn’t always about the title you hold.

If the person in charge is stuck, you don’t need to push them aside. Just walk beside them. Offer an idea. Ask a better question. Nudge the team forward.

Leaders carry weight. But they don’t have to carry it alone.

Marketing has lost its soul.

It became obsessed with funnels, metrics and conversion rates like the whole point was to trick people into clicking a button. We started treating humans like traffic. And somehow, that became normal.

But marketing, real marketing, is supposed to mean something. It’s supposed to challenge, to shift how people see the world. It should make us feel something. Want something better. Rethink the default.

Right now, too much of it feels like noise. Polished, A/B tested, SEO-optimized noise. And yeah, it might sell a few things, but at what cost? Trust? Meaning? Our collective attention span?

It doesn’t have to be like this.

We can do marketing that respects people. That starts with empathy, not urgency. That trades manipulation for real value. We can tell stories that actually matter and still grow a business. Shocking, I know.

Marketing doesn't need to be just about algorithms or tactics. 
It can be with and for humans.

Great teams don’t fail because of a lack of talent or effort. They fail because they’re unsure where to focus that effort.

If my team doesn’t know exactly what success looks like, that’s not their failure, it’s mine. If they’re unsure about priorities, if they’re hesitating, if they’re pulling in different directions, it’s because I haven’t made things clear enough.

People want to do great work. But they can’t read my mind. And “I already said it once” isn’t communication. That’s wishful thinking.

Clarity doesn’t mean I have to say something once. I have to say it until it sticks. Until there’s no confusion. Until everyone knows exactly what matters most.

Saying something once and expecting it to stick is like expecting a single gym session to get me in shape. 

Clarity needs repetition. So does leadership.

Most people begin their week on Monday. That’s the standard rhythm, and for a long time, I followed it too. But over time, I started feeling like I was never quite ahead of things.

So I made a quiet change. I started my week on Saturday.

It’s not about working more or trying to be different. It’s just that Saturday feels open. There’s less noise, fewer expectations. It’s easier to think. Easier to listen to what actually matters.

I don’t treat it like a grind. I don’t power through. I just use the stillness to get centered. To do the kind of work that needs space, not pressure.

I’m not chasing some perfect system or trying to squeeze more out of my days. I just find that starting earlier helps me carry a different kind of energy into the week. One that’s more intentional, more present.

By the time Monday arrives, I’ve already taken a few steps. I’ve already shaped a bit of the path. And that helps.

Today matters. What a great day to fight for your dreams, isn't it?

You’re always leading. The only question is: where?

Think of leadership like leaving footprints in fresh snow.

You take a step, others follow.
You veer off course, so do they.
You stand still, eventually, they freeze too.

And maybe you don’t notice it at first. The snow is soft. The path looks clean. But over time, the trail gets messy. People start hesitating. They’re not sure which direction is forward anymore. Some wander off, others just wait for someone (anyone) to walk like they mean it.
