That’s what happens when leaders stop leading by example.

Not because they’re bad people. But because they forget that every little action is part of the map others are following.

Leadership isn’t about clearing a path. It’s about walking one worth following.

So yeah, you’re always leading.

The only question is: are you taking your team somewhere they’ll be proud to end up? Or are you just dragging them through the snow?

Ever hired a team from a big agency, only to realize half the people on the call don’t need to be there?

That’s not a mistake. It’s the model.

Regional Plant Listener (sounds important). 
VP of Sandwich Logistics (vague, but impressive).
Chief Squirrel Whisperer (fancy title, but what do they actually do?).
A "specialist" (whatever that means).

Suddenly, you're paying for a small army.

Not because you need them. But because they need to hit their billable targets.

Don’t get me wrong, I’m not disregarding any specific role here. Most positions can be crucial in the right context and at the right time.

What I’m talking about here is the intentional practice of padding teams to justify inflated invoices. You know it well. 

Many big companies have mastered the art of over-selling. Over-staffing. Over-qualifying. It makes the invoice bigger, not the results better.

But do you want a show of force, or a team that actually gets things done?

You don’t need more people with fancy titles. You need the right people. Smart, focused, results-driven. People who deeply care about your project.

Always think twice when it comes to growing your team. More people don’t necessarily lead to better or greater results.

Still searching for that easy button?

There isn’t one. There’s no magic switch that makes everything easier or faster. The idea that success should come effortlessly is a myth. 

The real value lies in the struggle, the moments when you push through discomfort and uncertainty. That’s where the growth and the real results happen.

So, instead of looking for the easy way out, start looking for the opportunities to learn, to fail, and to try again. 

The hard path often leads to the most meaningful progress.

A job application is more than just a form filled and a CV. It’s hope. It’s effort. It’s someone taking a step toward a future they believe in.

Yet too often, that step is met with silence. No rejection. No feedback. Just nothing.

Imagine preparing for an exam and never getting your results. Training for a marathon and not knowing if you finished. Investing time, energy, and emotion into something, only to be met with a void. That’s what job seekers face when applications go unanswered.

Acknowledgment matters. Even a simple rejection brings clarity. A short piece of feedback can help someone refine their approach, improve their skills, and take the next step with confidence. Silence does none of that. Silence keeps people in limbo.

Every application represents potential. Talent. Ambition. Dedication. Ignoring it doesn’t just affect one human. It affects the culture we build in the workplace and beyond.

A rejection is better than silence. Feedback is even better. But nothing? Nothing is unacceptable. 

Respect the effort. Respond.

What happens when no one believes in you?

When your ideas are met with silence. When the people around you don’t see what you see. When doubt surrounds you, and even you start to wonder if you’re on the right track.

That’s what we explored last night at the 10th edition of Thunder Talks: Trusting yourself when nobody does.

It’s a tough road. It takes resilience. And sometimes, it takes hearing someone else’s story to remind you that you’re not alone.

That’s why Madalina’s presence was so powerful. She shared her journey with honesty and vulnerability, offering a glimpse into the moments that tested her. It was raw. It was real. And it reminded us all that trust is something you build, step by step.

To all of you who showed up, whether you spoke, listened, or joined us with your presence, thank you. These conversations matter because of you.

For those who couldn’t be there, I’ll leave you with a thought. I’ve always liked mathematics, and to me: Trust = certainty + faith.

Certainty in who you are, what you stand for, and the work you put in.
Faith that even when no one sees your impact, it's still real.

And here’s something to reflect on: How much of your lack of confidence is actually a lack of preparation?

See you at the next Thunder Talks.

I was lucky to have parents who encouraged me to explore, experiment, and grow in different areas of life.

Early on, I worked with my father on construction projects and helped my mother run a store. Later, I refereed football games, managed festival finances, and took on roles that seemed unrelated to programming. Yet, every experience sharpened my skills and accelerated my growth.

We’re told careers are ladders. Pick one and climb. But, from my point of view, they feel more like trees.

Branches extend in different directions: skills, careers, passions. All interconnected. We don’t just climb up. We move sideways, explore, adapt. Sometimes what feels like stagnation is just horizontal growth before a leap forward.

If another branch calls you, go for it. Changing direction is not failure. It’s leverage. Everything you’ve learned will serve you in ways you can’t yet see.

Broad knowledge creates unexpected advantages. Those who understand the whole tree move with confidence.

Somewhere along the way, we started acting like someone else’s win was our loss. Like success was a tiny pie, and every slice given to someone else meant less for us.

That’s nonsense.

Someone else’s win doesn’t take away from yours. There is no finish line where only one person gets to succeed. In fact, the more you celebrate others, the more you grow.

A friend lands a big opportunity? Cheer them on. A colleague puts in the work and delivers something great? Acknowledge it. A stranger makes a difference? Applaud them.

The true winners are not the ones who keep praise for themselves, but the ones who show up, acknowledge others' victories, and understand that helping others succeed only makes their own success more meaningful.

So root for people. Loudly. Genuinely. Often.

Because when we make a habit of celebrating the good in others, we create more of it in the world. And that’s a win for everyone.

You’ve got the best developers on your team. They’re smart, capable, and full of potential. So why are they still underperforming?

The problem is not their skills. But what can it be?

Way too many times the missing piece is psychological safety.

When team members don’t feel safe to speak up, raise concerns, or admit mistakes, problems go unnoticed, and innovation stagnates. Fear takes over, and instead of open conversations, you end up with silence. The silence of hidden problems that grow larger over time.

Every successful product is built on the foundation of vulnerability, trust, and a culture where sharing ideas and asking questions is encouraged. Where every voice is heard.

Without it, your team may be technically brilliant, but they won’t reach their full potential. Instead of pushing boundaries, they’ll play it safe. Instead of solving problems, they’ll avoid them.

If you want to reach your destination, make sure your route is paved with trust and openness. Put people first.

Agile. Scrum. Stand-ups. Sprints. Retros.

These are supposed to help us work faster and smarter. But when process becomes the goal instead of the tool, we lose sight of what really matters: our people.

If the team is drowning in rituals but still struggling to deliver, the problem isn’t their execution. It’s the system we’ve built around them. Process should serve the team, not the other way around.

A daily stand-up that doesn’t spark alignment is just a meeting. A sprint that ignores real-world constraints is just a deadline. A retrospective that doesn’t lead to change is just a history lesson.

People don’t burn out because they have too much work. They burn out because they’re forced to follow rules that don’t serve them. When a framework becomes more important than flexibility, we lose the very agility we set out to achieve.

We don’t win by following a framework. We win by working together in a way that makes sense for us.

The process itself should never be the priority. People should. And they should be supported to build systems that work for them, not against them.

A talented developer writes code, excited about the challenge ahead. But before they can even start, a message pops up.

"Hey, can you send me an update?"

A few lines in, another ping.

"Let’s hop on a quick call to go over your approach."

By noon, they’ve spent more time justifying their work than actually doing it.

This is what micromanagement looks like. Not leadership. Not guidance. Just an invisible leash, tightening with every unnecessary check-in.

Control kills creativity. When developers feel watched instead of trusted, they stop taking risks. They stop innovating. They do exactly what they’re told. Nothing more, nothing less.

The irony is, the managers who micromanage the most are often the ones who fear losing control. But control isn’t the goal. Impact is.

Give your people the right tools and the trust to get the job done.

They’ll do more than just work, but only if you let them.

You’re not bad at getting a job. 
School just didn’t prepare you for it.

For years, we’ve been sold the dream: go to school, get good grades, graduate, and a job will magically appear. But that system was built for a world that doesn’t exist anymore.

School didn’t teach you how to create opportunities. It taught you how to fill out forms, sit still, and memorize stuff you’ll never use again. And employers don’t care about your grades. They care about your hustle, creativity, and how well you handle failure.

The real world doesn’t ask, “What’s your grade in math?” It asks, “What problem can you solve, and why are you the one to do it?”

So if you’ve been struggling, don’t blame yourself. Blame the system that thought test scores and busywork would prepare you for anything.

Or better yet, take ownership. Because waiting for the system to change won’t get you anywhere. Learning real skills, taking risks, failing, adapting, and showing up for the work that matters, that will. And then, one day, you might change the system as well.

Your success isn’t printed on a piece of paper. It's in your ability to figure stuff out when things go sideways. It’s in your hands. And that’s a way better place to be.

Some people see service as a chore. A duty. Something they owe.

But I see it differently.

Being able to serve, whether through skills, time, or simply showing up, is a privilege. It means I have something to offer. It means I’m in a position to contribute, to make a difference, even in a small way.

Not everyone gets that chance. Some wish they could help but don’t have the means. Some are waiting for the right moment. Others don’t realize that even the simplest act of service (listening, sharing, supporting) has value.

I find real meaning in serving, and I deeply respect those who do the same. The ones who give without keeping score. The ones who use what they can instead of focusing on what they lack.

Because in the end, service is about impact. A powerful reminder that we have something worth giving.

And that’s a gift in itself.

Who are you serving today?

The status quo has a way of defending itself. It’s comfortable. Predictable. Safe.

And that’s exactly why it’s dangerous.

Because ‘this is just how things are done’ is not a reason anymore. It’s a warning sign. A signal that progress has stalled, that innovation is being choked by habit, that potential is being wasted in the name of familiarity.

In the dev industry, the stakes are even higher.

Old systems become shackles. Outdated processes don’t just slow us down, but they strangle what’s possible. The phrase ‘we’ve always done it this way’ turns from an explanation into an excuse.

And the worst part? Most people see it. They know what’s broken. But they stay quiet. Because change is uncomfortable. Because speaking up is risky. Because pushing forward means stepping into the unknown.

But silence? That’s the real risk.

Because the best systems, technical, cultural, and everything in between, aren’t built to preserve the past. They’re built to create the future.

So challenge the defaults. Question the assumptions. Reject the rules that no longer serve us.

The future isn’t waiting for permission. 
It belongs to those bold enough to build it. And you can be one of them.

For me, it’s hard to understand why businesses pour time and resources into products but overlook their people. It just doesn’t make sense.

Let’s break it down. Investing in people means investing in growth—both theirs and yours. When people feel supported and valued, they do excellent work. And when they do excellent work, they create work that makes a product stand out.

But if you focus only on the product and ignore the people behind it? You end up with something... decent. Functional, but forgettable. Because people who feel undervalued and overwhelmed won’t do their best work. And they won’t stick around long enough to make a real impact.

So, the equation is clear: invest in your people, and you’ll see the impact in your product.

But without that investment? You’re just chasing the next thing, hoping it’ll work. And deep down, we all know that’s never how greatness happens.

I get goosebumps every time I re-read this statement. Here’s why.

Who I am as a person is more a result of others' contributions than my own work.

No matter how hard you work, without mentors and colleagues it’s way harder to grow.

I see mentoring as an honour and being mentored as an immense privilege.

At first glance, you might think being a lifeguard means helping others when they ask for help, but it’s more than that.

A lifeguard actively looks for people who might be drowning.

It’s a proactive state of being. It’s a role I admire and I strive to fulfil.

Everything started with a dream.
And to this day, I wake up to fight for that dream.

A vision of all of us. Of us doing work that truly matters while caring for each other, not just chasing the big number.

I dream of a world where we all find meaning in our work. And that’s what drives me to keep going, to give back, to serve.

Call me crazy, but I strongly believe we can change the way we work, and in doing so, change the world around us.

I know we have a long way to go. But if not now, when? If not us, who?

I believe our work can be a vehicle. One that serves our collective missions, and not just pays the bills. A vehicle that helps transform society for the better.

While far too many companies are solely profit-driven, I believe in a world where people matter most, and where they come first.

And, funny enough, my experience with Thunder has proven that such work is not only more creative but also more productive. More and better things get done when people who care about each other come together.

We committed to putting our colleagues first, and that created a safe and encouraging environment where we can serve our partners—a culture where we can innovate.

In a way, our mission at Thunder is to prove that work can be meaningful. In that sense, Thunder itself is the mission. And every day matters, not just the big number.

We are here to serve, to chase meaning, to create better things.

I hope you, too, live or fight for such a dream. Don’t settle for a job that simply pays the bills. Seek work that gives you purpose.

Some will call you crazy. But some will join.

Most people do what’s required. They check the boxes. They meet expectations. And on paper, that’s enough.

But the work that sticks, the work people talk about, the work that changes things, that’s never just ‘enough’. It’s something more.

Early in my journey, I learned this the hard way. I saw what happened when people delivered exactly what was asked and nothing more. It was fine. Acceptable. But it never sparked loyalty. Never built momentum. Never turned customers into advocates or teams into movements.

Then I noticed something: the people who went the extra mile. Who added the thoughtful detail, the unexpected touch, the small moment of delight.

They were remembered.

Overdelivering was never about working harder, but about caring deeper. Showing up with generosity, with thoughtfulness, with the kind of effort that says, this matters. And when people feel that? Trust is built. Loyalty grows. A simple project turns into a lasting impact.

So the next time you’re tempted to do just enough, pause. Ask yourself:

What if ‘good enough’ is just the starting line?
What if the real opportunity lies beyond expectations?
What if today, you made something unforgettable?

Because the work that matters, the work that lasts, is never just enough. It’s always a little more. A little braver. A little better. A little bolder.

I grew up watching my parents care about the people around them, always finding ways to support the greater good, whether through work or just by being kind and caring.

Then I grew up some more. And, surprise! The world didn’t seem to work that way. Everywhere I turned, I saw people playing the “me, myself, and I” game like it was the only rule that mattered.

Still, I stuck to what I learned at home. I kept believing that collective success is worth more than individual wins. And, honestly? It’s been one of the best decisions of my life.

Of course, that didn’t stop people from warning me:

"You’re going to get taken advantage of."
"People will just use you."
"You’ll look like a fool."

In other words: "Be selfish like the rest of us, or you’ll regret it!"

Well, guess what? Jokes on them. Not only do I feel fulfilled when I help others, but it turns out that success has a funny way of showing up when you work with people, not against them. 

In our team at Thunder, we fought to build something bigger than any of us—not by stepping on each other, but by lifting each other up.

The truth is, deep down, I think we all have that instinct to work together. It’s just been buried under fear, insecurity, and a world that keeps screaming, “Compete! Win! Take what’s yours!”

Change is already happening. More and more people are realizing that we’re stronger together than alone.

So if you’ve ever felt that pull toward collective success, don’t let the world gaslight you into thinking it’s a flaw. It’s not. It’s exactly what we need.

We owe it to ourselves, to nature, to each other, to build a society that’s about us, not just me. 

No one left behind. No one forgotten.

It’s easy to get lost in the tech.

In so many startup teams, I see it happen—people are fantastic at writing code, but when it comes to working together? That’s when things start to fall apart. 

We’ve become so obsessed with the tools, the frameworks, the perfect solution, that we forget the most powerful thing we have: each other.

The truth is, no matter how great your coders are, they can’t do it alone. Tech is just a tool. It’s the way we collaborate, communicate, and align with the vision that really drives success.

The best code in the world is worthless if it’s built in isolation or doesn’t move the project forward in a meaningful way.

Focus less on how fast you can write the perfect code, and more on how well you can work as a unit. That’s where the real innovation is.

Humans first.

Innovation doesn’t wait for approval.

It doesn’t wait in line. It doesn’t come from someone else’s green light, endless meetings, or playing it safe.

It comes from ownership. It comes from someone who sees a gap and steps in. Someone who stops waiting for direction and starts creating possibility.

When you truly own the work, everything changes. You stop asking, ‘What’s the plan?’, as if someone else holds the answers. Instead, you ask, ‘What’s possible?’, because now, the future is yours to shape.

And yet, in so many workplaces, innovation is suffocated before it can even start. Micromanaged. Controlled. Boxed in by process and permission.

Ownership is not something granted. It’s a mindset. A decision. A commitment to take responsibility, embrace uncertainty, and create something that matters.

Want innovation? Stop managing. Start trusting. Give people the space to own their work, not just execute it. Let them lead, experiment, and push beyond what’s been done before.

Because when people truly own what they create, innovation is inevitable.

You’ve seen it before. Someone reaches the top, they’re winning, they’re unstoppable… until suddenly, they’re not.

Why? Did they anger the universe? Did their luck run out? Nope. Most of the time, they just got comfortable.

They hit a milestone, kicked back, and thought, "Well, that’s it! I’ve made it! Time to coast forever." But forever actually lasted just about a couple of years, if not months.

This is why I remind myself of a brilliant concept from a book I once read: The Second Curve.

The idea is simple: When you’re at the top of your game (or even right before), that’s exactly when you should start building what’s next. Always anticipate the peak of your success so you can adjust your direction before you start declining.

Got a promotion? Awesome. Don’t just frame your new title—make sure you’re leveling up your skills to match it. Just won an award? Fantastic. Now use that momentum to kick off an even bigger project instead of basking in the glow of your own greatness.

The problem? People assume things will stay good forever. They don't.

(they don't stay bad forever either, keep going, you got this!)

So, if you’re not growing, you’re slowly becoming that person who talks about their one big success from ten years ago.

Success is not a golden ticket to autopilot mode. It’s fuel. 
Use it before it expires.

And, most importantly, use it to help others and give back.

I’ve always believed in giving our team the freedom to own their work.

It’s a blessing I cherish. Not because it’s easy, but because it’s powerful.

Handing over control doesn’t mean stepping back entirely. It means having the courage to trust that they’ll step forward with their own vision and take responsibility for what they do.

Most people think leadership requires a tight grip on everything. Many leaders assume that by controlling every detail, they can guide the team to success.

The way my dad led his three-man team in a remote village, far from any leadership book, taught me otherwise.

I’ve learned that leadership thrives in moments of detachment. When I let go, I give my team space to lead, to make mistakes, and to find their own solutions. That’s where innovation takes root.

Watching my team take ownership is transformational. When they have the freedom to create, they rise to the occasion. They become more invested, more driven, and more passionate about the work.

It becomes their mission, and my role is to serve them.

Without a mission, what are you working for?

Or even a better question, why not aiming for purpose-driven work?

I just don’t get it. How could I make sense of working for years towards nothing?

- A bigger salary is not a dream, it’s barely an objective.
- A fancy role title doesn’t mean anything in the end.
- Equity from a vehicle that goes nowhere will never bring you fulfilment.

If you’re just starting your career, I’m with you, then you might be forced to accept a mediocre job to pay the bills. We all need to start somewhere.

But, but.. years into the process you just can’t stay in a boat that goes circles just for the sake of making a profit. Like.. you can, but why would you?

What is the most epic mission that drives you crazy about it?

In the beginning, those types of questions freaked me out. The weight of the responsibility that comes with them is huge.

But, you know what’s even scarier? The bill of regret we might get later on if we don’t intentionally decide on a mission for our career and life.

I bet you won’t be happy with just getting by.

If you never had such conversations with yourself, have them today.

Start with some sort of clarity. Pick a direction and then start moving.

The vision will change in time for sure, but, not moving shouldn’t be an option.

If you feel alone on your path, keep moving, you’ll eventually find people chasing similar north stars. Keep your steps moving.

Crazy things happen when you start talking about where you’re going and why you want to get there. The naysayers start to judge, but, sooner or later, the right people for you will appear. You’ll find yourselves.

The price of fulfilling a mission includes the judgment of those who don’t believe it. 
Some will, some won’t, so what?

A mission sets our souls on fire. We simply yearn to be part of a collective mission.

Every project has deliverables: code shipped, designs finalized, campaigns launched. That’s what shows up on the invoice. That’s what gets measured.

But the real work? The work that leaves a mark? It happens in the spaces between.

It’s how you show up in every conversation. How you listen, collaborate, and care. How you turn tasks into partnerships and transactions into trust.

Because great work is built with intention.

Anyone can hit deadlines. Anyone can tick boxes. But the teams people want to work with, the ones they recommend, remember, and return to, are the ones who bring more to the table than what’s expected. They bring curiosity. Generosity. Humanity.

Progress isn’t driven by deliverables alone. It’s fueled by connection. By people who care about the work and the people they’re doing it for.

At the end of the day, the product will speak for itself. But what people will remember most is how you made them feel along the way.

That’s what turns projects into partnerships. That’s what makes the work matter. And that's what I stand for.

Each step you climb on your career ladder should deepen your sense of responsibility to give back and serve others.

Having people work for or with you is an immense privilege, not a reason to feel entitled.

Serve them. Care about them. Make time for them.

And, most importantly, ensure that the vision you’re chasing as a team includes their becoming, not just yours.

They gave you their trust. You owe them.

There is one key aspect I never overlook in any retrospective.

Recently, our colleague Iuliana Pap wrapped up a long term journey of multiple years on a challenging project.

Most likely you can't have it today, but today you can decide that you will.

And today you can also start taking small steps in the direction you believe makes you happy.

What's your excuse?

[Translated from Romanian] I'm glad to see more and more companies and organizations around whose main goal is no longer profit at any cost.

Places where people are respected, appreciated and can do meaningful work alongside colleagues and leaders who value both collective and individual goals.

If this doesn't sound like the community you're part of, maybe it's a good time to think that you too deserve such a work context.

Maybe you need to develop some new skills, deepen some you already have, or take on a few extra responsibilities.

None of this should be a real obstacle if you truly believe you deserve it. The biggest problem is that many people have been wrongly convinced that they don't deserve it.

No matter how long it's been since you gave up having strong confidence in yourself, don't forget you're only one decision away from being confident in your own strength again.

Choose to believe in yourself. Choose to believe you deserve more.

[Translated from Romanian] In leadership, the end doesn't justify the means.

It's irrelevant if you are about to miss a goal.
Nothing excuses offensive, abusive or disrespectful behavior.

Human values and meaningful relationships between members must always come first.

Any other approach is a hypocrisy we must stop accepting.

[Translated from Romanian] It's time to stop working for bosses obsessed with control, and work for leaders who promote relationships based on respect, trust and transparency.

If you know you are serious, responsible and very good at what you do, it's time to stop accepting to work buried in micromanagement.

Choose to go into work contexts where you are truly appreciated as a person, and not seen only as a resource.

[Translated from Romanian] Beware of organizations that consider soft skills a nice to have.

In a healthy work culture, it is vital to be human and to be able to build meaningful connections with your colleagues.

[Translated from Romanian] If you want accelerated growth, it's essential to find a mentor.
A good mentor is practically a cheat sheet.

When it comes to choosing a mentor, here are 3 ideas I encourage you to keep in mind.

- They should want a better future for you than you dare to dream of.
- They should have a vision of long-term collaboration with you.
- They should have walked the path you want to walk.

There is a big difference between someone trying to manipulate you for their own interest and a true mentor. If you are attentive enough, you will feel the difference.

[Translated from Romanian] When it comes to leadership, the mental and emotional state of the people on the team says more about the quality of the leader than your technical skills.

Still, I see a growing trend around me toward real leadership and that makes me very happy.

Slowly, slowly we are having the courage to understand that a team that wants to work Agile can't be run like a factory from the 1960s.

What traits do you think are essential for a leader?

[Translated from Romanian] For me, one way to define success would be the ability to get back up and keep doing good, giving and helping, even if you went through hard trials that you can't find meaning in and that are unfair and at odds with your kindness.

How do you define success?

[Translated from Romanian] Art is the intentional act of using your humanity to create a change for the better in another person.

I read this description in one of Seth Godin's books and found in it my vision of what it means to be an artist.

For me art is not found only in a few categories of activities like painting or sculpture. I see it rather as a remarkable level at which you can do any work.
Remarkable doesn't necessarily mean very well paid, but having high intrinsic value.

A person who paints a copy of a photo (or of another painting) is not an artist, just a mediocre painter who let themselves be convinced they don't have enough "talent" to create. They put no humanity into that copy and nothing that makes them unique, only time.

On the other hand, a person who has the courage to follow a different vision, invests passion, time and resources and manages to devise a strategy that revolutionizes an aspect of health, is certainly an artist.

In my view, in every field there are people who embrace mediocrity (most) and people who are artists (few).
Being an artist is a decision, not a trait you are born with.

What do you choose to be?

[Translated from Romanian] If you read a book a week, it practically costs you about 35 lei to have at least one hour of quiet and disconnection every day while you grow and gain knowledge that will surely impact your life in a decisive way.

I simply don't think there is an investment with a better return.

[Translated from Romanian] Even if today you are not doing the work you'd like, don't underestimate the power of respect for a job well done.

How you treat the work is much more important than your job title.
No matter what stage of your career you're in, choose to give your all.

[Translated from Romanian] Every wave matters, because you never actually know which one is the last.

I try to always keep a feeling of gratitude lit inside me.

Often we let things of little importance completely spoil our perspective on life.

No matter how hard some moments are and how misunderstood some events in our lives are, I still believe we always have many reasons to be thankful.

You never solve a wrong with another wrong. No matter how hard it is for you, create good and share it with others too.

[Translated from Romanian] Among the many good things I learned from my mother, one essential one was that in her view people were always equal.

Neither she nor my father ever made distinctions between people based on their financial situation, ethnicity, spiritual orientation or any other aspect of life.

In many contexts in life we find ourselves in competition with other people, and in essence I don't think that is something bad, as long as the competition doesn't become toxic.

I understood from a young age that even when I won I remained equal to the one I defeated, and that always helped me stay grounded at the end of any success.

And, at the same time, when I was the one losing, I still felt equal to the one who beat me.
In other words I didn't see myself as a whole failure.

Practically, I managed not to identify with my results. And for that I don't have enough words to express the gratitude I feel toward my parents.

You are not defined by your results, neither when you succeed nor when you fail. You are much more than that.

You are who you are, not what you achieve.

[Translated from Romanian] Sooner or later in our lives, moments appear that totally change the reality of our lives in a way we don't want.

What are you doing today to be prepared for those moments?

You won't always have the chance to change something. Sometimes there will be no solutions left.

Sometimes the only price we are given the chance to pay is acceptance.

At the end of a failed exam, a business failure, a breakup or any kind of critical moment in your life, the choice to accept reality and keep living by your principles belongs to you.

The sadness you feel when you find out you were betrayed can change you into a dishonest person or can encourage you even more to be a trustworthy person.

You can see any problem as a reason to give up or as an opportunity to continue.

The choice always belongs to you.

[Translated from Romanian] An unusual piece of advice that will make a difference in your career.

Every time a colleague of yours has a success, be sincerely happy for them and show them appreciation and gratitude.

The idea that other colleagues' successes imply your failure is an illusion.
In reality you compete only with yourself.

Supporting an environment where effort and successes are recognized means putting your shoulder to a culture in which you too will be appreciated in turn.

[Translated from Romanian] I'm increasingly looking to develop my knowledge in all aspects of life.

I believe it's essential to be able to understand as big a picture as possible, and not be a specialist who only knows their own niche.

Basically, I'm looking to be a good generalist. That doesn't mean I don't have a main direction, only that I'm interested in understanding, at a general level, other sectors in my field or even adjacent fields.

I've felt this has helped me a lot, both personally and professionally, in the role I have within the Thunder team.

What do you think? Do you think it's important to invest time in accumulating this kind of knowledge?

[Translated from Romanian] Every time I set a goal, I choose to give myself more attempts than it seems necessary.

If you are determined not to give up, your chances of succeeding increase.

[Translated from Romanian] When you decide to build something remarkable, the force of resistance makes its presence felt immediately. It is most likely also the reason why we often end up giving up very quickly.

The status quo, our insecurities and our fears together form this force of resistance. It fights to keep things as they are and is never interested in a better solution, especially when the rewards come only in the long term.

Basically, even if for certain moments you manage to beat it and take steps in the direction of your vision, it will always come back with other arguments meant to make you give up.

The force of resistance tries with all its might to make you procrastinate, on the idea that "late is the first step to never". It will make you look for perfection, or ship something completely unprepared so that it fails as fast as possible. It will create excuses related to lack of resources or bad timing. It will tell you that you or the people on the team are not ready enough for what you want to build. It will make you worry about what other people will say about you.

All these arguments, and many other extremely creative ones, come from our reptilian brain, which is not very curious to do remarkable work, but rather mediocre work with minimum effort.

Whatever change you want to make in your life, you must be ready for this almost continuous fight against resistance.

My strategy in this fight is based on my vision for the future (my dreams).

This vision is built around the essential principles of my life, so the counterarguments I bring to this whole internal discussion are very strong ones.

It sounds stupid, but it's a way of beating myself using who I am.

How do you fight resistance?

[Translated from Romanian] The success indicator should be wellbeing, not a number.

What good is a company with dozens of unhappy but profitable employees?

What do you do with a big pile of money if you don't have close people next to you with whom to use it meaningfully?

How does a well-paid job you can't wait to escape help you?

How long will you keep believing it's about things and not about people?

[Translated from Romanian] I meet quite often people who want to change their job, saying they feel plateaued and want more.

I usually ask them whether they have explicitly expressed their wish for more responsibility and more opportunities to the people in the current company who are in a position to offer them.

Strangely, most of the time their answer is negative.
Basically they wait for everything to come on its own, without proactively seeking their own growth.

I'm convinced there are cases where companies have no interest in creating a favorable context for people's development.
In those situations, changing the company is most likely the best decision you can make.

However, in many other cases, all it takes is a change in your attitude to get out of that plateau.

Once you've changed your attitude, and with it your perspective on the situation, all you have to do is ask. In many cases there will most likely be opportunities you can take on.

If you truly want responsibilities, you will ask for them.
Otherwise, you most likely just want to be perceived as a person with responsibilities.

You can basically find another job in the same place, if your attitude changes.
[Translated from Romanian] I believe any form of success also brings the responsibility of helping others succeed. Together we are always better off.

[Translated from Romanian] I recently found this idea in a book I read and I love it incredibly.

I believe an important aspect of success lies in the idea of "together".

For me, people have always been a meaning of my life.

I have always sought to be around them, to try to help them, or simply to live experiences alongside them.

That's exactly why I'm very grateful to all the people at @thethunderteam, and I'm glad to have the chance to work and grow alongside them.

At the end of the day, they are actually the company, they are actually the meaning.

[Translated from Romanian] I'm increasingly trying to focus on the good I can do, instead of having a victim attitude and constantly complaining about the quality of some aspects of our society today.

I agree that the Romanian state is almost synonymous with the 'state for nothing', and I think we must be proactive in seeking to sanction the abuses it commits.

But I think it's at least as important to do the good that is within our reach.

For example, not having up-to-date libraries in all schools in the country is certainly a serious problem, but that shouldn't be my excuse not to choose to give, as far as I can afford, valuable books to children every month.

We can all be useful where we are.

[Translated from Romanian] If you want to change, start by improving a few habits.
And I don't mean major habits, but almost banal but consistent changes.

It's important to dream, but as soon as you have an idea of your vision, you must return to the present and start with small steps.

Big words said in a void won't take you far at all, but a few small successful actions can produce a remarkable domino effect.

Later, your identity will change as a natural consequence of the actions you choose to repeat.

[Translated from Romanian] Change doesn't happen, it is created.

For 30 years we've sat with our hands in our laps waiting for change to appear around the corner. I think we can all consider that we've learned the secret: change doesn't come if we don't create it.

Choose to focus on the difference you can make daily near you. Help a person in need, make time to mentor a young person, give as much as you can give, take your responsibilities seriously, read about what rights you have and seek to have them respected.

Instead of waiting for some miraculous change to come overnight, I think we should fight so that today is a little better than yesterday, and tomorrow a little better than today.

[Translated from Romanian] Don't be fooled by the status quo.

Do the things your colleagues avoid. Look to show yourself available for effort.
Be punctual. Say yes to challenges. Offer your help and support.

Choose to do the basics well and with respect for the work.
[Translated from Romanian] The leadership role comes with the responsibility of serving people, not the power to command them.

[Translated from Romanian] Who doesn't like a good story? I certainly do.

Seth Godin is one of my favorite authors. I've already read over 10 of the 20 books he's written, yet I keep discovering new valuable ideas in every book.

I'll leave here a few notes I wrote as I read the book, which I think are worth each of us reflecting on.

- A vote is a statement about the voter, not about the candidate.

- Marketing is an art, not a science, because the answers are never obvious.

- The first impression is extremely important, but since we don't know when it happens (not the first contact, but the first impression) it is essential to use all the tools and means we have to convey one and the same message, to tell one and the same story.

[Translated from Romanian] I think we too often choose to see life as good or bad, when it is actually never good or bad, but always both good and bad.

I believe, however, that a perspective that takes into account both the good and the bad parts is much more useful.

Especially when we go through a very hard period, loaded with failures and/or reasons for upset, I think it's essential to remind ourselves of the things we should still be grateful for.

So choose to see the rainbow even if you're still in the middle of the rain.

[Translated from Romanian] Usually, in the face of any problem, all you need is someone.

Whether it's a close friend, a stranger who brings a kind word at the right moment, family or a life partner, it is always people who actually make the difference.

A failure weighs on us much harder when we are alone, and a success doesn't mean much if you have no people to enjoy it with.

This "zero sum game" is actually a big deception. There's no point in winning 10 lei by making someone else lose 10 lei. Being alone at the top is probably the most painful form of failure.

[Translated from Romanian] In traffic, the green light means "go!". In our lives, green lights are the affirmation of the personal way in which we live. They tell us "yes" and give us what we want.

Green lights can, however, be disguised as yellow or red traffic lights. A moment of introspection, a detour, a pause to rethink something, a disagreement, an illness, a pain. Standing still, a failure, suffering, death. We don't like yellow and red lights. They slow us down or interrupt our flow. They are hard to manage. On the timeline, what yesterday was a red light can lead us today toward a green light. Every destruction leads to new constructions, every death leads to birth and every pain leads to a lesson that enlightens.

It all depends on how we understand the challenge in front of us and how we relate to it. Do we persist, recenter or give up? The choice is ours alone.

[Translated from Romanian] I very often meet people who have a lot to offer, but who have been frightened enough that they choose to hold back and stay indifferent, thus indirectly supporting the status quo.

Through many of the things I do, I try to help these people rediscover the courage to be the change.

I've read several statistics in different books saying that, on average, it would be enough for around 25% of people to opt for a change for it to later become the choice of the masses.

Opting for a change doesn't mean voting in a LinkedIn poll that you want it. It means being that change every day.

I believe that in Romania we are 25% of people who want and feel that we deserve a much better country. But, most likely, we are not vocal and active enough when something doesn't happen around us the way we feel common sense and fairness say it should.

We are too passive when someone throws trash on the ground.
We are too absent when it would be essential to support certain initiatives that would back this change.
We are too silent in the face of corruption.
We feel too small and too few, but actually that's not the case at all.

For example, in recent months I have increasingly chosen to change my bad habit of feeling inferior and giving up when a public servant (and not only) behaves with a total lack of respect and doesn't feel like having a simple conversation to give me the information I need, even though they are paid to do so.

In practice, I try to be less tolerant of things that aren't right.

What other simple changes like this do you think we could implement?
What do you do to support change?

[Translated from Romanian] I believe that more and more in the coming years, for companies and not only, the conversation about success will move further away from profit and closer to meaning, contribution to the community and impact on the environment.

That doesn't mean a company shouldn't be profitable, only that profit at any price will no longer be a widely accepted solution.

If you want to create such a company, you are unlikely to succeed with a culture built on many rules and a strict system that always keeps people within easily quantifiable indicators. Or, in other words, inside a box.

Rather, I'd say you need a culture built on principles like trust, transparency, empathy or generosity.

I know, it sounds naive, but it isn't. We've accepted for too long this boss-who-gives-orders approach used by many financially wealthy people.

We've reached the point where it's hard, if not impossible, for us to imagine that another variant could work. I believe it can be done differently, and that is what I'm trying to build together with my colleagues at Thunder.

To make a real change, I think you need to offer people a context in which they feel that failure is part of the process. An essential part when you want to challenge the status quo.

So I believe we should start putting more and more value on the uniqueness of the people we work with and stop treating them as mere numbers.

Every person matters.

[Translated from Romanian] The most essential thing I've understood about passion is that it is simply a decision.

Looking around, I see many people running from one place to another, failing to "find" their passion. At the same time, I know people who bring passion with them through every door they walk through.
In other words, passion is not "project-specific" but "people-specific".

A few aspects that can influence your decision to be passionate:
- The vision of the company you work for.
- The quality of your relationships with the people on your team (and not only).
- How appreciated and respected you feel.
- The impact you feel your work has (or doesn't have).
- How fairly you are rewarded for your effort and time.

These factors, and/or others that matter to you, play an important role in shaping how much passion you can put into your work.

But, no matter how high the indicators for these aspects are, everything rests on the foundation of your decision to be passionate.

If you don't feel passionate about what you do, you may be in one of the following two contexts:
- You work in a toxic environment where it's hard, or you don't even feel it makes sense, to decide to be passionate. The solution is a simple one and it's also a decision: to leave.
- You have a healthy environment with many opportunities but you're looking for passion in the wrong place: on the outside. You are passionate if you decide to be, not if something external makes you be.

For me, passion is born from respect for a job well done, from love for people and from gratitude for the opportunities we all have.

And I decide to put passion into absolutely everything I do.

What do you decide to be passionate about?

[Translated from Romanian] I have the chance to work alongside people I consider true friends. I see work as a privilege, a joy, and not as something I should do everything possible to get away from.

Work takes up so much of our life that I consider it unacceptable not to seek meaningful work, alongside people with whom you share a vision and a clear set of values.

If you're not happy with your work, if you don't feel you resonate with your colleagues, if your boss is a jerk, if you're not offered any opportunity to evolve, to make a difference or to build a better future for yourself, what is your exit plan?

If you don't have a plan, decide today that it's time to make one.

If you can't manage on your own, ask for help.

If you have no one close who could guide you, leave me a message and I'll try to help you as much as I can.

[Translated from Romanian] We are all weird in many ways, and I think it's important to let our uniqueness represent us, and not to try to fit into boring templates that many people try to impose on others for the sake of profit.

When it comes to marketing, those whom Seth calls weird are actually the 'early adopters' that your product or service should focus on at the beginning.

Obviously, the knowledge in the book transcends the field of Marketing, and can certainly be useful in many other aspects of life.

Here are a few notes I found in the book that struck me as interesting.

What matters is not only how big the average is, but often how big the deviation from the average is.

Being rich means being able to make choices, not having a sum of money.

Success is increasingly won by feeding niches, not by imposing normality on the masses.

Seen up close, normality disappears.

Do you fight for the status quo or do you support the weird ones?

You are weird and that should make you happy.

[Translated from Romanian] Very many people (companies) simply seek to do a lot, fast and at any price. Practically all meaning is sacrificed for the sake of gain, and most of the time that is a purely financial one.

I've met many people who own companies that could very easily create much better working conditions for their people, and help much more with their professional and personal development. Yet they choose not to, probably because they validate their success only through the holy profit and nothing more.

How much is a human smile worth? Too little, unfortunately, in many cases.

The limit beyond which one doesn't go when it comes to investing in people's development is extremely low. I wonder, could this have something to do with the level of the society we live in?

I think we should define success more often by the quality of the relationships we have with our colleagues, by the mission our work supports, by the meaning produced by our effort, or by the wellbeing we manage to build both in our own life and in that of others.

Growth at any price should not be the principle on which a business is built.

For anyone who runs a smaller or larger business in one form or another, I'm leaving here a question that I think is worth asking quite regularly.

As a result of the growth decision you're about to make, will the company improve or only expand?

[Translated from Romanian] A large part of what we don't like about today's Romania is actually a status quo.

I don't think it's a very good strategy to expect that certain people who have been shamelessly stealing for over 30 years will simply stop on their own one Tuesday.

Just as I don't think it helps much to merely complain that things aren't different.

I think a better strategy would be to build the change.

To my joy, I believe we already have some weird ones who are slowly building a change. The change we all want.

Here I'm referring to people like Dragoș Pătraru, Paul Olteanu, Alex Nedea, and a few more, obviously together with the teams around them, because no person is an island.

I fight daily, and I like to think that sometimes I succeed, to be a weird one too.

I try to be part of this movement by focusing on the good and the difference I can make around me.

Don't think you're too small to be important.

We are the system. We are the change.

Do you fight for the status quo or do you support the weird ones?

[Translated from Romanian] I try to be as grateful for the clouds as I am for the sun.

I recently reread some notes I took while reading the book 4000 Weeks and I reminded myself how liberated I felt when I chose to look my finitude and limits in the eye and accept them.

I am a very ambitious person and I believe it's important to dream very big.

At the same time, I believe it's essential to understand that some things are, simply, not in our control. They don't depend on us, and we don't have the power to change them.

Accepting that you have some limits doesn't mean limiting yourself or giving up easily. It simply means having the courage to recognize when you are not given the chance to change certain aspects of your reality.

Instinctively it may seem comfortable to take on a victim attitude, but that surely only makes the situation worse.

When you go through periods with many clouds, try to find courage rather than feed a victim attitude.

Look for help. You don't have to be alone under those clouds. And don't forget that sooner or later the sun will appear again.

[Translated from Romanian] I was raised from a young age in a family that always sought, from the little it had, to give.

I learned early that a whole of mine is never more valuable than half for me and half given away.

If you give yourself the chance to truly experience the joy and power of generosity, I firmly believe your perspective on life will change.

Those who know me know that until around 21 I was very proud (actually foolish) that I didn't read. But a book received as a gift completely changed the trajectory of my life.

So, a few years ago I started, with small steps, to give books as gifts too. And today I keep doing it more and more.

All of these 100+ books, and many more to come, will go to as many people as possible. I look forward to giving them away together. 📚

[Translated from Romanian] I'm glad to see more and more companies and organizations around whose main goal is no longer profit at any price.

Places where people are respected, appreciated and where they can do meaningful work alongside colleagues and leaders who value both collective and individual goals.

If that doesn't sound like the community you are part of, maybe it's a good moment to consider that you too deserve such a work context.

Once you have truly decided that you deserve it, it's only a matter of time until you find such an opportunity.

Maybe you need to develop some new skills, deepen some skills you already have, or take on a few extra responsibilities.

None of this should represent a real obstacle if you truly believe you deserve it. The biggest problem is that many people have been wrongly convinced that they don't deserve it.

No matter how long it's been since you gave up having strong confidence in yourself, don't forget you are only one decision away from being confident in your own strengths again.

Choose to believe in yourself. Choose to believe you deserve more.

A fixed mindset keeps you stuck where you are now.

On the other hand, in a growth mindset, you always strive to improve your abilities, learn new things, and improve your skills.

Embracing a growth mindset is essential if you seek to speed up your career growth significantly.

Everybody in your company is a brand ambassador.

Don’t make the mistake of believing that only the branding and marketing team(s) work on that aspect of your business.

I once bought a tennis racket from a sports shop, and it came with its own bag.

Mistakes happen. We all make them. Even though I didn’t like that I had to go back to the shop to remove the tags, that wasn’t the worst part.

The worst part was that the employee I discussed with when I arrived back in the store (a different one than the guy who forgot the tag on it) had no intention to apologise for the hassle.

She knew it wasn't her fault, so what was there to apologise for?

Nobody taught her that it would have been beneficial for her and the company’s brand to apologise in her colleague's name.

It wasn’t the Instagram marketing campaign that screwed that company’s image in my eyes. Instead, it was the overworked (and probably underpaid) cashier.

First, create a culture in which everybody matters. Respect and care about everyone involved in the company.

Second, help them understand they are all responsible for the company’s brand.

Third, always reward those who step up to cover their colleagues' mistakes in order to protect the brand.

Time is an essential resource, no matter what you try to achieve in your career or as an entrepreneur.

I believe indecision has two significant downsides in anybody’s journey. First, it puts doubt in your mind, and second, it makes you lose time because you postpone your next action.

For me, the main reason behind indecision was always fear of failure. 

We all know failure is part of any process. There is no way around it. Yet, a lot of the time, we are still scared to fail.

However, what helped me the most in my journey was that I realised there are two types of failures.

Some failures screw everything up, and some can be managed and overcome.

So, whenever I have to decide, my first goal is to understand what type of failure could result from that decision. 

Doing that, you’ll probably notice that in most cases, the decisions we have to make are not the ones which lead to a complete failure. Instead, many of them are decisions you can afford to mess up.

Thus, making these non-crucial decisions faster wins you time and allows you to learn from the mistakes that occur along the way while still being able to move forward without overthinking a single situation.

On the other hand, if you stay indecisive in those situations, you’ll stop yourself (and your team) from achieving your goals.

If it’s not critical, then make decisions fast. You’ll be able to adapt and overcome the small failures you might experience.

#thehumandeveloper #bedicisive #adapt #overcomefailures #grow

The internet changed the game forever. We are now one click away from an incredible amount of knowledge, inspiration and tools.

In one way or another, many of us picked one or more mentors that we admire and from whom we might try to learn valuable lessons.

If you feel like you understood their words but get stuck when trying to apply them in your life, it could be because you didn’t study deep enough their thinking process.

I think it’s essential to take the time and study their journey to understand their messages better.

Here is a quote from @garyvee “You're not lazy, you just don't love what you do.”

This statement certainly sends a bold message about the importance of loving what you do. Reading it, you could start to believe that once you find what you love doing, your laziness will go away in an instant.

I doubt that is going to happen. However, after years of studying Gary, reading his books and trying to understand his mindset, here is how this statement translates to me:

“The work you love brings you energy when you get to do it. It’s the kind of work that inspires you when you think about your long-term journey. In the macro, you should have fun doing it, making you feel fulfilled, happy and driven, even if in the micro, you might feel like not doing it sometimes. “

I’m not trying to tell you what Gary wanted to say. The point was to illustrate that after you deeply study your mentors, you’ll manage to read between the lines. 

You’ll see the meaning behind the expressions, extract more value from them and most importantly, grab some precise action points to take in your life.

#thehumandeveloper #inspirationalpeople #mentors #quotestoliveby #godeeper

Taking on teaching responsibilities was one of the best decisions for my career as a developer.

In the beginning, I didn’t feel prepared (most probably I wasn’t), I was scared, and I thought I wouldn’t be able to help at all. But, regardless of my doubts, I said yes.

My first attempt was at an internship program within a company I worked for.

I did my best to create an action plan for every technical lesson and be ready for possible unexpected questions from the interns. Of course, I forgot the plan, and indeed there were questions I had no answers for.

In the end, the internship wasn’t as good as it could have been if a more experienced colleague had done it. But that would have been a short-term decision for both myself and the company. We all know that short-term thinking affects the long-term journey.

Fast forward to this day, I believe it’s essential not to create a fake impression of you knowing everything. 

So stop waiting to become a genius before starting to teach others. That’s not what they are looking for. They need a kind mentor who cares about them.

Seeing their mentor being comfortable with making mistakes and not having all the answers makes them realise you are as human as they are. Such a context gives them the courage to fail and raise questions, which ultimately leads to greater progress.

On the other hand, all these experiences helped me solidify my knowledge, learn new things, develop new abilities and create more clarity within my thoughts.
It was a game-changer.

You are ready to teach.
